webcpp::document brings JavaScript programmers the wonders of C++ without the risks of C++. It is a header-only JSON document for C++20, one of the libraries of webcpp, whose behaviour is JavaScript’s: what JSON.parse, property access, assignment, delete, the array methods and JSON.stringify do in JavaScript, document does in C++, with the same key order and the same text out, so that a JavaScript peer and a C++ program agree byte for byte.

Its tree lives in one relocatable image, built through an allocator, so that a document can live in a memory segment, be made durable, be shared between threads and processes, and travel as binary and be opened where it lands, with no parse. It reads and writes JSON and NDJSON streams, keeps numbers exact, seals images with a CRC, and answers queries over ordered keys, from C++ and from JavaScript. Its core never throws: every operation that can fail returns its error as a value.

This page teaches document concept by concept, from JavaScript’s side: what each part does, its smallest example, its variations and its rules. Every C++ program it shows was compiled and run, natively and, where the program does not need Boost.Asio, Boost.Cobalt, threads, shared memory or xactor, on emscripten and for wasm32-wasip2 and wasm32-wasip3 too (Testing), and printed the output shown under it, which is what Node prints for the same JavaScript wherever the page does not say otherwise. The listings of the JavaScript module are copied from the tests that run it. The reference that closes it lists every name the headers declare.

Introduction

webcpp::document brings JavaScript programmers the wonders of C++ without the risks of C++.

The wonders are what JavaScript does not give:

  • JSON and NDJSON streams, read as the bytes arrive, in chunks of any size (Streams of documents).

  • Exact numbers: a number is stored as the decimal that was written, and getDecimal reads it back in full (Numbers).

  • Images sealed by a CRC, so that a byte changed by accident is refused when an image is opened (Sealed images).

  • Memory you manage: one relocatable image, reserve and capacity, shrink_to_fit and compact, pools of blocks, and no garbage collector in the way (Images).

  • Shared documents, counted by reference and copied on write, between threads and between processes (Sharing).

  • Binary transmission: an image is sent as it is and opened in place, with no parse and no allocation on receipt (Images on the wire).

  • Ordered-index queries: lower bounds, equal ranges and prefix queries over an object’s keys, with no sorting (Keys in order).

The risks are the ones of C++: a pointer that dangles, a buffer that overflows, behaviour that is undefined. document leaves them out. A handle never fails, a write completes or changes nothing, the core never throws, and a full buffer is an error value: a failure is a value the program tests, and not a crash (Handles).

Where it wins outright is binary transmission, where moving an image costs nothing or a memory copy: between a page and its Worker, between the threads of a process, through shared memory between processes, and from a socket into a pool block on a machine or a fast local link whose receiver’s CPU is the bottleneck (What C++ gives JavaScript). It is honest about where it loses. It parses more slowly than Boost.JSON. An image is many times larger than its JSON text, so over a network the JSON text, compressed, is the smaller payload. And a seal is a CRC against accidental damage, not authentication: never open an image from a source you do not trust (Where document does not win).

The JavaScript programmer also keeps JavaScript’s ways with JSON. A web application speaks JSON with JavaScript, and JavaScript decides what that JSON means: the order in which an object’s keys come out, what JSON.stringify writes for a number, what splice removes. A C++ program that is to agree with a JavaScript peer byte for byte needs a JSON document that makes the same decisions. document is that document: what JSON.parse, property access, assignment, delete, the array methods and JSON.stringify do in JavaScript, it does in C++, with the same key order and the same text out. Its module for JavaScript is taught in Using it from JavaScript.

Why not Boost.JSON

Boost.JSON is the JSON library of Boost, and document reads JSON with its parser. Its document, boost::json::value, is another matter, for the closer compatibility with JavaScript that document was written for. Measured on Boost 1.92:

  • Key order. boost::json::object keeps keys in the order they were inserted. JavaScript puts the keys that are array indices first, ascending, then the others in the order they were created: JSON.parse('{"b":1,"2":2,"a":3,"1":4}') holds {"1":4,"2":2,"b":1,"a":3} (Key order).

  • Erasing reorders. object::erase moves the last member into the erased one’s place: erasing a from {"a":1,"b":2,"c":3,"d":4} leaves {"d":4,"b":2,"c":3}, where JavaScript’s delete leaves {"b":2,"c":3,"d":4}.

  • Numbers are doubles. 0.1000000000000000000000000000000001 is read into a double and written back as 1E-1. JavaScript rounds it too, to 0.1; document keeps it exact by default, and writes every number as JavaScript writes it (Numbers).

  • Hash flooding. An object’s index hashes its keys, so a crafted input of 4 MB, keys that collide, took 9.23 s to parse. Keys come from the network; document indexes them in ordered trees, which no input degrades.

  • Pointers. A boost::json::value holds pointers, so it can neither live in a memory segment shared between processes nor travel as binary. document’s tree lives in one relocatable image, every pointer in it an offset (Images).

document uses Boost.JSON’s SAX parser, boost::json::basic_parser, and nothing else of it. Compared with Boost.JSON puts the two side by side, program by program, and says what Boost.JSON does better.

A first document

This program parses a JSON text, reads two members, writes one, pushes an element onto an array, and writes the document back with an indent of 2. It begins with the library’s header and an alias for its namespace:

#include <webcpp/document.hpp>

#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <string_view>

namespace wd = webcpp::document;

wd::parse is JSON.parse. Its result holds the document, or the error that made none: the core of document never throws, and every operation that can fail returns wd::result, Boost.System’s result:

// JSON.parse, whose result holds the document or the error.
wd::result<wd::document> made =
    wd::parse(R"({"name":"Ada","born":1815,"langs":["Analytical"]})");
if (made.has_error()) {
    std::cout << "error: " << made.error().message() << '\n';
    return 1;
}
wd::document& doc = *made;

doc["name"] is a handle, the place doc.name names. value_or is JavaScript’s ??: the value as the type of the fallback, or the fallback when nothing is there, or when what is there is not of that type:

// doc.name ?? "nobody", and doc.born ?? 0.
std::cout << doc["name"].value_or(std::string_view("nobody")) << " was born in "
          << doc["born"].value_or(std::int64_t{0}) << '\n';

set is assignment, and push is Array.prototype.push. Each returns its result, which converts to true on success; a write that fails changes nothing:

// doc.known = true; doc.langs.push("Note G"); each write returns its result.
if (!doc["known"].set(true) || !doc["langs"].push("Note G")) {
    std::cout << "error: the document is full\n";
    return 1;
}

stringify(2) is JSON.stringify(doc, null, 2):

// JSON.stringify(doc, null, 2).
std::cout << doc.stringify(2) << '\n';

It prints:

Ada was born in 1815
{
  "name": "Ada",
  "born": 1815,
  "langs": [
    "Analytical",
    "Note G"
  ],
  "known": true
}

The new member known comes last, as JavaScript adds it, and the text is byte for byte what Node writes for the same operations.

Requirements

  • A C++20 compiler. document’s tests and examples are built and run natively with Clang and GCC, on emscripten under node, and for wasm32-wasip2 and wasm32-wasip3 with the Clang of wasi-sdk, under wasmtime (Testing).

  • Boost 1.92 or newer: Interprocess for the image’s heap and its offsets, MultiIndex for the tree’s indices, Decimal for exact numbers, System for result and the error codes, Charconv for reading and writing doubles, and JSON for its parser. document is header-only; of Boost, only JSON’s parser and Charconv are compiled, once, by webcpp’s build. A b2 project uses document through /webcpp/document//document, which brings all of them.

  • webcpp’s configuration, config, whose <webcpp/config.hpp> every header of document includes first.

  • Exceptions are the program’s choice. The core never throws, in a build with exceptions or without; the sugar that throws as JavaScript does exists only with them (The sugar that throws).

  • Optional: Boost.Asio, for the readers and writers of streams and images, and Boost.Cobalt for its coroutines, in <webcpp/document/asio.hpp>, which builds natively only (With Boost.Asio); xactor for the actor example (In an actor system); Emscripten, for the JavaScript module (Using it from JavaScript).

  • Nothing else: no threads, no clock, no file, no global or static mutable state.

Reading this page

<webcpp/document.hpp> includes every public header, whose names are in the namespace webcpp::document. The code of this page writes them wd::parse and wd::document, as after namespace wd = webcpp::document;.

What C++ gives JavaScript lists what C++ gives JavaScript, and Using it from JavaScript teaches the module that brings it to a page, a Worker and Node. Traits chooses what a document stores; Images shows the binary image, Images on the wire sends it, and Sharing shares it. Compared with Boost.JSON compares document with Boost.JSON, The sugar that throws teaches the sugar that throws, and Errors lists every error. Testing shows how document is tested, Benchmarks what it costs, and the reference closes the page.

What C++ gives JavaScript

webcpp::document brings JavaScript programmers the wonders of C++ without the risks of C++. A JavaScript programmer who reaches for C++ gets control over memory, exact arithmetic, shared memory and bytes that move without a parse, and pays for them with pointers that dangle, buffers that overflow and behaviour that is undefined. document keeps the first and refuses the second: a handle never fails, a write completes or changes nothing, the core never throws, and a full buffer is an error value (Handles).

This section lists what document gives that JavaScript does not, each with the smallest program that shows it and a link to the section that teaches it. The programs are C++; the same document is reached from JavaScript by the module of Using it from JavaScript, which gives a page or a Worker the points that need no C++ to write. Binary transmission comes first, because it is where document wins outright, and the last subsection says where it does not.

Binary transmission

A document is its own wire format. doc.image() is its bytes, and a receiver opens them where they landed: wd::open(buffer), or Document.open(bytes) in JavaScript, reads a header of 64 bytes and, for a sealed image, a CRC, and the document is there. Nothing is parsed and no tree is built, and the receiver allocates nothing per value and nothing per message. A JSON text must be parsed on arrival, and a parse allocates for every value it holds.

That is where document wins outright, in the places where moving the image costs nothing or a memory copy:

  • A page and its Worker. The image crosses as a transferred ArrayBuffer, which moves in constant time, where postMessage of an object makes a structured clone of every node (An image sent to a Worker).

  • Threads of one process. A document moves through a queue as a small handle, and its image stays where it is (Threads).

  • Processes of one machine. A pool of blocks in shared memory, and the offset of a block sent through a queue (Processes).

  • A socket, on one machine or a fast local link. A reader fills a block of a pool straight from the stream and opens the image there, so the receiver’s CPU, which is the bottleneck on such a link, spends none of its time parsing (Images on the wire).

This program copies an image into a buffer of the program’s own and opens it there, with no parse; Boost.JSON, for which a value points into its memory resource, can only be serialized and parsed again:

constexpr std::string_view text = R"({"user":"Ada","langs":["Analytical","Note G"]})";
wd::result<wd::document> made = wd::parse(text);
if (made.has_error()) {
    return false;
}
const std::span<const std::byte> image = made->image();
// A buffer of the program's, 16-aligned, large enough for the image.
alignas(16) std::array<std::byte, 8192> buffer{};
if (image.size() > buffer.size()) {
    return false;
}
std::ranges::copy(image, buffer.begin());
// Opened in place: the buffer becomes the document, with no parse.
wd::result<wd::basic_document<wd::default_traits, wd::external>> opened =
    wd::open(std::span<std::byte>(buffer.data(), image.size()));
if (opened.has_error()) {
    return false;
}
std::cout << "5. An image copied to another buffer and opened in place\n";
print_document(opened->stringify());
// A Boost.JSON value points into its memory resource, so its bytes cannot be copied: the
// only way to move it is to serialize it and parse it again.
print_boost(boost_text(made->stringify()));
5. An image copied to another buffer and opened in place
  document:   {"user":"Ada","langs":["Analytical","Note G"]}
  Boost.JSON: {"user":"Ada","langs":["Analytical","Note G"]}

Over a network the text is the smaller payload. An image is several times the size of the JSON text it holds, since it keeps a node of 192 bytes for each value (Memory per value), and it is still larger once both are compressed (The sizes on the wire). On a link that carries the bytes, compressed JSON is smaller and arrives sooner, unless the receiver’s parse costs more than the extra bytes take to cross.

JSON and NDJSON streams

JavaScript reads one JSON text with JSON.parse, and reads a stream by cutting it into texts first. wd::stream_parser takes the bytes of a stream as they arrive, in chunks of any size, split anywhere, and delivers each document as soon as the bytes that end it are in: NDJSON, JSON text sequences, and concatenated JSON with or without whitespace between the documents (Streams of documents). A bad line can be dropped, with its line number reported, and the stream goes on (Errors). Reading NDJSON by hand takes a loop over next():

/**
 NDJSON: each document ends at its line's newline, so a line may end in CRLF, a line may be empty,
 and the last line may lack its newline, which finish closes.
*/
bool read_ndjson() {
    std::cout << "NDJSON, taken with next():\n";
    wd::stream_options options;
    options.framing = wd::framing::lines;
    wd::stream_parser p(options);
    constexpr std::string_view text =
        "{\"id\":1,\"tags\":[\"a\",\"b\"]}\n"
        "{\"id\":2,\"note\":\"first\\nsecond\"}\r\n"
        "\n"
        "[3,4.5]\n"
        "null";
    if (!write_in_pieces(p, text, options.on_error)) {
        return false;
    }
    if (const wd::result<std::size_t> finished = p.finish(); finished.has_error()) {
        report_error(p, finished.error());
        return false;
    }
    take_ready(p, options.on_error);
    return true;
}
NDJSON, taken with next():
{"id":1,"tags":["a","b"]}
{"id":2,"note":"first\nsecond"}
[3,4.5]
null

The same parser reads from Boost.Asio, Boost.Cobalt and an actor system, and a JavaScript sender can feed it chunk by chunk (With Boost.Asio, Streams).

Exact numbers

A JavaScript number is a double, and 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004. document stores a number as the decimal that was written, in a decimal128, writes it as JavaScript writes a number, and leaves the arithmetic to the program: in the traits’ own number type it is exact, and get<T>() refuses to round. js_traits stores doubles, to read a number as JavaScript would (Numbers):

// 0.1 + 0.2, computed by the program in the traits' own number type, then stored.
wd::result<wd::document> exact = wd::parse(R"({"a":0.1,"b":0.2})");
wd::result<wd::basic_document<wd::js_traits>> js =
    wd::parse<wd::js_traits>(R"({"a":0.1,"b":0.2})");
if (exact.has_error() || js.has_error()) {
    return 1;
}
using decimal = boost::decimal::decimal128_t;
const wd::result<decimal> a = (*exact)["a"].get<decimal>();
const wd::result<decimal> b = (*exact)["b"].get<decimal>();
const wd::result<double> x = (*js)["a"].get<double>();
const wd::result<double> y = (*js)["b"].get<double>();
if (!a || !b || !x || !y || !(*exact)["sum"].set(*a + *b) || !(*js)["sum"].set(*x + *y)) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << exact->stringify() << '\n' << js->stringify() << '\n';
{"a":0.1,"b":0.2,"sum":0.3}
{"a":0.1,"b":0.2,"sum":0.30000000000000004}

A JavaScript peer reads the exact digits of a number back with getDecimal, where get gives the Number that rounds them (Exact numbers).

Sealed images

An image is a function of the operations that made it, the same bytes on every target. seal() writes the CRC-32C of those bytes into its header, and opening checks it, so a bit flipped on a disk or a wire, a torn write or a stray write is refused as errc::damaged_document before any of the image is read (Sealed images):

// A sealed image with one byte changed is refused as damaged, by open and by from_image.
const auto found =
    std::ranges::search(bytes, std::as_bytes(std::span(std::string_view("Ada"))));
if (found.empty()) {
    return false;
}
found.front() = std::byte{'a'};
if (!refused("one byte changed", wd::open(bytes))) {
    return false;
}
one byte changed: damaged_document, a sealed image whose bytes do not match its seal

A seal is a CRC against accidental damage and is not authentication: anyone can compute a valid seal for any bytes. Never open an image from a source you do not trust; data from an untrusted source enters as JSON text, which the parser checks entirely (What is refused).

Memory you manage

A document lives in one block of memory, a single relocatable image, and there is no garbage collector in the way: the program decides when the memory grows, when it shrinks and when it goes. reserve grows the image once for a batch (the way std::vector::reserve does) and capacity says how large it is; shrink_to_fit gives back the free space at its end, and compact rewrites the image without the holes that deleted values leave (Compacting); free() in JavaScript releases a document at once, where the collector would. A pool of blocks, allocated once, leases a block to each image that arrives and takes it back, zeroed, when the document goes (Images on the wire):

wd::result<wd::document> made = wd::parse("{}");
if (made.has_error()) {
    return false;
}
for (std::uint64_t i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) {
    if (!(*made)[std::to_string(i)].set(std::string(100, 'x'))) {
        return false;
    }
}
const std::uint64_t grown = made->image().size();
if (!made->root().set(wd::object{{"kept", true}}) || !made->shrink_to_fit()) {
    return false;
}
std::cout << "grown to " << grown << " bytes, shrunk to " << made->image().size() << ": "
          << made->stringify() << '\n';

// Blocks never move: a deep copy into a new document packs the content.
wd::result<wd::document> packed = wd::document::create();
if (packed.has_error() || !packed->root().set(*made)) {
    return false;
}
std::cout << "packed: " << packed->image().size() << " bytes\n";
grown to 524288 bytes, shrunk to 352864: {"kept":true}
packed: 4096 bytes
/** A pool of two blocks: the most the client leases at once. */
wd::image_pool pool_of_two() {
    return wd::image_pool::create(block_bytes, 2).value();
}

Shared documents with copy on write

wd::shared_document is std::shared_ptr for a document: copies share one image, a count in the block’s header says how many hold it, and the last one gives the block back. A holder that wants to write calls make_mutable, which copies the image into a block of its own when others hold it, so the others keep the document as it was. The count lives in the pool, so it is the same in every thread and every process that maps it (Sharing):

// make_mutable copies the image into a block of the writer's own when other holders exist, so the
// writer changes its copy and the others keep the document as it was. The library does not
// synchronise writers: a block with several writers, or a writer and readers of that same block,
// must wait for each other by the program's own means, such as a mutex. This writer changes only
// its copy, which no other holder reads.
void writer_task(wd::shared_document<> holder, std::string& out) {
    if (holder.make_mutable().has_error() || holder["name"].set("Lovelace").has_error()) {
        out = "error";
        return;
    }
    out = describe(holder);
}
writer: Lovelace was born in 1815
after the writer: Ada was born in 1815, use_count 1, 6 of 7 blocks free
last copy dropped: 7 of 7 blocks free

Ordered-index queries

An object is kept in two orders at once: JavaScript’s, which iteration follows, and key order, which by_key() gives with lower_bound, upper_bound and equal_range. A prefix query is two bounds, and nothing is sorted: a JavaScript program sorts every key to get the same answer, and gets it again at each query (Keys in order):

// by_key is the same object in key order, by UTF-16 code units, with bounds for ranges of keys.
// A JavaScript program sorts every key to get any of these; here the tree keeps them sorted.
wd::result<wd::document> catalog_made = wd::parse("{}");
if (catalog_made.has_error()) {
    return fail(catalog_made);
}
wd::document& catalog = *catalog_made;
wd::result<wd::object_ref> as_catalog = catalog.root().as_object();
if (as_catalog.has_error()) {
    return fail(as_catalog);
}
const wd::object_ref catalog_obj = *as_catalog;
const std::array<std::string_view, 13> names{
    "user_3", "admin",  "user_1", "guest",  "user_9", "user",   "user_2",
    "owner",  "user_7", "user_5", "user_4", "user_8", "user_6",
};
for (const std::string_view key : names) {
    const auto added = catalog_obj.insert(key, true);
    if (added.has_error()) {
        return fail(added);
    }
}
std::cout << "JavaScript order:";
for (const auto& member : catalog_obj) {
    std::cout << ' ' << member.first;
}
std::cout << '\n';
const auto keys = catalog_obj.by_key();
std::cout << "by_key order:";
for (const auto& member : keys) {
    std::cout << ' ' << member.first;
}
std::cout << '\n';

// The keys with the prefix "user_" lie from its first key up to the first key at or after
// "user`", the character after '_'.
const std::ranges::subrange users(keys.lower_bound("user_"), keys.lower_bound("user`"));
std::cout << "prefix user_: " << std::ranges::distance(users) << " keys, from "
          << users.begin()->first << " to " << std::ranges::prev(users.end())->first << '\n';

const auto [exact, exact_end] = keys.equal_range("user_5");
std::cout << "equal_range user_5: " << std::ranges::distance(exact, exact_end) << " member, "
          << exact->first << '\n';

std::cout << "lower_bound p: " << keys.lower_bound("p")->first << '\n';
const std::ranges::subrange between(keys.lower_bound("g"), keys.lower_bound("v"));
std::cout << "keys from g up to v: " << std::ranges::distance(between) << '\n';
JavaScript order: user_3 admin user_1 guest user_9 user user_2 owner user_7 user_5 user_4 user_8 user_6
by_key order: admin guest owner user user_1 user_2 user_3 user_4 user_5 user_6 user_7 user_8 user_9
prefix user_: 9 keys, from user_1 to user_9
equal_range user_5: 1 member, user_5
lower_bound p: user
keys from g up to v: 12

Where document does not win

document is a different trade from Boost.JSON and from JavaScript’s own objects, and some of it is a loss:

  • Parsing is slower than Boost.JSON’s and than JSON.parse. Every value is a node of a tree of indices inside the image, which the parse must build; Boost.JSON appends to contiguous arrays. The benchmarks measure it, natively, in Node and in Chrome (Reading the results).

  • An image is larger than its JSON text, many times larger, and still larger when both are compressed. On a narrow network, compressed JSON is the smaller payload and the better choice (The sizes on the wire).

  • A seal is not authentication. It is a CRC against accidental damage. An image is trusted input, and an image from a source that is not trusted must never be opened (What is refused).

  • A lookup walks a tree where JavaScript and Boost.JSON hash, and an array splice renumbers the positions after it (Reading the results).

What document asks for in return is what the other sections teach: a document that behaves as JavaScript does, that moves as bytes, that lives in memory its program manages, and that cannot make the program crash.

Using it from JavaScript

document is also a JavaScript module. js/webcpp-document.mjs is an ES module that wraps the library, compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten, in two classes, Document and StreamParser, and runs in Node, in a page and in a Worker. A JavaScript program keeps JavaScript’s values and JavaScript’s errors, and gets what JavaScript lacks: exact numbers, queries over ordered keys, a binary image it can send to a Worker with no parse, and memory it frees when it chooses. This section teaches the module; the sections before it teach the C++ library behind it.

The listings of this section are literal, and are not compiled by this page: each is copied from a test or from the example of libs/document/js, where Node’s test runner runs the tests and a headless Chromium runs the example, so that what they show is checked. The files are named above each listing.

The package is built, and its tests run, with b2 and Emscripten’s toolset; the module is the webcpp-document-core program, an ES module, which webcpp-document.mjs imports and awaits when it loads:

b2 toolset=emscripten libs/document/js//package
b2 toolset=emscripten libs/document/test/js//js-tests

The tests are the own lane js of the library (libs/document/test/js), which runs on Emscripten’s toolset: js-tests and shared-tests run Node’s test runner on the packages, npm-package-test tests the npm package as a user receives it, and js-chrome and shared-chrome run the examples in headless Chromium.

Documents

A Document is made by Document.parse(text), which is JSON.parse and throws the SyntaxError that JSON.parse throws, or by Document.open(bytes) (Images). A place in the document is a path: an array of string keys and non-negative integer indices from the root, [] being the root itself. A path that leads to nothing reads undefined, as property access does. get, set, erase, push, splice, length and stringify do what their names do in JavaScript:

Copied from js/test/api.test.mjs
const doc = Document.parse('{"user":{"name":"Ada","age":36,"langs":["C"]},"n":null,"t":false}')
assert.equal(doc.get(['user', 'name']), 'Ada')
assert.equal(doc.get(['user', 'age']), 36)
assert.deepEqual(doc.get(['user', 'langs']), ['C'])
assert.equal(doc.get(['n']), null)
assert.equal(doc.get(['missing', 'deeper']), undefined)
assert.equal(doc.get(['user', 'langs', 0]), 'C')
doc.free()

get returns a scalar as its JavaScript value and a container as a copy, and toJSON() is get([]), so JSON.stringify(doc) works on a document. set writes what JSON.stringify writes for its value, so undefined erases a member, and -0 is 0. erase says whether the key was there:

Copied from js/test/api.test.mjs
const doc = Document.parse('{"user":{"name":"Ada"},"langs":[]}')
doc.set(['user', 'age'], 30)
doc.set(['user', 'tags'], { a: [1, 'two', null] })
doc.set(['pi'], 3.14159)
doc.set(['zero'], -0)
assert.equal(doc.get(['user', 'age']), 30)
doc.set([], [true])
assert.equal(doc.stringify(), '[true]')
doc.free()

push returns the new length, as Array.prototype.push does, and splice takes the arguments of Array.prototype.splice, negative positions and clamped counts included, and returns the elements it removed:

Copied from js/test/api.test.mjs
const doc = Document.parse('{"langs":["C","Rust","Go"]}')
assert.equal(doc.push(['langs'], 'Note G'), 4)
assert.equal(doc.length(['langs']), 4)
assert.deepEqual(doc.splice(['langs'], 0, 1), ['C'])
assert.deepEqual(doc.splice(['langs'], -1, 1, 'JS', 'Lisp'), ['Note G'])
assert.equal(doc.stringify(), JSON.stringify({ langs: ['Rust', 'Go', 'JS', 'Lisp'] }))
doc.free()

stringify(indent) is JSON.stringify(doc, null, indent), with the same bytes, and the key order is JavaScript’s (Key order).

Errors

An operation that fails throws the error JavaScript would throw for it: SyntaxError for malformed text, RangeError for a number out of range or for no room left in a buffer, and TypeError for a value of another kind, a write through something that is not a container, a value that is not JSON (a function, a symbol, a BigInt), a path that is not an array of keys and indices, bytes that are not an image, a sealed image that is damaged, and a document that was freed. These are the errc values of Errors, each under the name JavaScript gives it. An operation that throws changes nothing:

Copied from js/test/api.test.mjs
const doc = Document.parse('{"obj":{"a":1},"arr":[1,2],"num":5,"str":"s"}')
assert.throws(() => doc.set(['missing', 'x'], 1), TypeError)
assert.throws(() => doc.push(['obj'], 1), TypeError)
assert.throws(() => doc.erase(['arr', 0]), TypeError)
assert.throws(() => doc.splice(['num'], 0, 1), TypeError)
assert.throws(() => doc.set(['f'], () => 1), TypeError)
assert.throws(() => doc.get(['arr', 1.5]), TypeError)
doc.free()

Exact numbers

get gives the Number of a JSON number, which rounds a number that a double cannot hold. getDecimal gives the number exactly, as the text of its decimal, so a price or an identifier of thirty digits survives a round trip through a JavaScript program (Numbers):

Copied from js/test/api.test.mjs
const text = '0.1234567890123456789012345678901234'
const doc = Document.parse(`{"price":${text},"small":1.50}`)
assert.equal(doc.getDecimal(['price']), text)
assert.equal(doc.get(['price']), Number(text))
assert.equal(doc.getDecimal(['small']), '1.5')
assert.equal(doc.get(['small']), 1.5)
doc.free()

Ordered keys

The keys of an object are also kept in key order, so a range of keys is found without sorting them. keysInRange(path, low, high) gives the keys from low up to, and not including, high; a prefix query is the range from the prefix to the prefix followed by ￿ (Keys in order):

Copied from js/test/api.test.mjs
const doc = Document.parse('{"users":{"user_2":{},"user_10":{},"admin":{},"user_1":{},' +
    '"user_":{},"user`":{}}}')
assert.deepEqual(doc.keysInRange(['users'], 'user_', 'user_￿'),
    ['user_', 'user_1', 'user_10', 'user_2'])
assert.deepEqual(doc.keysInRange(['users'], 'x', 'y'), [])
doc.free()

Images

A document is its image, and the module hands the image to the program. doc.byteLength is its size, and doc.image() is a Uint8Array that views the bytes where they are in WebAssembly memory, with no copy: it stays valid until the memory grows or the document changes, so a program that keeps the bytes copies them with slice(). Document.open(bytes) makes a document of an image. When the bytes are a view of WebAssembly memory, 16-aligned, such as another document’s image(), it opens them in place and shares them; otherwise it copies them into the module’s memory first, which is a memory copy and no parse. A document opened from bytes is its own, and the bytes it was opened from may change or go. seal() writes the CRC of the image into it, which open checks, and refuses a sealed image whose bytes changed with a TypeError (Sealed images):

Copied from js/test/api.test.mjs
const doc = Document.parse('{"a":[1,2,3]}')
assert.equal(doc.byteLength, doc.image().byteLength)
assert.equal(doc.seal(), undefined)
const image = doc.image().slice()
assert.equal(Document.open(image).stringify(), '{"a":[1,2,3]}')
image[image.length - 1] ^= 0xff
assert.throws(() => Document.open(image), TypeError)
doc.free()

An image is trusted input. open refuses bytes that are not an image, and a seal catches bytes that changed by accident; it does not authenticate them, and an image from a source that is not trusted must never be opened (What is refused).

Memory

A document lives in WebAssembly memory, outside the heap that JavaScript’s collector manages, in one relocatable image. Memory is therefore a thing the program holds, not a thing the collector finds:

  • doc.free() releases the image at once, and a second free() does nothing. A freed document refuses every operation with a TypeError. A program that makes many documents, such as one per message of a stream, frees each when it is done.

  • A document that is never freed is released when the collector collects its object, through a FinalizationRegistry, which runs when the engine chooses and not when the program needs the memory. It is a safety net and not a plan.

  • The module’s memory grows on demand, up to 4 GB, and WebAssembly never returns memory to the system; a freed image returns to the module’s allocator, for the next document to use.

  • image() is a view of that memory and byteLength its size, so a program knows what a document costs, and a document that is to travel as bytes is already the bytes.

A parsed document starts at 4096 bytes and grows as it needs. doc.capacity is the number of bytes its image can hold before a change must move it, and doc.reserve(bytes) makes the image hold at least that many, so a program that knows how large a document will grow pays for the room once (Reserving). A size that is not a non-negative integer, or that is past the document’s limit, is a RangeError, and nothing changes. shrink_to_fit and compact of the C++ library, which pack an image, are not in the module.

Copied from js/test/api.test.mjs
const doc = Document.parse('{"a":1}')
const before = doc.capacity
assert.ok(before >= doc.byteLength)
assert.equal(doc.reserve(before * 4), undefined)
assert.ok(doc.capacity >= before * 4)
assert.equal(doc.stringify(), '{"a":1}')
doc.free()

An image sent to a Worker

A page parses a document, copies its image into an ArrayBuffer of its own and transfers the buffer to a Worker. The transfer moves the buffer in constant time and detaches it from the sender, where postMessage of an object would clone every value of it. The copy is made first because a view of WebAssembly memory cannot be transferred. The Worker opens the image in its own memory, which is one memory copy, and reads from it: nothing is parsed there. The page is js/example/page.mjs:

Copied from js/example/page.mjs
const doc = Document.parse(text)
doc.set(['user', 'age'], 36)
const bytes = doc.image().slice()
doc.free()

worker.postMessage({ image: bytes.buffer }, [bytes.buffer])

and the Worker, js/example/worker.mjs, which answers with what the document holds:

Copied from js/example/worker.mjs
self.onmessage = ({ data }) => {
    const doc = Document.open(new Uint8Array(data.image))
    self.postMessage({
        name: doc.get(['user', 'name']),
        age: doc.get(['user', 'age']),
        langs: doc.get(['user', 'langs']),
        price: doc.getDecimal(['price']),
        text: doc.stringify(),
    })
    doc.free()
}

A headless Chromium runs the example and fails unless the Worker answered what the document holds and the transfer detached the buffer. How the transfer compares with postMessage of an object is measured in Benchmarks.

Documents shared between workers

The transfer above gives each Worker a copy of the image, and one Worker’s copy is its own. A second build of the module, js/shared/webcpp-document-shared.mjs, shares documents instead: its WebAssembly memory is one SharedArrayBuffer, and every Worker the program creates can join it. Several Workers then read the same document at once, in place: nothing is transferred and nothing is copied, and the image a Worker reads is at the address, in that memory, where the page parsed it. It is the shared_document of Sharing, taught from JavaScript.

Every document of this module is in the memory’s pool, whose blocks are the room of an image, and a Document is one reference to a document, as a std::shared_ptr is: useCount counts the references of every Worker, and the last one given up, by free() or by the collector, gives the block back. A write is every holder’s, since they read the same bytes. makeMutable() first makes the document the writer’s own: a copy in a block of its own when others hold it, the same block when none does, while the others go on reading the original (Copy on write).

The page starts the module when it imports the file, and hands a Worker two things in a message: connection(), which the Worker joins, and a token for the document. The Worker awaits join(connection), which runs the module on the shared memory in that Worker, and then adopts the token. The page, js/shared/example/page.mjs, parses a document and gives its token to four Workers:

Copied from js/shared/example/page.mjs
const free = pool.available
const doc = Document.parse('{"user":{"name":"Ada","langs":["C","Note G"]},"price":1.50}')
const address = doc.image().byteOffset
say(`page: parsed into one block of the pool, use count ${doc.useCount}`)

const workers = Array.from({ length: 4 }, start)
const adopted = await Promise.all(workers.map(worker =>
    worker.send({ command: 'adopt', connection: connection(), token: doc.share() })))

and a Worker, js/shared/example/reader.mjs, joins, adopts, and writes on a copy of its own:

Copied from js/shared/example/reader.mjs
const commands = {
    async adopt({ connection, token }) {
        await join(connection)
        doc = SharedDocument.adopt(token)
        return describe()
    },
    // The document made this worker's own, a copy in a block of its own, then changed.
    write({ name }) {
        doc.makeMutable()
        doc.set(['user', 'name'], name)
        return describe()
    },
    free() {
        doc.free()
        return {}
    },
}

A Worker that is done calls leave(): it drops every reference it holds, gives its slot back and may join again. A Worker that calls free() on a document drops that reference alone.

A token is what share() returns: a small object, { offset, ticket, generation }, that postMessage clones, and that keeps one reference to the document until a thread adopts it. SharedDocument.adopt(token) takes the reference over, once; SharedDocument.drop(token) gives it back without adopting it, as a receiver does that does not want the document. A token that was adopted or dropped is spent, and adopt and drop refuse it with a TypeError, even when its block holds another document by then, as does anything that is not a token:

Copied from js/shared/test/sharing.test.mjs
const doc = Document.parse(text)
const token = doc.share()
SharedDocument.drop(token)
assert.equal(doc.useCount, 1)
assert.throws(() => SharedDocument.adopt(token), TypeError)
assert.throws(() => SharedDocument.drop(token), TypeError)

A headless Chromium runs the example, and fails unless the page prints these lines, in which the four Workers read the page’s own address and the one that wrote does not:

Copied from js/shared/example/shared-workers.expected
cross-origin isolated: true
page: parsed into one block of the pool, use count 1
worker 1: reads Ada and C, Note G, at the page's address: true, in a SharedArrayBuffer: true
worker 2: reads Ada and C, Note G, at the page's address: true, in a SharedArrayBuffer: true
worker 3: reads Ada and C, Note G, at the page's address: true, in a SharedArrayBuffer: true
worker 4: reads Ada and C, Note G, at the page's address: true, in a SharedArrayBuffer: true
page: use count 5, blocks in use 1
worker 4: makeMutable, then set: reads Grace, at the page's address: false
page: reads Ada, use count 4, blocks in use 2
page: every worker freed its reference, use count 1
page: freed, every block back in the pool: true

A SharedArrayBuffer exists only in a page that is cross-origin isolated, which the server asks of the browser with two headers on the page and on every file it loads: Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp. Without them the module does not start. Node needs neither.

The memory is laid out once, by the thread that starts the module, and has limits:

  • The memory is fixed at 128 MiB and does not grow, as growing a shared memory would make every Worker refresh its views of it. A full heap is an error, a RangeError, and not an abort.

  • The pool has 64 blocks of 512 KiB. A document is one block, so an image can be no larger than the room of a block: a change past it is a RangeError, and so is makeMutable() or Document.parse when no block is free. pool.available, pool.blocks and pool.blockBytes tell what is left.

  • At most 32 Workers are joined at once; a thirty-third join is a RangeError until one leaves. At most 1024 tokens are in flight at once.

  • A Worker that is terminated without calling leave() keeps its references and its slot for the life of the memory: its documents are not given back. A Worker that is done calls leave() first.

  • join.js, the Emscripten library that lets a Worker the program creates run the module, reads internals of Emscripten 6.0.11 (createWasm, wasmMemory, updateMemoryViews), so the module is tied to that version of Emscripten until it is checked against another.

Streams

StreamParser is the stream parser of Streams of documents, with the same framings, concatenated (the default), lines for NDJSON and rfc7464, and the same policy on errors, onError stop or skip, the latter for the framings that can go on. StreamParser.from(source, options) is an async generator that takes a ReadableStream of bytes or strings, such as a response body, or any async iterable of them, and yields a Document as soon as the bytes that end it arrive, whatever the chunks:

Copied from js/test/stream.test.mjs
for await (const doc of StreamParser.from(chunked(encoder.encode(lines), size), { framing: 'lines' })) {
    assert.ok(doc instanceof Document)
    out.push(doc.toJSON())
}

A bad line throws a SyntaxError once the documents before it are yielded, and under onError skip it is dropped and counted in parser.dropped. The end of the source ends the stream, as finish() does, so a top-level number or a last line without its newline is delivered (Errors).

The parser can also be driven by hand, which is how a sender written in JavaScript feeds the parser compiled from C++: write takes a chunk, read gives the next complete document or undefined, and finish ends the stream:

Copied from js/test/stream.test.mjs
const parser = new StreamParser({ framing: 'lines' })
parser.write(encoder.encode('{"a":'))
assert.equal(parser.read(), undefined)
parser.write(encoder.encode('1}\n'))
assert.deepEqual(parser.read().toJSON(), { a: 1 })
assert.equal(parser.read(), undefined)
parser.finish()

Each document read or from gives is a Document, in WebAssembly memory like any other, which the program frees when it has used it.

From JavaScript

document’s interface is JavaScript’s ways with JSON, written in C++: a name of JavaScript becomes a member function of the same meaning, and an operation that JavaScript makes throw returns its error instead. A program that knows how JavaScript reads and writes a parsed object knows how document does. This section is for the C++ programmer who knows JavaScript; the JavaScript programmer who wants document in a page, a Worker or Node reads Using it from JavaScript, and what C++ gives that JavaScript does not is in What C++ gives JavaScript.

JavaScript, then C++

Each row is a JavaScript expression and what a program of document writes for it, v being a handle (Handles) and doc a document:

JavaScript document

JSON.parse(text)

wd::parse(text), which returns a result; wd::parse_or_throw(text) throws, with exceptions only (Parsing)

JSON.stringify(v, null, 2)

v.stringify(2), wd::stringify(doc, 2), and wd::stringify_to(doc, sink, 2) in pieces (Writing JSON)

v.key, v["key"], v[3]

v["key"], v[3]: a handle, which never fails

v.at(-1)

v.at(-1)

typeof v, Array.isArray(v), v === null

v.kind(), v.is_array(), v.is_null(), and an is_ function for every kind

v === undefined

v.is_undefined()

v ?? fallback

v.value_or(fallback)

"key" in v

v.contains("key")

v.length, of an array or a string

v.length(), in UTF-16 code units for a string

Object.keys(v).length

v.size()

Number.isInteger(v)

v.is_integer()

v.key = x

v["key"].set(x); v["key"] = x throws, with exceptions only (The sugar that throws)

delete v.key

v.erase("key"), or v["key"].set(wd::undefined)

Object.assign(v, source)

v.assign_from(source)

Object.entries(v), Object.keys(v), Object.values(v)

v.entries(), v.keys(), v.values()

for (const x of a)

for (wd::const_value x : a)

structuredClone(doc)

doc.clone()

a.push(x), a.splice(1, 2) and the other array methods

the same names (Arrays)

{key: 1}, [1, 2]

wd::object{{"key", 1}}, wd::array{1, 2}

The program below prints each JavaScript expression beside what document gives for it, with this helper, which writes undefined where nothing is there, as JavaScript prints it:

/** Prints a JavaScript expression and the value it reads, `undefined` when nothing is there. */
void show(std::string_view expression, const wd::const_value& v) {
    std::cout << expression << " -> " << (v.is_undefined() ? "undefined" : v.stringify()) << '\n';
}

Handles walks through the program; every line it prints is what Node prints for the same JavaScript.

Where document differs, on purpose

A few things JavaScript does would make a document either unsafe or unlike JSON. document does otherwise there, and each difference keeps the text JSON.stringify writes, but where the table says it does not:

JavaScript document Why

a.x = b.y makes both name one object

a["x"].set(b["y"]) copies the subtree, and so does h = other with exceptions

A document is a tree, as JSON is: no value is shared, and no cycle exists.

a.splice(0, 1, a) inserts the array into itself, a cycle

it inserts a copy of the array as it was

The same: a tree has no cycle.

o.x = undefined keeps the key x, which JSON.stringify omits

erases x

Nothing stores undefined. The text is the same; Object.keys would differ.

[undefined] holds undefined, written [null]

stores null

The same text.

arrays may have holes

null fills them, and pop or shift of what was a hole returns null, where JavaScript returns undefined

Arrays are dense (Arrays); the text is the same.

arr["0"] is element 0, and obj[3] the member "3"

arr["0"] names nothing, nor does obj[3]: a key reaches a member, an index an element

A handle names a member or an element, never both.

numbers are doubles

exact with the default traits; JavaScript’s doubles with js_traits

What is stored is what was sent (Numbers).

JSON.parse of 40 digits rounds, and of 1e999 gives Infinity

the default traits refuse 40 digits with errc::range, and store 1e999 exactly, which a JavaScript peer reads as Infinity; js_traits round 40 digits and make 1e999 Infinity, written null, as JavaScript does

The default traits keep what was sent; js_traits read it as JavaScript does (What each refuses).

-0

0

JSON.stringify(-0) writes 0 too.

JSON.parse('"\ud800"') keeps the lone surrogate

refused with errc::syntax, with either encoding; set keeps one with utf16

Boost.JSON’s parser, which document uses, cannot deliver one (Lone surrogates).

a Uint8Array is written {"0":1,"1":2}

bytes are written as base64 by default

The traits’ bytes policy; javascript_bytes restores JavaScript’s text (Strings, dates and bytes).

prototypes, getters, symbols, toJSON, a replacer, a reviver, Map, Set, BigInt

none

Out of scope: a document holds JSON’s values, and dates and bytes.

The program shows four of them: an index written as a key, a key written as an index, -0, and the lone surrogate the parser refuses:

wd::result<wd::document> made = wd::parse(R"({"list":[10,20],"o":{"3":"three"},"z":-0})");
if (made.has_error()) {
    return false;
}
wd::document& doc = *made;
show("doc.list['0']", doc["list"]["0"]);  // JavaScript: 10, an index written as a key
show("doc.o[3]", doc["o"][3]);            // JavaScript: "three", a key written as an index
show("doc.z", doc["z"]);                  // -0 is 0, as JSON.stringify writes it
say(R"(JSON.parse('"\ud800"') refused)", wd::parse(R"("\ud800")").error() == wd::errc::syntax);
doc.list['0'] -> undefined
doc.o[3] -> undefined
doc.z -> 0
JSON.parse('"\ud800"') refused -> true

JSON.parse gives 10, "three" and 0 for the first three, and keeps the lone surrogate.

Handles

A document holds one value, and a program reaches the values inside it through handles: wd::value, which reads and writes, and wd::const_value, which reads. doc.root(), doc["key"], doc[3] and every navigation from a handle return one. A handle names one place in one document, and is cheap to copy: it holds the document’s address and the ids of nodes, not a pointer into the tree.

Navigation never fails

In JavaScript, doc.user.nick is undefined when user has no nick, and doc.n.x.y throws a TypeError when doc.n is a number. A handle never fails: it names one of three things, and reads undefined where nothing is there.

A handle names Made by Reads, and set does

a node

navigation to a value that exists

the value; set replaces it

a missing member or element of a container that exists

obj["absent"], or arr[9] past the end

undefined; set creates the member, or the element, filling the elements between with null

nothing

navigation through undefined, a scalar, or an erased value

undefined; set fails with errc::type, JavaScript’s TypeError

The program of From JavaScript parses a user and a number, and navigates:

constexpr std::string_view text = R"({"user":{"name":"Ada","tags":["math"]},"n":3})";
wd::result<wd::document> made = wd::parse(text);
if (made.has_error()) {
    return false;
}
wd::document& doc = *made;
wd::value user = doc["user"];

show("user.name", user["name"]);
show("user.nick", user["nick"]);        // a missing member: set creates it
show("doc.n.x.y", doc["n"]["x"]["y"]);  // nothing: JavaScript throws a TypeError here
show("user.tags[0]", user["tags"][0]);
show("user.tags.at(-1)", user["tags"].at(-1));
user.name -> "Ada"
user.nick -> undefined
doc.n.x.y -> undefined
user.tags[0] -> "math"
user.tags.at(-1) -> "math"

A handle resolves its place again at every call, so it reads what is there now: user["nick"] reads undefined until a set creates the member, and the same handle then reads the new value. A handle stays valid while the document grows and its image moves to a larger buffer; it reads undefined once its value is erased; and it is invalid once its document is moved from or destroyed, as a container’s iterators are.

Reading

kind() is JavaScript’s typeof, with null, arrays, dates and bytes told apart: one of the enumerators of wd::kind, undefined, null, boolean, number, string, date, bytes, array and object, each with an is_ function. get<T>() reads the value as T and returns a result: errc::type for another kind, and errc::range for a number that T cannot hold exactly. T is bool, any integer type, a Boost.Decimal type, the traits’ number type, std::string, std::string_view, std::u16string, std::u16string_view, wd::date_ms, std::vector<std::byte> or std::span<const std::byte> (Strings, dates and bytes).

value_or(fallback) is JavaScript’s ??: the value get<T>() gives, T being the fallback’s type, or the fallback when nothing is there, when the value is null, or when it cannot be read as T. contains(key) is key in v for an object, size() an object’s key count or an array’s length, and length() an array’s length or a string’s in UTF-16 code units, as JavaScript counts them:

say("typeof user.name === 'string'", user["name"].is_string());
say("'tags' in user", user.contains("tags"));
if (const wd::result<std::uint64_t> length = user["name"].length()) {
    say("user.name.length", *length);
}
say("doc.n ?? 0", doc["n"].value_or(std::int64_t{0}));
say("user.nick ?? 'none'", user["nick"].value_or(std::string_view("none")));
say("Number.isInteger(doc.n)", doc["n"].is_integer());
typeof user.name === 'string' -> true
'tags' in user -> true
user.name.length -> 3
doc.n ?? 0 -> 3
user.nick ?? 'none' -> none
Number.isInteger(doc.n) -> true

A std::string_view that get returns, and a key that keys() gives, are views into the document’s image: each is valid until the document’s next change, which may move the image.

Writing

set(x) is assignment. It takes bool, any integer type, the Boost.Decimal types, the traits’ number type, text (std::string_view, const char*, std::string, std::u16string_view), bytes (std::span<const std::byte>), a wd::date_ms, nullptr or wd::null, the literals wd::object and wd::array, which are JSON written in C++, a handle or a document of the same traits, which it copies, and wd::undefined. A character is not a number: set('a') does not compile, nor does set of a float, nor of a double unless the traits’ number type is one.

erase(key) is delete, and returns whether the key was there. set(wd::undefined) erases a member too: JavaScript keeps a member whose value is undefined, and writes nothing for it, while a document never stores undefined. In an array, it stores null, the text JavaScript writes for it; at the root, the document holds undefined, and writes nothing. assign_from(source) is Object.assign: each member of the source is set here, in its order, as one operation that completes or changes nothing; an array’s elements are its members "0" to "n-1", and null or undefined add nothing.

// user.nick = "Countess"; user.age = 36; user.tags.push("poetry"); user.home = {...};
if (!user["nick"].set("Countess") || !user["age"].set(36) || !user["tags"].push("poetry") ||
    !user["home"].set(wd::object{{"city", "London"}, {"rooms", wd::array{1, 2}}})) {
    return false;
}
show("user", user);

// delete user.age; user.nick = undefined, which erases it; Object.assign(user, {...}).
const wd::result<bool> erased = user.erase("age");
if (!erased || !user["nick"].set(wd::undefined)) {
    return false;
}
say("delete user.age", *erased);
wd::result<wd::document> defaults = wd::parse(R"({"lang":"en","name":"Lovelace"})");
if (defaults.has_error() || !user.assign_from(defaults->root())) {
    return false;
}
show("user", user);
user -> {"name":"Ada","tags":["math","poetry"],"nick":"Countess","age":36,"home":{"city":"London","rooms":[1,2]}}
delete user.age -> true
user -> {"name":"Lovelace","tags":["math","poetry"],"home":{"city":"London","rooms":[1,2]},"lang":"en"}

Every writing function returns a result and is [[nodiscard]]. It completes, or it changes nothing: it finds the room it needs in the image before it allocates (Images), so a full image, a value of the wrong kind or a number out of range leave the document as it was.

Copies, never aliases

JavaScript’s doc.copy = doc.user makes two names of one object, so that a change through one is seen through the other. A document is a tree, as JSON is, so set of a handle copies the subtree:

// doc.copy = doc.user shares one object in JavaScript; here it is a copy of the subtree.
if (!doc["copy"].set(user) || !doc["copy"]["name"].set("Byron")) {
    return false;
}
show("user.name", user["name"]);
show("copy.name", doc["copy"]["name"]);
user.name -> "Lovelace"
copy.name -> "Byron"

A copy reads its source before it changes anything, so a value may be copied into its own subtree. Between documents, copies need the same traits, and any storage. doc.clone() copies a whole document into a new owned one, as structuredClone would.

A wd::value is not a regular value: with exceptions, x = y writes where x points, and never makes it point elsewhere (The sugar that throws). It must not be swapped or sorted: std::swap(x, y) assigns through both handles, leaving both places holding the value of y, and std::sort over a range of handles writes the document’s values the same way. Read the values out, sort them, and set them back.

Iteration and equality

entries(), keys() and values() are Object.entries, Object.keys and Object.values, in the order of the traits’ object policy (Key order), and a for over an array’s handle visits its elements. A key is a std::string_view with UTF-8 strings, and a std::u16string_view with UTF-16 ones (Traits):

// for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(user))
for (auto [key, value] : user.entries()) {
    std::cout << key << ": " << value.stringify() << '\n';
}
// for (const tag of user.tags)
for (const wd::const_value tag : user["tags"]) {
    std::cout << "tag " << tag.stringify() << '\n';
}
name: "Lovelace"
tags: ["math","poetry"]
home: {"city":"London","rooms":[1,2]}
lang: "en"
tag "math"
tag "poetry"

A range reads the document as it is when each step is taken, so changing the container it walks is undefined, as it is for a standard container.

== compares two values structurally, which JavaScript does not: the same kind; numbers by value, so 1, 1.0 and 1e0 are equal; strings, dates and bytes by value; arrays element by element; objects with the same keys, each holding an equal value, in any order. Two documents compare their roots.

Numbers

JavaScript’s numbers are doubles: JSON.parse rounds every number to the nearest one, so a peer that sends 34 exact digits receives 17. With its default traits, document stores every number exactly as it was sent, and writes it back as JavaScript would write that value; with js_traits, it holds JavaScript’s own doubles, and agrees with JavaScript on every digit.

Stored by value

A number is stored in one of two forms, chosen by its value, never by its spelling: an integer that fits the traits’ integer, std::int64_t, is one; any other number is the traits’ number, Boost.Decimal’s decimal128_t by default, normalised, without trailing zeros. So 1, 1.0 and 1e0 are one stored value, as they are one number in JavaScript, and 18446744073709551615, past std::int64_t, is an exact number. Parsing reads a number from its text, never through a double: more than 34 significant digits, or an exponent past the range of decimal128_t, is errc::range.

Writing follows JavaScript’s Number::toString on the stored digits, with k significant digits and the decimal point after position n:

When Written as Example

k <= n <= 21

the digits, then n - k zeros

1e20 writes 100000000000000000000

0 < n <= 21

the digits, with a point after n of them

123.45

-6 < n <= 0

0., then -n zeros, then the digits

0.000001

otherwise

one digit, a point and the others if any, e, the sign, n - 1

1e+21, 1e-7, 1.5e+300

So every number JSON.stringify writes, the shortest text of a double, is written back byte for byte as JavaScript writes it, and a number a double cannot hold stays exact. The program parses one text with each traits:

constexpr std::string_view text =
    "[0.1000000000000000000000000000000001,18446744073709551615,4611686018427387904,"
    "1e21,1.50,1E-7,1.0,-0]";
parsed("default_traits", wd::parse(text));
parsed("js_traits     ", wd::parse<wd::js_traits>(text));
default_traits: [0.1000000000000000000000000000000001,18446744073709551615,4611686018427387904,1e+21,1.5,1e-7,1,0]
js_traits     : [0.1,18446744073709552000,4611686018427388000,1e+21,1.5,1e-7,1,0]

With js_traits, the numbers are what Node holds, written as Node writes them: the 34 digits round to 0.1, and 262, 4611686018427387904, is written 4611686018427388000. A number under js_traits is first rounded to a double, then stored as an integer when that double is integral and fits std::int64_t, so it writes back as Node writes the double.

What each refuses

The default traits refuse a number they cannot store exactly: more than 34 significant digits, or an exponent past the range of decimal128_t, beyond about 1e6144. Within it they store every number exactly, 1e999 included, which a JavaScript peer reads as Infinity. js_traits refuse no number: they round as JSON.parse does, and a number past a double’s range is Infinity, as JSON.parse makes it, which stringify writes null, as JSON.stringify does:

constexpr std::string_view forty_digits = "1234567890123456789012345678901234567890";
parsed("40 digits, default_traits", wd::parse(forty_digits));
parsed("40 digits, js_traits     ", wd::parse<wd::js_traits>(forty_digits));
parsed("1e999, default_traits    ", wd::parse("1e999"));
parsed("1e999, js_traits         ", wd::parse<wd::js_traits>("1e999"));
40 digits, default_traits: a number or index out of range
40 digits, js_traits     : 1.2345678901234568e+39
1e999, default_traits    : 1e+999
1e999, js_traits         : null

set refuses a NaN or an infinity of a Boost.Decimal type with errc::range. A double’s NaN and infinities, which arithmetic makes, and a parse past a double’s range, are stored under js_traits, and written null, as JavaScript writes them.

Reading a number

get<T>() gives a number as any integer type, a Boost.Decimal type, or the traits’ number type, when T holds it exactly, and errc::range otherwise: a number that is not an integer, or does not fit, is never truncated or rounded into T. is_integer() is Number.isInteger, true for a number such as 1e30 too:

wd::result<wd::document> made =
    wd::parse(R"({"small":300,"big":18446744073709551615,"half":0.5,"huge":1e30})");
if (made.has_error()) {
    return 1;
}
const wd::document& doc = *made;
read("small as int64_t", doc["small"].get<std::int64_t>());
read("small as int8_t", doc["small"].get<std::int8_t>());
read("big as uint64_t", doc["big"].get<std::uint64_t>());
read("big as int64_t", doc["big"].get<std::int64_t>());
read("half as int64_t", doc["half"].get<std::int64_t>());
std::cout << "Number.isInteger(huge): " << std::boolalpha << doc["huge"].is_integer() << '\n';
small as int64_t: 300
small as int8_t: a number or index out of range
big as uint64_t: 18446744073709551615
big as int64_t: a number or index out of range
half as int64_t: a number or index out of range
Number.isInteger(huge): true

A double is read or set only when the traits’ number type is one: the default traits have no conversion from or to double, nor to float ever, so a program cannot lose digits by accident.

Arithmetic

A document stores numbers; it computes nothing. A program reads a value in the traits’ own number type, computes, and stores the result, so the arithmetic is the number type’s: exact in decimal, binary in a double.

// 0.1 + 0.2, computed by the program in the traits' own number type, then stored.
wd::result<wd::document> exact = wd::parse(R"({"a":0.1,"b":0.2})");
wd::result<wd::basic_document<wd::js_traits>> js =
    wd::parse<wd::js_traits>(R"({"a":0.1,"b":0.2})");
if (exact.has_error() || js.has_error()) {
    return 1;
}
using decimal = boost::decimal::decimal128_t;
const wd::result<decimal> a = (*exact)["a"].get<decimal>();
const wd::result<decimal> b = (*exact)["b"].get<decimal>();
const wd::result<double> x = (*js)["a"].get<double>();
const wd::result<double> y = (*js)["b"].get<double>();
if (!a || !b || !x || !y || !(*exact)["sum"].set(*a + *b) || !(*js)["sum"].set(*x + *y)) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << exact->stringify() << '\n' << js->stringify() << '\n';
{"a":0.1,"b":0.2,"sum":0.3}
{"a":0.1,"b":0.2,"sum":0.30000000000000004}

Strings, dates and bytes

JSON has strings; JavaScript programs also send dates and bytes through it, as text. A document stores strings in the encoding its traits choose, and holds dates and bytes as values of their own, which it writes as JSON.stringify writes a Date and, by its traits, a Uint8Array.

Strings

The traits’ string is the stored encoding of strings and keys: wd::utf8, the default, or wd::utf16, the code units JavaScript holds, which js_traits choose. Either way, length() counts UTF-16 code units, as JavaScript does: UTF-8 is decoded to count them. Text is validated where it enters: the parser refuses invalid UTF-8, and set refuses text invalid in its encoding with errc::type.

A view reads a string as it is stored, and cannot transcode: get<std::string_view>() reads UTF-8 strings only, and get<std::u16string_view>() UTF-16 ones; get<std::string>() and get<std::u16string>() transcode from either. Keys come out as the encoding’s view. The sugar’s as_string() reads UTF-8 strings only: under js_traits, a program uses as<std::u16string_view>() or as<std::string>() (The sugar that throws).

constexpr std::string_view text = R"(["é😀","tab\there \"q\" \u0001"])";
wd::result<wd::document> utf8 = wd::parse(text);
wd::result<wd::basic_document<wd::js_traits>> utf16 = wd::parse<wd::js_traits>(text);
if (utf8.has_error() || utf16.has_error()) {
    return false;
}
// "é😀".length is 3 in UTF-16 code units, whatever the stored encoding.
read("UTF-8 length ", (*utf8)[0].length());
read("UTF-16 length", (*utf16)[0].length());
read("UTF-8 as std::string_view", (*utf8)[0].get<std::string_view>());
read("UTF-8 as std::u16string_view", (*utf8)[0].get<std::u16string_view>());
read("UTF-16 as std::u16string_view", (*utf16)[0].get<std::u16string_view>());
read("UTF-16 as std::string", (*utf16)[0].get<std::string>());
std::cout << "both write: " << utf8->stringify() << ' ' << utf16->stringify() << '\n';

// A lone surrogate: kept by UTF-16 and written as JSON.stringify writes it; refused by UTF-8.
constexpr std::array<char16_t, 1> lone{0xD800};
const std::u16string_view surrogate(lone.data(), lone.size());
print("UTF-16 set", (*utf16)[2].set(surrogate));
print("UTF-8 set ", (*utf8)[2].set(surrogate));
std::cout << "UTF-16 writes: " << (*utf16)[2].stringify() << '\n';
UTF-8 length : 3
UTF-16 length: 3
UTF-8 as std::string_view: é😀
UTF-8 as std::u16string_view: a value of another kind
UTF-16 as std::u16string_view: 3 code units
UTF-16 as std::string: é😀
both write: ["é😀","tab\there \"q\" \u0001"] ["é😀","tab\there \"q\" \u0001"]
UTF-16 set: ok
UTF-8 set : a value of another kind
UTF-16 writes: "\ud800"

Both encodings write the same text, escaped as JSON.stringify escapes it: a quotation mark and a backslash with a backslash; \b, \f, \n, \r and \t; any other character below U+0020 as \u and four lowercase hexadecimal digits; nothing else, so /, text beyond ASCII and U+2028 and U+2029 are written as they are.

A lone surrogate is a UTF-16 code unit of a pair whose other half is missing, which JavaScript’s strings may hold. UTF-8 cannot encode one, so set refuses it with wd::utf8; wd::utf16 keeps it, and writes it as \u and its four digits, as JSON.stringify has since ES2019. The parser refuses one with either encoding (Lone surrogates).

Dates

A date is a wd::date_ms, milliseconds since the epoch, 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, as a JavaScript Date holds it, and its range is JavaScript’s, 8.64e15 ms on either side: set past it is errc::range. It is written as Date.prototype.toJSON writes it, "2026-10-12T03:04:05.678Z", with a year outside 0 to 9999 written as six digits and a sign, "+275760-09-13T00:00:00.000Z".

JSON has no dates, so a parse keeps every string a string, as JSON.parse does, unless parse_options::revive_dates, which turns a string in exactly that format into a date. get<wd::date_ms>() reads such a string as a date too, revived or not:

constexpr std::string_view text = R"({"at":"2026-10-12T03:04:05.678Z","day":"2026-10-12"})";
wd::parse_options revive;
revive.revive_dates = true;
wd::result<wd::document> plain = wd::parse(text);
wd::result<wd::document> revived = wd::parse(text, revive);
if (plain.has_error() || revived.has_error()) {
    return false;
}
std::cout << "is_date: " << std::boolalpha << (*plain)["at"].is_date() << ' '
          << (*revived)["at"].is_date() << ' ' << (*revived)["day"].is_date() << '\n';
// A string in Date.prototype.toJSON's format reads as a date, revived or not.
const wd::result<wd::date_ms> at = (*plain)["at"].get<wd::date_ms>();
std::cout << "ms since the epoch: " << (at ? at->time_since_epoch().count() : 0) << '\n';

const wd::date_ms last{std::chrono::milliseconds{8'640'000'000'000'000}};
print("set the last date", (*plain)["last"].set(last));
print("set one ms later ", (*plain)["later"].set(last + std::chrono::milliseconds{1}));
print("written", plain);
is_date: false true false
ms since the epoch: 1791774245678
set the last date: ok
set one ms later : a number or index out of range
written: {"at":"2026-10-12T03:04:05.678Z","day":"2026-10-12","last":"+275760-09-13T00:00:00.000Z"}

Bytes

Bytes are a std::span<const std::byte> that set stores raw in the image, and that an image carries as they are. stringify writes them as the traits’ bytes policy says:

Policy Written as

wd::base64, the default

base64 of RFC 4648, with padding

wd::base64url

base64url of RFC 4648, section 5, without padding

wd::javascript_bytes, in js_traits

what JSON.stringify writes for a Uint8Array: an object of the indices and the bytes

parse_options::revive_bytes turns a string valid in the policy’s text back into bytes, and, with javascript_bytes, an object whose keys are exactly "0" to "n-1" holding integers from 0 to 255. get<std::vector<std::byte>>() reads such a value as bytes too, and get<std::span<const std::byte>>() reads bytes in place:

const std::array<std::byte, 4> raw{
    std::byte{0xde},
    std::byte{0xad},
    std::byte{0xbe},
    std::byte{0xef},
};
const std::span<const std::byte> view(raw);
wd::result<wd::document> base64 = wd::document::create();
wd::result<wd::basic_document<canonical_traits>> base64url =
    wd::basic_document<canonical_traits>::create();
wd::result<wd::basic_document<wd::js_traits>> js = wd::basic_document<wd::js_traits>::create();
if (base64.has_error() || base64url.has_error() || js.has_error() ||
    !base64->root().set(view) || !base64url->root().set(view) || !js->root().set(view)) {
    return false;
}
print("base64          ", base64);
print("base64url       ", base64url);
print("javascript_bytes", js);

// revive_bytes turns text of the bytes policy back into bytes.
wd::parse_options revive;
revive.revive_bytes = true;
wd::result<wd::document> revived = wd::parse(R"({"key":"3q2+7w=="})", revive);
if (revived.has_error()) {
    return false;
}
const wd::result<std::vector<std::byte>> key = (*revived)["key"].get<std::vector<std::byte>>();
std::cout << "revived: " << std::boolalpha << (*revived)["key"].is_bytes() << ", "
          << (key ? key->size() : 0) << " bytes\n";
base64          : "3q2+7w=="
base64url       : "3q2-7w"
javascript_bytes: {"0":222,"1":173,"2":190,"3":239}
revived: true, 4 bytes

The program’s canonical_traits choose base64url (Traits).

Key order

The order of an object’s keys is what makes two JSON.stringify texts equal or not, and JavaScript’s is not the order of insertion. Its OrdinaryOwnPropertyKeys gives the keys that are array indices first, ascending, then every other key in the order it was created. Measured in Node 26, JSON.parse('{"b":1,"2":2,"a":3,"1":4}') holds {"1":4,"2":2,"b":1,"a":3}, and a document writes the same.

Array indices

An array index is a key that is the canonical decimal spelling of an integer from 0 to 4,294,967,294: "0", "7" and "10" are, and "01", "-1", "1.0", " 1" and "4294967295" are not, so they keep their place among the other keys. Assigning an existing key keeps its place. Erasing a key and creating it again puts it where a new key goes: last among the other keys, or back among the indices, ascending, for an index.

The policies

The traits’ object chooses the order:

Policy The order of an object’s keys

wd::javascript_order, the default

JavaScript’s: array indices ascending, then the other keys in the order they were created

wd::insertion_order

the order each key was created, the text’s order for a parsed object, whatever the key

wd::sorted

by the keys’ UTF-16 code units, with either encoding, as JavaScript’s sort() and RFC 8785 order them: for canonical JSON, signatures and hashes

A repeated key in parsed text is accepted as JSON.parse accepts it: the last value, in the first one’s place. The program parses one text under each policy, the last two through traits of its own (Traits), then erases and creates again a key and an index:

constexpr std::string_view text = R"({"b":1,"2":2,"a":3,"1":4,"01":5})";
print("javascript_order", wd::parse(text));
print("insertion_order ", wd::parse<insertion_traits>(text));
print("sorted          ", wd::parse<canonical_traits>(text));

// An index key erased and created again goes back among the indices; any other key, last.
wd::result<wd::document> made = wd::parse(text);
if (made.has_error() || !made->root().erase("b") || !(*made)["b"].set(6) ||
    !made->root().erase("1") || !(*made)["1"].set(7)) {
    return false;
}
print("erased, created ", made);
javascript_order: {"1":4,"2":2,"b":1,"a":3,"01":5}
insertion_order : {"b":1,"2":2,"a":3,"1":4,"01":5}
sorted          : {"01":5,"1":4,"2":2,"a":3,"b":1}
erased, created : {"1":7,"2":2,"a":3,"01":5,"b":6}

Every operation keeps the order: set, erase, assign_from, a copy and the parser. An object’s members are kept in ordered indices, never in a hashed one, since keys come from untrusted text: no input makes a lookup slower than its logarithm.

Arrays

A handle of an array has JavaScript’s array methods, under their JavaScript names, with JavaScript’s index rules. Each is a core function: it returns a result, completes or changes nothing, and fails with errc::type, JavaScript’s TypeError, on anything but an array.

JavaScript document Returns

a.push(x, y)

a.push(x, y)

result<std::uint64_t>: the new length

a.pop()

a.pop()

result<document>: a new document holding the removed element, or holding undefined when the array was empty

a.shift()

a.shift()

the same, from the front

a.unshift(x, y)

a.unshift(x, y)

result<std::uint64_t>: the new length

a.splice(start, count, x, y)

a.splice(start, count, x, y)

result<document>: the array of the removed elements

a.splice(start)

a.splice(start)

the same, removing every element from start

a.reverse()

a.reverse()

result<void>

a.slice(start, end)

a.slice(start, end)

result<document>: a new array of copies of the elements

a.concat(b, x)

a.concat(b, x)

result<document>: a new array of this array’s elements, then each argument’s, an array’s elements or the value itself

a.at(i)

a.at(i)

a handle, which names nothing out of range

a.length = n

a.set_length(n)

result<void>: truncates, or appends null

a[i] = x past the end

a[i].set(x)

result<void>: the elements between become null

The values a method takes are what set takes (Writing), each copied into the array; a method that returns removed or copied elements returns them in a new owned document, so that they outlive the array. The program logs each call, what it returned and the array after it:

/** The text of a value, `undefined` when nothing is there. */
std::string text(const wd::const_value& v) {
    return v.is_undefined() ? "undefined" : v.stringify();
}

/** Prints a call, what it returned and the array after it. */
void log(std::string_view call, std::string_view returned, const wd::const_value& a) {
    std::cout << call << " -> " << returned << ", a = " << text(a) << '\n';
}

/** Prints a call that returns a document: the removed values, or a new array. */
void log(std::string_view call, const wd::result<wd::document>& r, const wd::const_value& a) {
    log(call, r.has_value() ? text(r->root()) : r.error().message(), a);
}

/** Prints a call that returns a new length. */
void log(std::string_view call, const wd::result<std::uint64_t>& r, const wd::const_value& a) {
    log(call, r.has_value() ? std::to_string(*r) : r.error().message(), a);
}

/** Prints a call that returns nothing. */
void log(std::string_view call, const wd::result<void>& r, const wd::const_value& a) {
    log(call, r.has_value() ? "undefined" : r.error().message(), a);
}
wd::value a = made->root();
log("a.push(6, 7)", a.push(6, 7), a);
log("a.pop()", a.pop(), a);
log("a.shift()", a.shift(), a);
log("a.unshift(0)", a.unshift(0), a);
log("a.splice(1, 2, 'x', 'y', 'z')", a.splice(1, 2, "x", "y", "z"), a);
log("a.reverse()", a.reverse(), a);
log("a.slice(-2)", a.slice(-2), a);
log("a.concat([8, 9], 10)", a.concat(wd::array{8, 9}, 10), a);
log("a.at(-1)", text(a.at(-1)), a);
a.push(6, 7) -> 7, a = [1,2,3,4,5,6,7]
a.pop() -> 7, a = [1,2,3,4,5,6]
a.shift() -> 1, a = [2,3,4,5,6]
a.unshift(0) -> 6, a = [0,2,3,4,5,6]
a.splice(1, 2, 'x', 'y', 'z') -> [2,3], a = [0,"x","y","z",4,5,6]
a.reverse() -> undefined, a = [6,5,4,"z","y","x",0]
a.slice(-2) -> ["x",0], a = [6,5,4,"z","y","x",0]
a.concat([8, 9], 10) -> [6,5,4,"z","y","x",0,8,9,10], a = [6,5,4,"z","y","x",0]
a.at(-1) -> 0, a = [6,5,4,"z","y","x",0]

Indices

Indices follow JavaScript exactly. A negative start counts from the end and is clamped at 0, and a start past the length is the length; an omitted count removes to the end, and a negative one is 0. The end of slice follows the same rules as start, and at counts a negative index from the end:

if (!a.set(wd::array{1, 2, 3, 4, 5})) {
    return 1;
}
log("a.splice(-2, 1)", a.splice(-2, 1), a);
log("a.splice(10, 0, 'end')", a.splice(10, 0, "end"), a);
log("a.splice(1, -5)", a.splice(1, -5), a);
log("a.splice(3)", a.splice(3), a);
a.splice(-2, 1) -> [4], a = [1,2,3,5]
a.splice(10, 0, 'end') -> [], a = [1,2,3,5,"end"]
a.splice(1, -5) -> [], a = [1,2,3,5,"end"]
a.splice(3) -> [5,"end"], a = [1,2,3]

Dense arrays

JavaScript’s arrays may have holes, elements that were never set; JSON has none, and writes a hole as null. A document’s arrays are dense, the traits’ only array policy, wd::dense: a longer length, or a write past the end, fills the elements between with null, which writes the same text. So pop or shift of an element that was a hole returns null, where JavaScript returns undefined:

log("a.length = 1", a.set_length(1), a);
log("a.length = 3", a.set_length(3), a);
log("a[5] = 6", a[5].set(6), a);
log("a.pop()", a.pop(), a);
log("a.pop()", a.pop(), a);  // JavaScript: undefined, the element of a hole
a.length = 1 -> undefined, a = [1]
a.length = 3 -> undefined, a = [1,null,null]
a[5] = 6 -> undefined, a = [1,null,null,null,null,6]
a.pop() -> 6, a = [1,null,null,null,null]
a.pop() -> null, a = [1,null,null,null]

Copies and empty arrays

pop and shift of an empty array return a document that holds undefined, as JavaScript returns undefined. And since a document is a tree, a.splice(0, 1, a) inserts a copy of the array as it was before the call, where JavaScript inserts the array itself, a cycle; the copy is a value of its own:

if (!a.set(wd::array{})) {
    return 1;
}
log("a.pop()", a.pop(), a);  // a document that holds undefined
// JavaScript inserts the array itself, a cycle; a document inserts a copy of it.
if (!a.set(wd::array{1, 2})) {
    return 1;
}
log("a.splice(0, 1, a)", a.splice(0, 1, a), a);
log("a[0].push({})", a[0].push(wd::object{}), a);  // the copy, not a
a.pop() -> undefined, a = []
a.splice(0, 1, a) -> [1], a = [[1,2],2]
a[0].push({}) -> 3, a = [[1,2,{}],2]

A method that inserts many values, push, unshift, splice or concat, finds the room for all of them first: in a full external buffer, it returns errc::capacity and the array is as it was (Images).

Containers

The handles of Handles read and write a document as JavaScript does. A C++ program that walks a document also wants the interface its containers have, and document gives it: as_object() makes of an object a view that is a sorted map, as_array() makes of an array a view that is a vector, and both are ranges that the standard algorithms and views read. They are views of the document and own nothing, wd::object_ref and wd::array_ref, and every operation that can fail returns its result as the rest of the library does.
