The program of this section is example/document_containers.cpp, and prints the same lines on every target.

Its helpers print the message of a failed result and the document after an operation:

/** Prints the message of a failed result, and yields the exit code of main. */
template <class Result>
int fail(const Result& r) {
    std::cout << "error: " << r.error().message() << '\n';
    return 1;
}

/** Prints an operation and the document after it, as JSON. */
void step(std::string_view what, const wd::document& doc) {
    std::cout << what << " -> " << doc.stringify() << '\n';
}

An object is a sorted map

insert and try_emplace answer the member and whether it was inserted, and a key that is there keeps its value; insert_or_assign assigns to it, as JavaScript’s o[key] = v does. find answers the member’s iterator, or end(), contains whether the key is there, and erase how many members it removed. Iteration follows JavaScript’s order, so a new key comes last, and so does a key that is erased and inserted again (Key order):

// An object is a sorted map: insert and try_emplace answer the member and whether it was
// inserted, and insert_or_assign assigns to it as JavaScript's o[key] = v does.
wd::result<wd::document> made = wd::parse("{}");
if (made.has_error()) {
    return fail(made);
}
wd::document& doc = *made;
wd::result<wd::object_ref> as_object = doc.root().as_object();
if (as_object.has_error()) {
    return fail(as_object);
}
const wd::object_ref obj = *as_object;

const auto name = obj.insert("name", "Ada");
if (name.has_error()) {
    return fail(name);
}
std::cout << "insert name: " << name->second << '\n';

// A key that is there keeps its value.
const auto again = obj.insert("name", "Grace");
if (again.has_error()) {
    return fail(again);
}
std::cout << "insert name again: " << again->second
          << ", name = " << doc["name"].value_or(std::string_view("nobody")) << '\n';

const auto assigned = obj.insert_or_assign("name", "Augusta Ada");
if (assigned.has_error()) {
    return fail(assigned);
}
std::cout << "insert_or_assign name: " << assigned->second
          << ", name = " << doc["name"].value_or(std::string_view("nobody")) << '\n';

const auto born = obj.try_emplace("born", 1815);
if (born.has_error()) {
    return fail(born);
}
std::cout << "try_emplace born: " << born->second << '\n';

// find answers the member's iterator, or the end; contains answers whether the key is there.
const wd::object_ref::iterator found = obj.find("born");
std::cout << "find born: " << found->second.value_or(std::int64_t{0}) << '\n';
const wd::object_ref::iterator missing = obj.find("nope");
std::cout << "contains born: " << obj.contains("born")
          << ", find nope is end: " << (missing == obj.end()) << '\n';

const auto erased = obj.erase("born");
if (erased.has_error()) {
    return fail(erased);
}
std::cout << "erase born: " << *erased << ", contains born: " << obj.contains("born") << '\n';

// A new key comes last, and so does a key erased and inserted again: the members iterate in
// JavaScript's order, which is the order they were added in.
const auto langs = obj.insert("langs", wd::array{"Analytical", "Note G"});
if (langs.has_error()) {
    return fail(langs);
}
const auto known = obj.insert("known", true);
if (known.has_error()) {
    return fail(known);
}
const auto born_again = obj.insert("born", 1815);
if (born_again.has_error()) {
    return fail(born_again);
}
for (const auto& [key, handle] : obj) {
    std::cout << key << " = " << handle.stringify() << '\n';
}
insert name: true
insert name again: false, name = Ada
insert_or_assign name: false, name = Augusta Ada
try_emplace born: true
find born: 1815
contains born: true, find nope is end: true
erase born: 1, contains born: false
name = "Augusta Ada"
langs = ["Analytical","Note G"]
known = true
born = 1815

An array is a vector

push_back, emplace_back, insert, erase and resize change an array as they change a std::vector, and at checks the index: an index past the end is an error value and not an undefined element. erase answers the iterator of the element after the one it removed, and resize to a larger size fills with null (Dense arrays):

// An array is a vector: push_back, emplace_back, insert, erase and resize change it as
// std::vector does, and at checks the index.
wd::result<wd::document> list_made = wd::parse("[1,2,3]");
if (list_made.has_error()) {
    return fail(list_made);
}
wd::document& list_doc = *list_made;
wd::result<wd::array_ref> as_array = list_doc.root().as_array();
if (as_array.has_error()) {
    return fail(as_array);
}
const wd::array_ref list = *as_array;

const auto pushed = list.push_back(4);
if (pushed.has_error()) {
    return fail(pushed);
}
step("push_back(4)", list_doc);

const auto emplaced = list.emplace_back(5);
if (emplaced.has_error()) {
    return fail(emplaced);
}
step("emplace_back(5)", list_doc);

const auto placed = list.insert(std::ranges::next(list.begin(), 1), 9);
if (placed.has_error()) {
    return fail(placed);
}
step("insert(begin + 1, 9)", list_doc);

// erase answers the iterator of the element after the one it removed.
const wd::array_ref::iterator after = list.erase(std::ranges::next(list.begin(), 1));
step("erase(begin + 1)", list_doc);
const wd::value next_element = *after;
std::cout << "erase returns the element after: " << next_element.value_or(std::int64_t{0})
          << '\n';

const auto shrunk = list.resize(3);
if (shrunk.has_error()) {
    return fail(shrunk);
}
step("resize(3)", list_doc);
std::cout << "front " << list.front().value_or(std::int64_t{0}) << ", back "
          << list.back().value_or(std::int64_t{0}) << '\n';

const wd::result<wd::value> third = list.at(2);
if (third.has_error()) {
    return fail(third);
}
std::cout << "at(2) = " << third->value_or(std::int64_t{0}) << '\n';
// An index past the end is an error value, not an undefined element.
const wd::result<wd::value> beyond = list.at(10);
std::cout << "at(10) is errc::range: "
          << (beyond.has_error() && beyond.error() == wd::errc::range) << '\n';

const auto grown = list.resize(5);
if (grown.has_error()) {
    return fail(grown);
}
step("resize(5)", list_doc);
push_back(4) -> [1,2,3,4]
emplace_back(5) -> [1,2,3,4,5]
insert(begin + 1, 9) -> [1,9,2,3,4,5]
erase(begin + 1) -> [1,2,3,4,5]
erase returns the element after: 2
resize(3) -> [1,2,3]
front 1, back 3
at(2) = 3
at(10) is errc::range: true
resize(5) -> [1,2,3,null,null]

Ranges

An object and an array are each a std::ranges::bidirectional_range, so the standard algorithms and the views over them read their members as they read a vector or a map:

// An object and an array are ranges: the standard algorithms and the views over them read
// their members, as they read a vector.
wd::result<wd::document> shop_made = wd::document::create();
if (shop_made.has_error()) {
    return fail(shop_made);
}
wd::document& shop = *shop_made;
const auto shop_set = shop.root().set(wd::object{
    {"prices", wd::array{3, 8, 12, 5, 20}},
    {"stock", wd::object{{"apple", 4}, {"pear", 0}, {"plum", 7}}},
});
if (shop_set.has_error()) {
    return fail(shop_set);
}
wd::result<wd::array_ref> as_prices = shop["prices"].as_array();
if (as_prices.has_error()) {
    return fail(as_prices);
}
const wd::array_ref prices = *as_prices;
wd::result<wd::object_ref> as_stock = shop["stock"].as_object();
if (as_stock.has_error()) {
    return fail(as_stock);
}
const wd::object_ref stock = *as_stock;

const auto above_five = [](const wd::value& v) { return v.value_or(std::int64_t{0}) > 5; };
const auto doubled_value = [](const wd::value& v) { return 2 * v.value_or(std::int64_t{0}); };
std::cout << "prices above 5: " << std::ranges::count_if(prices, above_five) << '\n';
std::cout << "prices above 5, doubled:";
// The view is built and iterated in one statement: a filter view has no const iteration.
for (const std::int64_t twice :
     prices | std::views::filter(above_five) | std::views::transform(doubled_value)) {
    std::cout << ' ' << twice;
}
std::cout << '\n';

const auto empty = std::ranges::find_if(
    stock, [](const auto& member) { return member.second.value_or(std::int64_t{0}) == 0; });
std::cout << "first out of stock: " << empty->first << '\n';
prices above 5: 3
prices above 5, doubled: 16 24 40
first out of stock: pear

What a change leaves valid is more than the standard containers leave: an insertion, and any growth of the image, keeps every iterator and handle valid and invalidates only the views (std::string_view) read from a value; an erase invalidates the iterators to the erased member and its subtree. A range reads the document as it is when each step is taken, so changing the container it walks is undefined, as it is for a standard container.

Keys in order

An object is kept in JavaScript’s order, and also in key order: by_key() is the same object ordered by key, by UTF-16 code units whatever the encoding, with find, lower_bound, upper_bound and equal_range. Each step and each bound is a search of a tree, so a query costs O(log n), and nothing is sorted: a JavaScript program sorts every key to get any of these answers, and gets it again each time. A prefix query is a range from the first key at or after the prefix up to the first key at or after the prefix with its last character raised by one:

// by_key is the same object in key order, by UTF-16 code units, with bounds for ranges of keys.
// A JavaScript program sorts every key to get any of these; here the tree keeps them sorted.
wd::result<wd::document> catalog_made = wd::parse("{}");
if (catalog_made.has_error()) {
    return fail(catalog_made);
}
wd::document& catalog = *catalog_made;
wd::result<wd::object_ref> as_catalog = catalog.root().as_object();
if (as_catalog.has_error()) {
    return fail(as_catalog);
}
const wd::object_ref catalog_obj = *as_catalog;
const std::array<std::string_view, 13> names{
    "user_3", "admin",  "user_1", "guest",  "user_9", "user",   "user_2",
    "owner",  "user_7", "user_5", "user_4", "user_8", "user_6",
};
for (const std::string_view key : names) {
    const auto added = catalog_obj.insert(key, true);
    if (added.has_error()) {
        return fail(added);
    }
}
std::cout << "JavaScript order:";
for (const auto& member : catalog_obj) {
    std::cout << ' ' << member.first;
}
std::cout << '\n';
const auto keys = catalog_obj.by_key();
std::cout << "by_key order:";
for (const auto& member : keys) {
    std::cout << ' ' << member.first;
}
std::cout << '\n';

// The keys with the prefix "user_" lie from its first key up to the first key at or after
// "user`", the character after '_'.
const std::ranges::subrange users(keys.lower_bound("user_"), keys.lower_bound("user`"));
std::cout << "prefix user_: " << std::ranges::distance(users) << " keys, from "
          << users.begin()->first << " to " << std::ranges::prev(users.end())->first << '\n';

const auto [exact, exact_end] = keys.equal_range("user_5");
std::cout << "equal_range user_5: " << std::ranges::distance(exact, exact_end) << " member, "
          << exact->first << '\n';

std::cout << "lower_bound p: " << keys.lower_bound("p")->first << '\n';
const std::ranges::subrange between(keys.lower_bound("g"), keys.lower_bound("v"));
std::cout << "keys from g up to v: " << std::ranges::distance(between) << '\n';
JavaScript order: user_3 admin user_1 guest user_9 user user_2 owner user_7 user_5 user_4 user_8 user_6
by_key order: admin guest owner user user_1 user_2 user_3 user_4 user_5 user_6 user_7 user_8 user_9
prefix user_: 9 keys, from user_1 to user_9
equal_range user_5: 1 member, user_5
lower_bound p: user
keys from g up to v: 12

The module of Using it from JavaScript gives the same query to JavaScript as keysInRange.

Reserving room

A batch of insertions of a known size is made with the image reserved once, as a vector is reserved: the insertions then move nothing, where without the reservation the same insertions grow the image and move it. The example of this section measures it with reserve and capacity (Reserving).

Writing JSON

wd::stringify(v, indent) is JSON.stringify(v, null, indent), and writes its exact bytes: the keys in the policy’s order (Key order), strings escaped as JSON.stringify escapes them (Strings, dates and bytes), numbers as JavaScript writes them (Numbers), a date as Date.prototype.toJSON writes it, and bytes by the traits’ policy. It is a function of a handle or of a document, and a member of both, doc.stringify(2) and doc["user"].stringify():

// JSON.stringify(doc, null, 2).
std::cout << doc.stringify(2) << '\n';

The indent is JavaScript’s: 0 writes compactly, a larger one is clamped to 10 spaces, and an empty array or object is written [] or {} at any indent. A value that is undefined, a handle of nothing or a document that holds undefined, writes no text, as JSON.stringify(undefined) returns none. stringify returns a std::string, so its only failure is the standard library’s std::bad_alloc; a program that must not meet even that writes to a sink of its own.

In pieces, to a sink

wd::stringify_to(v, sink, indent, chunk) writes the same bytes as stringify, in pieces of at most chunk bytes, 4096 unless told otherwise, to a sink: any callable that takes a std::string_view and returns void or wd::result<void>. A failure the sink returns stops the writing and is returned; an exception it throws propagates. The document is unchanged either way, and a writer holds no recursion, so a document nested as deep as memory allows is written:

// The same bytes as stringify, in pieces of at most 8 bytes, to a sink that prints each.
const wd::result<void> written =
    wd::stringify_to(*made, [](std::string_view piece) { std::cout << piece << '|'; }, 0, 8);
if (written.has_error()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << '\n';

// A sink that returns a failure stops the writing, and stringify_to returns that failure.
std::string kept;
const wd::result<void> stopped = wd::stringify_to(
    *made,
    [&kept](std::string_view piece) -> wd::result<void> {
        if (!kept.empty()) {
            return wd::errc::capacity;
        }
        kept = piece;
        return {};
    },
    0, 8);
std::cout << kept << " then " << stopped.error().message() << '\n';
{"name":|"Ada","t|ags":["m|ath"],"n|":1500}|
{"name": then no room left

The first sink writes a bar after each piece of 8 bytes; the second keeps the first piece, then fails, which stops the writing there.

Parsing

wd::parse(text, options) is JSON.parse(text): it reads JSON text into a new owned document and returns it in a result. It accepts what RFC 8259 and JSON.parse accept, and nothing else: no comments, no trailing commas, and whitespace of space, tab, line feed and carriage return only. A key written twice keeps the last value in the first one’s place, as JavaScript does. A document’s parser never throws: its input is the network’s, and every failure is a value.

wd::parse<Traits> parses into a document of other traits, as wd::parse<wd::js_traits>(text) does in Numbers; wd::parse_into(buffer, text) parses into a buffer the program owns (Images); and wd::parse_or_throw(text), with exceptions only, throws as JSON.parse does (The sugar that throws).

Limits and revivers

wd::parse_options holds the limits of a parse, each of which is errc::capacity when it is passed, and the revivers:

Member What it is

max_depth

The deepest nesting of arrays and objects, 256 unless told otherwise.

max_bytes

The most bytes of text, every chunk counted; no limit unless told otherwise.

max_document_bytes

The largest image an owned document grows to, 64 MiB unless told otherwise.

revive_dates

Whether a string in exactly the format of Date.prototype.toJSON becomes a date (Dates).

revive_bytes

Whether text of the traits’ bytes policy becomes bytes (Bytes).

Memory per value

Every value of a document is a node of the image’s tree, and a node takes 192 bytes of the image whatever it holds: a number, true, null, an empty string, an empty array or object alike. A string’s bytes, and a key’s, take a block of their own besides: 48 bytes for a string of 8 bytes, 112 for one of 100. So "abcdefgh" takes 240 bytes, and {"k":0}, an object and a member with its key, 432. These are the image’s sizes on every target, measured, as an image is the same bytes everywhere (Images).

A short value costs far more in the image than in its text. Measured, 2 MB of text, [0,0,...] with 1,048,576 zeros, makes an image of 268 MB, 128 times the text, which shrink_to_fit() brings to 201 MB; and while an owned image grows, its old and new buffers are held at once. So the default max_document_bytes is 64 MiB, which refuses input from the network early: it is reached by 700 KB of such text, which a native release build reads for 0.4 seconds with 137 MB resident before it fails, where a limit of 1 GiB would take 11 MB of text, 9 seconds and 2.2 GB. A program that parses larger documents raises max_document_bytes to what it can afford, and sets max_bytes with it: a parse past either fails with errc::capacity. A document the program builds itself, with create, keeps a limit of 1 GiB (Images).

In chunks

wd::parser is the parser itself, wd::basic_parser<Traits, Storage> for other traits or a buffer of the program’s: write(chunk) takes the text in chunks of any size, split anywhere, inside a string, a number, an escape or a character’s bytes, down to one byte at a time, and finish() ends the text and returns the document. The document a parser builds is the one a whole parse builds, however the text is split:

wd::parser p;
// The text {"name":"Ada","tags":["math"],"n":1.5e3}, split inside a string and a number.
for (const std::string_view chunk :
     {R"({"name":"Ad)", R"(a","tags":["ma)", R"(th"],"n":1.)", R"(5e3})"}) {
    if (const wd::result<void> written = p.write(chunk); written.has_error()) {
        std::cout << "error: " << written.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
}
wd::result<wd::document> made = p.finish();
if (made.has_error()) {
    std::cout << "error: " << made.error().message() << '\n';
    return 1;
}
std::cout << made->stringify() << '\n';
{"name":"Ada","tags":["math"],"n":1500}

The parser builds the document node by node as each chunk arrives, so the document may grow and its image move between two chunks; finish returns it. reset() makes the parser ready for another text, its selectors kept (Selectors).

Errors and offsets

Malformed text is errc::syntax, JavaScript’s SyntaxError. offset() is the count of bytes consumed, which after a syntax error is the offset where it was found, the same however the text was split, and cause() is the code of Boost.JSON’s parser behind it. A number the traits refuse is errc::range (What each refuses), and a limit passed errc::capacity.

A parser reads one text: anything but whitespace after it is errc::syntax, whose cause() is Boost.JSON’s extra_data, at the offset where the second text begins, whether it comes in the same chunk or a later one, so "1 2" and "[1] " then "[2]" are refused, and no selector sees the second text. A parser that failed stays failed: every later write and finish returns the same error, until reset. A finished parser takes no more text, which is errc::syntax, until reset. And max_bytes counts every chunk written, not each one alone:

p.reset();
report("write [1,2", p.write("[1,2"), p);
report("write ,]", p.write(",]"), p);  // the error, at the byte where it was found
std::cout << "cause: " << p.cause().message() << '\n';
report("write 3]", p.write("3]"), p);  // a failed parser stays failed
p.reset();
report("write [1]", p.write("[1]"), p);
const wd::result<wd::document> one = p.finish();
std::cout << "finish: " << (one.has_value() ? one->stringify() : one.error().message()) << '\n';
report("write [2]", p.write("[2]"), p);  // a finished parser takes no more text
wd::parse_options limits;
limits.max_depth = 2;
limits.max_bytes = 8;
wd::parser limited(limits);
report("write [[1],", limited.write("[[1],"), limited);
report("write [2]]", limited.write("[2]]"), limited);  // 9 bytes in all
std::cout << "[[[1]]]: " << wd::parse("[[[1]]]", limits).error().message() << '\n';
write [1,2: ok
write ,]: malformed JSON text at 5
cause: syntax error
write 3]: malformed JSON text at 5
write [1]: ok
finish: [1]
write [2]: malformed JSON text at 3
write [[1],: ok
write [2]]: no room left at 5
[[[1]]]: no room left

Lone surrogates

JSON.parse('"\ud800"') gives a string holding a lone surrogate, half of a UTF-16 pair. document’s parser refuses it with errc::syntax, with either encoding, utf16 included, which could store it. That is a limit of Boost.JSON’s parser, which document reads JSON with, and a deliberate choice: the parser cannot deliver a lone surrogate, but only refuse it, or, with allow_invalid_utf16, replace it with U+FFFD, which would change the text without a word. So it is documented, not worked around. A program that must hold one, with wd::utf16, stores it with set of a std::u16string_view, and stringify writes it as JSON.stringify does (Strings).

Streams of documents

A stream of documents is a stream of bytes that holds JSON texts one after another: a socket that a server writes NDJSON to, a log file of JSON lines, the output of a program that prints indented documents. wd::stream_parser, wd::basic_stream_parser<Traits> for other traits, in <webcpp/document/stream.hpp>, takes the bytes in chunks of any size, split anywhere, down to one byte at a time, and delivers each document as soon as the bytes that end it are consumed. It reads one document at a time: at a document’s end it delivers it and begins the next on the bytes that follow, in the same chunk, so a stream of any length needs the memory of the documents not yet taken and of the one being read.

Each document is parsed as wd::parse parses one text (Parsing), with the same key order, numbers and revivers, into a new owned document, and is held to the same limits on its own: max_depth, max_document_bytes, and max_bytes, which counts the bytes of one document from its first, not those of the stream (Limits and revivers). wd::stream_options holds those options, and two of its own: the framing, which says how the documents are told apart, and the policy on errors.

Framings

wd::framing The stream

concatenated

Documents one after another, with any JSON whitespace between them, or none: indented JSON, {"a":1} {"b":2}, {"a":1}{"b":2}, [1][2] and "x""y" alike. A document ends where its value closes; a top-level number ends at the next byte that cannot continue it, so 1 2 is two documents and 12 one, however it is split. The default.

lines

NDJSON, also called JSON Lines: one document per line.

rfc7464

JSON text sequences, RFC 7464: each document in a record that the byte 0x1E opens.

NDJSON

A line of NDJSON holds one document, and a document ends at its line’s \n. JSON never holds a raw \n inside a string, where it is always the escape \n, so a raw \n in the stream always ends a line. With framing::lines:

  • a document ends at its line’s \n, or at \r\n: the \r, and any other JSON whitespace before or after the document on its line, is ignored;

  • an empty line, or one of whitespace only, is ignored;

  • the last line may end without its \n: finish() closes it;

  • two documents on one line are an error for that line, and so is a document not complete at its \n. Indented JSON is therefore not NDJSON: { alone on a line is an error, and so is each line after it, until a line holds a whole document again.

A document of a line is delivered at the line’s \n, once the line is known to hold it alone.

JSON text sequences

With framing::rfc7464, a record starts at 0x1E, the ASCII record separator, and ends before the next 0x1E or at the stream’s end. Its document may span lines, indented, and is delivered as soon as its value closes; a top-level number closes at the \n that RFC 7464 puts after each text, at the next 0x1E, or at finish(). A record holds nothing but whitespace after its document; an empty record is ignored. Whitespace before the first record is ignored, and any other byte before it is an error.

Errors

A bad document is errc::syntax for malformed text, errc::range for a number the traits refuse, and errc::capacity past a limit, as in a parse (Errors and offsets). What follows it is the policy’s, wd::on_error:

wd::on_error What a bad document does

stop

It ends the stream: the documents before it are delivered, then every call returns its error, until reset(). The default, and the only policy of framing::concatenated, which has no place to go on from.

skip

It is dropped, and its error is delivered in its place, in the stream’s order; the stream goes on at the next line with framing::lines, and at the next 0x1E with framing::rfc7464.

A parser asked to skip with framing::concatenated is refused: every call of it returns boost::system::errc::invalid_argument. After an error is delivered, error_line() and error_offset() say where it was found, the line counted from 1 and the offset in bytes from the stream’s start, and error_cause() gives the code of Boost.JSON’s parser behind it, which is extra_data for a second document on a line or in a record.

finish() ends the stream: it closes a top-level number or a last line without its \n, and a document the end cuts short is errc::syntax. After it the parser takes no more bytes, which is errc::syntax, until reset(); an empty write and another finish() complete nothing.

Without I/O

The parser is sans-IO: it reads no socket and no file, so it serves any source, a socket read by hand, a file read in blocks, an actor’s messages, or JavaScript that hands chunks to a C++ function compiled with Emscripten. Its documents come out in one of two ways:

  • write(bytes) queues each document it completes, and next() takes the oldest: a result<std::optional<document>> that holds the document, nothing when none is complete, or an error, delivered as the policy says;

  • write(bytes, f) and finish(f), the push form, hand each document to f as it completes, after any that next() has not taken: f takes a result<document>, the document or, with on_error::skip, the error of one dropped, and returns void or result<void>, whose failure ends the stream with that error.

write and finish return how many documents, and dropped documents’ errors, they completed. line() is the line of the last byte consumed, offset() the bytes consumed, and documents() the documents delivered so far. The core never throws, as the rest of document: an exception that f throws propagates, with the bytes up to the document it was given consumed.

By hand

The program below reads each stream from a string, with no I/O at all. Its helpers print the error a call returned with the line it was found on, take every document the parser holds, and write the text in pieces of one, five, two and seven bytes in turn, as a socket might deliver it:

/** Prints the error a write, a finish or a take returned, with the line it was found on. */
void report_error(const wd::stream_parser& p, const boost::system::error_code& error) {
    std::cout << "error at line " << p.error_line() << ": " << error.message() << '\n';
}
/**
 Takes every document the parser holds, printing each as stringify writes it. Under
 on_error::skip a dropped document's error is printed and taking goes on; under on_error::stop the
 error comes back on every take, so taking ends at it.
*/
void take_ready(wd::stream_parser& p, wd::on_error policy) {
    for (;;) {
        wd::result<std::optional<wd::document>> taken = p.next();
        if (taken.has_error()) {
            report_error(p, taken.error());
            if (policy == wd::on_error::stop) {
                return;
            }
            continue;
        }
        const std::optional<wd::document>& held = *taken;
        if (!held.has_value()) {
            return;
        }
        std::cout << held->stringify() << '\n';
    }
}
/**
 Writes `text` to the parser in pieces of 1, 5, 2 and 7 bytes in turn, as a socket might deliver
 it, and takes the documents each piece completes. Returns false when the stream stopped.
*/
bool write_in_pieces(wd::stream_parser& p, std::string_view text, wd::on_error policy) {
    constexpr std::array<std::size_t, 4> sizes{1, 5, 2, 7};
    for (std::size_t turn = 0; !text.empty(); ++turn) {
        const std::string_view piece = text.substr(0, sizes[turn % sizes.size()]);
        text.remove_prefix(piece.size());
        if (const wd::result<std::size_t> written = p.write(piece); written.has_error()) {
            report_error(p, written.error());
            return false;
        }
        take_ready(p, policy);
    }
    return true;
}

NDJSON ends each document at its line’s newline, so a line may end in CRLF, a line may be empty, and the last line may lack its newline, which finish() closes. The documents are taken with next():

/**
 NDJSON: each document ends at its line's newline, so a line may end in CRLF, a line may be empty,
 and the last line may lack its newline, which finish closes.
*/
bool read_ndjson() {
    std::cout << "NDJSON, taken with next():\n";
    wd::stream_options options;
    options.framing = wd::framing::lines;
    wd::stream_parser p(options);
    constexpr std::string_view text =
        "{\"id\":1,\"tags\":[\"a\",\"b\"]}\n"
        "{\"id\":2,\"note\":\"first\\nsecond\"}\r\n"
        "\n"
        "[3,4.5]\n"
        "null";
    if (!write_in_pieces(p, text, options.on_error)) {
        return false;
    }
    if (const wd::result<std::size_t> finished = p.finish(); finished.has_error()) {
        report_error(p, finished.error());
        return false;
    }
    take_ready(p, options.on_error);
    return true;
}
NDJSON, taken with next():
{"id":1,"tags":["a","b"]}
{"id":2,"note":"first\nsecond"}
[3,4.5]
null

Concatenated JSON, with no separator or with indentation between the documents, is pushed to a callback, which sees each document as soon as its last byte is consumed:

/**
 Concatenated JSON, with no separator or with indentation between documents, pushed to a callback:
 each document is handed over as soon as its last byte is consumed, so a callback sees it before
 the rest of the piece is read.
*/
bool push_concatenated() {
    std::cout << "concatenated, pushed to a callback:\n";
    wd::stream_parser p;
    constexpr std::string_view text =
        "{\"a\":1}    {\"b\":2}\n"
        "[1][2]\n"
        "{\n"
        "  \"c\": [\n"
        "    3\n"
        "  ]\n"
        "}";
    const auto print = [](wd::result<wd::document> made) {
        std::cout << (made.has_value() ? made->stringify() : made.error().message()) << '\n';
    };
    for (std::size_t at = 0; at < text.size(); at += 3) {
        if (const wd::result<std::size_t> written = p.write(text.substr(at, 3), print);
            written.has_error()) {
            report_error(p, written.error());
            return false;
        }
    }
    if (const wd::result<std::size_t> finished = p.finish(print); finished.has_error()) {
        report_error(p, finished.error());
        return false;
    }
    std::cout << p.documents() << " documents\n";
    return true;
}
concatenated, pushed to a callback:
{"a":1}
{"b":2}
[1]
[2]
{"c":[3]}
5 documents

With on_error::skip, a bad line is reported with its line number and the stream goes on at the next line:

/**
 NDJSON with a bad line under on_error::skip: the bad line is reported with its line number, and the
 stream goes on from the next line.
*/
bool skip_bad_line() {
    std::cout << "NDJSON with a bad line, skipped:\n";
    wd::stream_options options;
    options.framing = wd::framing::lines;
    options.on_error = wd::on_error::skip;
    wd::stream_parser p(options);
    constexpr std::string_view text = "{\"ok\":1}\n{\"bad\":}\n[2]\n\"three\"";
    if (!write_in_pieces(p, text, options.on_error)) {
        return false;
    }
    if (const wd::result<std::size_t> finished = p.finish(); finished.has_error()) {
        report_error(p, finished.error());
        return false;
    }
    take_ready(p, options.on_error);
    return true;
}
NDJSON with a bad line, skipped:
{"ok":1}
error at line 2: malformed JSON text
[2]
"three"

And a stream of JSON text sequences, whose records open with the byte 0x1E and may span lines:

/**
 JSON text sequences, RFC 7464: each record opens with the byte 0x1E, and its document may span
 several lines.
*/
bool read_rfc7464() {
    std::cout << "rfc7464 records:\n";
    wd::stream_options options;
    options.framing = wd::framing::rfc7464;
    wd::stream_parser p(options);
    constexpr std::string_view text =
        "\x1e{\"a\":1}\n"
        "\x1e{\n  \"b\": [\n    2\n  ]\n}\n"
        "\x1e\"three\"\n";
    if (!write_in_pieces(p, text, options.on_error)) {
        return false;
    }
    if (const wd::result<std::size_t> finished = p.finish(); finished.has_error()) {
        report_error(p, finished.error());
        return false;
    }
    take_ready(p, options.on_error);
    return true;
}
rfc7464 records:
{"a":1}
{"b":[2]}
"three"

A bare number or other scalar that ends a concatenated stream is closed only by the end of the input. A document that is an object or an array ends where its value closes, but 42 has no byte that ends it: the number could go on in the next chunk. It is delivered when finish() is called, which the Asio and Cobalt readers of this section call when the stream reaches its end.

With Boost.Asio

<webcpp/document/asio.hpp> reads a stream of documents from Boost.Asio’s streams. It is the one header of document that includes Boost.Asio, which builds natively only, so <webcpp/document.hpp> leaves it out, and a program that uses it includes it and is built natively.

wd::async_read_document(stream, buffer, parser, token) reads the next document of stream, an AsyncReadStream such as a socket or a pipe. It takes the parser’s next document when the parser holds one, and otherwise reads from the stream into buffer and writes what it read into the parser, piece by piece, until a document is complete. The buffer is either of Boost.Asio’s two models: a DynamicBuffer_v2, such as what asio::dynamic_buffer makes of a string, is taken by value and only what it names must outlive the operation; a DynamicBuffer_v1, such as Beast’s multi_buffer, is taken by reference and must outlive it. Bytes the buffer already holds are read first, and a buffer made of several pieces is never joined into one. It is a composed operation that takes any completion token of Boost.Asio’s, a callback, asio::use_awaitable, asio::deferred or boost::cobalt::use_op among them, and completes with (boost::system::error_code, document):

Error The completion

none

The next document.

the error of a document dropped

With on_error::skip; the next call goes on with the stream.

the error that stopped the stream

With on_error::stop, every time, until the parser’s reset().

asio::error::eof

The stream ended, and the parser’s finish() delivered every document it held; every later call completes with it again.

another

The error of a read.

On an error the document is empty. A completion is never called inside async_read_document: one that needs no read is dispatched to the handler’s immediate executor, or posted to the stream’s. One operation at a time reads a stream, its buffer and its parser, which outlive it.

The program below runs a server and a client on the loopback address, in one thread. The server writes NDJSON, then concatenated JSON, in pieces of one, three, seven, two and thirteen bytes, so the client’s parser meets documents cut in the middle. The connection is a pair of sockets:

/**
 A TCP connection on the loopback address: the server's end, written to, and the client's end,
 read from.
*/
struct link {
    link(asio::io_context& io, tcp::acceptor& acceptor) : server(io), client(io) {
        client.connect(acceptor.local_endpoint());
        acceptor.accept(server);
    }

    tcp::socket server;
    tcp::socket client;
};

The server’s end is written in pieces, and after each piece the context is drained until the client has consumed it, so that the output does not depend on timing; the write side is then shut down, which the client reads as the end of the stream:

/**
 Writes `text` to the server's end in pieces of 1, 3, 7, 2 and 13 bytes in turn. After each piece
 the context is drained until the client's parser has consumed it, so the pieces arrive one at a
 time; then the write side is shut down, which the client reads as eof.
*/
bool send_in_pieces(asio::io_context& io, tcp::socket& server, std::string_view text,
                    const wd::stream_parser& parser) {
    constexpr std::array<std::size_t, 5> sizes{1, 3, 7, 2, 13};
    std::uint64_t sent = 0;
    for (std::size_t turn = 0; !text.empty(); ++turn) {
        const std::string_view piece = text.substr(0, sizes[turn % sizes.size()]);
        text.remove_prefix(piece.size());
        asio::write(server, asio::buffer(piece.data(), piece.size()));
        sent += piece.size();
        if (!drain_until(io, [&parser, sent] { return parser.offset() == sent; })) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    server.shutdown(tcp::socket::shutdown_send);
    return true;
}

The client reads the NDJSON in a coroutine, awaiting async_read_document in a loop until the completion is eof:

/**
 Reads the client's documents until eof, awaiting each read in turn. The parser's finish delivers
 its last document before the eof.
*/
asio::awaitable<void> read_in_coroutine(tcp::socket& client, wd::stream_parser& parser) {
    std::string storage;
    const auto buffer = asio::dynamic_buffer(storage);
    for (;;) {
        auto [ec, made] = co_await wd::async_read_document(client, buffer, parser,
                                                           asio::as_tuple(asio::use_awaitable));
        if (ec == asio::error::eof) {
            std::cout << "eof\n";
            co_return;
        }
        if (ec) {
            std::cout << "error: " << ec.message() << '\n';
            co_return;
        }
        std::cout << made.stringify() << '\n';
    }
}

/** Sends NDJSON over a link and reads it in a coroutine, one document printed per line. */
bool ndjson_in_coroutine(asio::io_context& io, tcp::acceptor& acceptor) {
    std::cout << "NDJSON, read in a coroutine:\n";
    link c(io, acceptor);
    wd::stream_options options;
    options.framing = wd::framing::lines;
    wd::stream_parser parser(options);
    constexpr std::string_view text =
        "{\"id\":1,\"tags\":[\"a\",\"b\"]}\n"
        "{\"id\":2,\"ok\":false}\r\n"
        "\n"
        "[3,null]\n"
        "\"last\"";
    bool done = false;
    asio::co_spawn(io, read_in_coroutine(c.client, parser),
                   [&done](const std::exception_ptr&) { done = true; });
    return send_in_pieces(io, c.server, text, parser) && drain_until(io, [&done] { return done; });
}
NDJSON, read in a coroutine:
{"id":1,"tags":["a","b"]}
{"id":2,"ok":false}
[3,null]
"last"
eof

and the concatenated JSON with a callback, which starts the next read by posting it, so that no read begins inside its own callback. The last document of this stream is the bare number 42, which arrives only when eof makes the reader finish the parser:

/**
 Reads documents with a callback, each read started after the one before it completes. The next
 read is posted rather than called, so no read is started from inside its own callback.
*/
class callback_reader {
public:
    callback_reader(tcp::socket& client, wd::stream_parser& parser, bool& done)
        : client_(client), parser_(parser), done_(done), buffer_(asio::dynamic_buffer(storage_)) {}

    /** Starts the read of the next document. */
    void start() {
        wd::async_read_document(client_, buffer_, parser_,
                                [this](boost::system::error_code ec, const wd::document& made) {
                                    if (ec == asio::error::eof) {
                                        std::cout << "eof\n";
                                        done_ = true;
                                        return;
                                    }
                                    if (ec) {
                                        std::cout << "error: " << ec.message() << '\n';
                                        done_ = true;
                                        return;
                                    }
                                    std::cout << made.stringify() << '\n';
                                    asio::post(client_.get_executor(), [this] { start(); });
                                });
    }

private:
    tcp::socket& client_;
    wd::stream_parser& parser_;
    bool& done_;
    std::string storage_;
    asio::dynamic_string_buffer<char, std::char_traits<char>, std::allocator<char>> buffer_;
};

/** Sends concatenated JSON over a link and reads it with a callback. */
bool concatenated_with_callback(asio::io_context& io, tcp::acceptor& acceptor) {
    std::cout << "concatenated JSON, read with a callback:\n";
    link c(io, acceptor);
    wd::stream_parser parser;
    constexpr std::string_view text =
        "{\"a\":1}    {\"b\":[true,null]}\n"
        "[1][2]\n"
        "{\n  \"c\": \"x\"\n}\n"
        "42";
    bool done = false;
    callback_reader reader(c.client, parser, done);
    reader.start();
    return send_in_pieces(io, c.server, text, parser) && drain_until(io, [&done] { return done; });
}
concatenated JSON, read with a callback:
{"a":1}
{"b":[true,null]}
[1]
[2]
{"c":"x"}
42
eof

After an HTTP header, with Boost.Beast

A response’s header is read with Boost.Beast, and the body that follows it is read as a stream of documents from the same buffer. Beast reads the socket in blocks, so the bytes of the body that arrived with the header are in the buffer when async_read_header returns. They stay there, past the header, and async_read_document takes them before it reads the socket again: nothing is copied out of the buffer, and nothing is lost.

The program below runs a server and a client on the loopback address, in one thread. The client sends a GET, and the server answers with a header that Beast writes and an NDJSON body in pieces. The header and the body’s first piece leave in one write, so the client’s first read holds both, which is the case this section is about:

/**
 Writes `bytes` to the socket; false when the write failed, after printing the error.
*/
asio::awaitable<bool> send_bytes(tcp::socket& socket, std::string_view bytes) {
    auto [ec, sent] = co_await asio::async_write(socket, asio::buffer(bytes.data(), bytes.size()),
                                                 asio::as_tuple(asio::use_awaitable));
    if (ec) {
        std::cout << "server: " << ec.message() << '\n';
        co_return false;
    }
    co_return true;
}

/**
 Answers the client's GET: the response header, written by Beast, and the NDJSON body in pieces of
 2, 5, 3 and 11 bytes; the write side is then shut down, which ends the body for the client, since
 the response has no Content-Length.
*/
asio::awaitable<void> serve(tcp::socket& socket) {
    constexpr std::string_view body =
        "{\"id\":1,\"name\":\"ada\"}\n"
        "{\"id\":2,\"tags\":[\"a\",\"b\"]}\n"
        "[3,null]\n"
        "\"last\"";

    beast::multi_buffer buffer;
    http::request<http::empty_body> request;
    auto [read_ec, read_bytes] =
        co_await http::async_read(socket, buffer, request, asio::as_tuple(asio::use_awaitable));
    if (read_ec) {
        std::cout << "server: " << read_ec.message() << '\n';
        co_return;
    }

    // Without a Content-Length the body ends with the connection, so the connection is not kept.
    http::response<http::empty_body> response{http::status::ok, request.version()};
    response.set(http::field::content_type, "application/x-ndjson");
    response.keep_alive(false);
    std::ostringstream header;
    header << response;

    // The header and the body's first piece leave in one write, so the client's first read can take
    // both: the bytes past the header are then in the client's buffer when Beast returns.
    constexpr std::array<std::size_t, 4> sizes{2, 5, 3, 11};
    std::string_view rest = body;
    std::string first = header.str();
    const std::string_view head_piece = rest.substr(0, sizes[0]);
    rest.remove_prefix(head_piece.size());
    first.append(head_piece);
    if (!co_await send_bytes(socket, first)) {
        co_return;
    }
    for (std::size_t turn = 1; !rest.empty(); ++turn) {
        const std::string_view piece = rest.substr(0, sizes[turn % sizes.size()]);
        rest.remove_prefix(piece.size());
        if (!co_await send_bytes(socket, piece)) {
            co_return;
        }
    }
    socket.shutdown(tcp::socket::shutdown_send);
}

The client reads the header into a beast::multi_buffer with a response_parser<empty_body>, and prints the status and the content type. Beast does not read the body: the same buffer goes on to async_read_document, with the document parser of the stream:

beast::multi_buffer buffer;
http::response_parser<http::empty_body> header;
auto [header_ec, header_bytes] = co_await http::async_read_header(
    socket, buffer, header, asio::as_tuple(asio::use_awaitable));
if (header_ec) {
    std::cout << "client: " << header_ec.message() << '\n';
    co_return;
}
const http::response<http::empty_body>& response = header.get();
std::cout << "status " << response.result_int() << ' ' << response.reason() << '\n';
std::cout << "content type " << response[http::field::content_type] << '\n';
// The buffer may already hold the first bytes of the body: whatever Beast read past the header
// stays in it. The reader writes those bytes into the parser before it reads the socket again,
// so the first document is parsed from them, and nothing is copied out of the buffer.
wd::stream_options options;
options.framing = wd::framing::lines;
wd::stream_parser documents(options);
for (;;) {
    auto [ec, made] = co_await wd::async_read_document(socket, buffer, documents,
                                                       asio::as_tuple(asio::use_awaitable));
    if (ec == asio::error::eof) {
        std::cout << "eof\n";
        co_return;
    }
    if (ec) {
        std::cout << "error: " << ec.message() << '\n';
        co_return;
    }
    std::cout << made.stringify() << '\n';
}
status 200 OK
content type application/x-ndjson
{"id":1,"name":"ada"}
{"id":2,"tags":["a","b"]}
[3,null]
"last"
eof

With Boost.Cobalt

async_read_document takes boost::cobalt::use_op as it takes any token, so a Cobalt task reads a stream of documents in the style of Cobalt, and cobalt::as_result turns the completion into a result whose error is the stream’s, eof included. One task writes the lines in pieces, another reads each document and prints it with its number, until the end of the stream, which the last line ends without a newline:

// Sends the text in pieces of 1, 3, 7, 2 and 13 bytes in turn, then shuts the sending side of the
// connection, which is the end of the stream for the reader.
cobalt::task<void> send(tcp::socket& socket, std::string_view text) {
    constexpr std::array<std::size_t, 5> sizes{1, 3, 7, 2, 13};
    for (std::size_t turn = 0; !text.empty(); ++turn) {
        const std::size_t size = std::min(sizes[turn % sizes.size()], text.size());
        co_await asio::async_write(socket, asio::buffer(text.data(), size), cobalt::use_op);
        text.remove_prefix(size);
    }
    socket.shutdown(tcp::socket::shutdown_send);
}
// Reads the documents one at a time and prints each with its number; the end of the stream is
// eof, which is not an error, and a failure of the stream is printed and ends the reader.
cobalt::task<void> read(tcp::socket& socket) {
    wd::stream_options options;
    options.framing = wd::framing::lines;
    wd::stream_parser parser(options);
    std::string storage;
    const auto buffer = asio::dynamic_buffer(storage);
    std::size_t count = 0;
    for (;;) {
        auto next = co_await cobalt::as_result(
            wd::async_read_document(socket, buffer, parser, cobalt::use_op));
        if (next.has_error()) {
            if (next.error() == asio::error::eof) {
                break;
            }
            std::cout << "error: " << next.error().message() << '\n';
            co_return;
        }
        ++count;
        std::cout << count << ' ' << next->stringify() << '\n';
    }
    std::cout << "eof after " << count << " documents\n";
}
// The connection is made before the coroutines start: the listening socket holds it until accept.
cobalt::main co_main(int /*argc*/, char** /*argv*/) {
    const auto executor = cobalt::this_thread::get_executor();
    tcp::acceptor acceptor(executor, tcp::endpoint(asio::ip::address_v4::loopback(), 0));
    tcp::socket writer(executor);
    tcp::socket reader(executor);
    reader.connect(acceptor.local_endpoint());
    acceptor.accept(writer);
    co_await cobalt::join(send(writer, ndjson), read(reader));
    co_return 0;
}
1 {"name":"Ada","tags":["math"],"n":1500}
2 [1,2.5,null,true,"x"]
3 "plain text"
4 {"z":1,"a":2}
5 {"last":true}
eof after 5 documents

In an actor system

A parser can live inside an actor, because it is sans-IO: the actor gives it bytes and takes its documents. The program below runs two actors on xactor’s FIFO driver, which makes its output the same on every run. The messages are the bytes of the stream, its end, a document the parser completed, and a line it dropped:

/** The bytes of the stream, as the host sends them. */
struct chunk {
    std::string text;
};

/** The end of the stream, which the parser closes. */
struct end_of_stream {};

/** A document the parser completed, moved to the consumer: its image stays where it is. */
struct parsed {
    wd::document value;
};

/** A line the parser dropped, and the line it was on. */
struct rejected {
    std::string reason;
    std::uint64_t line = 0;
};

using message = std::variant<chunk, end_of_stream, parsed, rejected>;

The parser actor writes each chunk it receives to a stream_parser, whose push form hands each document to a callback that sends it to the consumer. The document is moved in the message, and its image stays where it is. A line that is not JSON is dropped, and the actor reports it and goes on:

/** Parses the stream, and sends each document, or each line it drops, to the consumer. */
class parser final : public xactor::actor_logic<message> {
public:
    explicit parser(xactor::actor_ref consumer) : consumer_(consumer), stream_(lines_skipping()) {}

    /** The callback the parser hands each document to, and each dropped line's error. */
    auto hand(xactor::turn<message>& turn) {
        return
            [this, &turn](wd::result<wd::document>&& made) { return relay(turn, std::move(made)); };
    }

    xactor::result<void> handle(xactor::turn<message>& turn,
                                const xactor::envelope<message>& cause) override {
        if (const auto* bytes = std::get_if<chunk>(&cause.payload)) {
            const xactor::result<std::size_t> written = stream_.write(bytes->text, hand(turn));
            return as_void(written);
        }
        if (std::holds_alternative<end_of_stream>(cause.payload)) {
            const xactor::result<std::size_t> finished = stream_.finish(hand(turn));
            return as_void(finished);
        }
        return {};
    }

private:
    /** Sends a completed document, or the reason a line was dropped, to the consumer. */
    xactor::result<void> relay(xactor::turn<message>& turn, wd::result<wd::document>&& made) {
        if (made.has_value()) {
            return turn.send(consumer_, parsed{.value = std::move(*made)});
        }
        return turn.send(consumer_,
                         rejected{.reason = made.error().message(), .line = stream_.error_line()});
    }

    /** Keeps the failure of a call of the parser; the documents it completed went on already. */
    static xactor::result<void> as_void(const xactor::result<std::size_t>& counted) {
        if (!counted.has_value()) {
            return {boost::system::in_place_error, counted.error()};
        }
        return {};
    }

    xactor::actor_ref consumer_;
    wd::stream_parser stream_;
};

The consumer prints what it receives:

/** Prints each document with stringify, and each line the parser dropped. */
class consumer final : public xactor::actor_logic<message> {
public:
    xactor::result<void> handle([[maybe_unused]] xactor::turn<message>& turn,
                                const xactor::envelope<message>& cause) override {
        if (const auto* got = std::get_if<parsed>(&cause.payload)) {
            std::cout << got->value.stringify() << '\n';
        }
        if (const auto* dropped = std::get_if<rejected>(&cause.payload)) {
            std::cout << "line " << dropped->line << " dropped: " << dropped->reason << '\n';
        }
        return {};
    }
};

and the host delivers the chunks one at a time, cut inside a string, a number and a line, and runs the actors until they are idle after each:

xactor::scheduler<message> system(xactor::budgets{.fuel = 100});
const xactor::result<xactor::actor_ref> printing = xactor::create_actor<consumer>(system);
if (!printing.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
const xactor::result<xactor::actor_ref> reading =
    xactor::create_actor<parser>(system, *printing);
if (!reading.has_value()) {
    return 1;
}

// Two documents and a line that is not JSON, in chunks cut inside a string, a number and a
// line; a third document with an exponent, and a last one with no newline after it.
const std::array<std::string_view, 7> pieces{
    R"({"name":"Ad)",
    R"(a","born":181)",
    "5}\n{\"name\":\"Gr",
    R"(ace","langs":["COB)",
    "OL\"]}\nnot j",
    "son\n{\"name\":\"Alan\",\"n\":1.5",
    "e3}\n{\"name\":\"Edsger\"}",
};

xactor::fifo_driver<message> driver(system);
std::uint64_t delivery = 0;
for (const std::string_view piece : pieces) {
    const xactor::correlation_id execution{.value = ++delivery};
    if (!system.deliver(*reading, chunk{.text = std::string(piece)}, execution).has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }
    if (!driver.run_until_idle(nullptr).has_value()) {
        return 1;
    }
}
const xactor::correlation_id execution{.value = ++delivery};
if (!system.deliver(*reading, end_of_stream{}, execution).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
if (!driver.run_until_idle(nullptr).has_value()) {
    return 1;
}
{"name":"Ada","born":1815}
{"name":"Grace","langs":["COBOL"]}
line 3 dropped: malformed JSON text
{"name":"Alan","n":1500}
{"name":"Edsger"}

Fed from JavaScript

A sender written in JavaScript can feed the parser compiled from C++ chunk by chunk, and a ReadableStream such as a response body can be turned into an async iterable of documents. The module that does this is taught in Streams; the program below shows the same parser in a program of your own, compiled with Emscripten, which JavaScript drives through Embind.

The class wraps a stream_parser and holds two JavaScript functions. JavaScript writes the bytes of the stream to it, and its callback runs once for each document that a chunk completes, with the text stringify writes, or for each line it drops, with the line and the message. Embind turns a Uint8Array into the std::string of write, so a chunk may end inside a character:

/**
 A parser of a stream of documents that JavaScript writes to and that calls JavaScript back: the
 callback `on_document` is given each document as the text `stringify` writes, and `on_error` the
 line and the message of an error.

 The framing `lines` is NDJSON, whose bad line is dropped and reported while the stream goes
 on; any other name is a concatenated stream, whose first error ends it.
*/
class json_stream {
public:
    json_stream(const std::string& framing, emscripten::val on_document, emscripten::val on_error)
        : on_document_(std::move(on_document)),
          on_error_(std::move(on_error)),
          parser_(options_of(framing)) {}

    /** Takes a chunk of the stream, and calls back for each document it completes. */
    void write(const std::string& chunk) {
        const wd::result<std::size_t> written =
            parser_.write(chunk, [this](auto made) { deliver(std::move(made)); });
        if (written.has_error()) {
            report(written.error());
        }
    }

    /** Ends the stream, which closes a last line with no newline and a number at the end. */
    void finish() {
        const wd::result<std::size_t> finished =
            parser_.finish([this](auto made) { deliver(std::move(made)); });
        if (finished.has_error()) {
            report(finished.error());
        }
    }

private:
    static wd::stream_options options_of(std::string_view framing) {
        wd::stream_options options;
        if (framing == "lines") {
            options.framing = wd::framing::lines;
            options.on_error = wd::on_error::skip;
        }
        return options;
    }

    /** What the parser gives for each document it completes, or for each line it drops. */
    void deliver(wd::result<wd::document> made) {
        if (made.has_error()) {
            report(made.error());
            return;
        }
        on_document_(made->stringify());
    }

    void report(const boost::system::error_code& error) {
        on_error_(static_cast<unsigned>(parser_.error_line()), error.message());
    }

    emscripten::val on_document_;
    emscripten::val on_error_;
    wd::stream_parser parser_;
};
EMSCRIPTEN_BINDINGS(document_stream_js) {
    emscripten::class_<json_stream>("JsonStream")
        .constructor<const std::string&, emscripten::val, emscripten::val>()
        .function("write", &json_stream::write)
        .function("finish", &json_stream::finish);
}

Node loads the module and sends two streams in chunks, one of NDJSON, whose bad line is dropped and reported while the stream goes on, and one concatenated, whose last number only finish closes. The fifth chunk of the NDJSON stream ends with the byte 0xC3, the first of the two bytes of the é of Zoé:

// Sends a text to a C++ stream in chunks of the given size and prints what each chunk completes.
// The text is encoded first, so that a chunk may end inside a character, as a socket's may.
function send(framing, text, size) {
    let chunk = 0
    const stream = new module.JsonStream(framing,
        document => lines.push(`  chunk ${chunk}: ${document}`),
        (line, message) => lines.push(`  chunk ${chunk}: line ${line} dropped, ${message}`))
    const bytes = encoder.encode(text)
    lines.push(`${framing}, in chunks of ${size} bytes:`)
    for (let at = 0; at < bytes.length; at += size) {
        chunk += 1
        stream.write(bytes.subarray(at, at + size))
    }
    chunk += 1
    stream.finish()
    stream.delete()
}
send('lines', '{"id":1,"tags":["a","b"]}\n{"id":2,"name":"Zoé"}\n{"bad":}\n[3,4.5]\n"last"', 9)
send('concatenated', '{"a":1}    {"b":[2,3]}[4]"five" 6', 4)

Each line it prints says the chunk after which a document arrived. The last line of the NDJSON stream, and the last number of the other, arrive when finish ends the stream, as nothing before ends them:

lines, in chunks of 9 bytes:
  chunk 3: {"id":1,"tags":["a","b"]}
  chunk 6: {"id":2,"name":"Zoé"}
  chunk 7: line 3 dropped, malformed JSON text
  chunk 8: [3,4.5]
  chunk 9: "last"
concatenated, in chunks of 4 bytes:
  chunk 2: {"a":1}
  chunk 6: {"b":[2,3]}
  chunk 7: [4]
  chunk 8: "five"
  chunk 10: 6

The program is a driven test: webcpp.drive builds it with Emscripten and runs Node over it, in the own lane js (Using it from JavaScript), where Node compares what it prints with these lines.

Selectors

A stream of a million records should not need the memory of a million records. A parser’s selectors name places in the text, and deliver each value there as soon as it is complete, while the rest of the text is still to come: on delivers a value and drops it from the document being built, and observe delivers it and keeps it.

The language

A selector is a subset of JSONPath: $, the root, then any sequence of these steps.

Step What it matches

.name

The member name. A name starts with a letter, _, $ or a byte past ASCII, and goes on with those and digits.

['name']

The member name, any key, with \' and \\ as its only escapes.

[n]

The element n, written in decimal without a leading zero.

[*]

Every element of an array.

.*

Every member of an object.

So $.items[*].id matches the id of each element of items. A malformed selector is errc::type, returned by on or observe.

Delivery

A callback takes a wd::const_value, the value, which it reads but cannot change, and a wd::path_view, where the value is in the text, valid during the call; to_string() writes it as a selector of that place, $['items'][0], which on parses back. A key’s ' and \ are escaped and its other bytes written as they are, control characters included, so the text is not RFC 9535’s normalized path. A callback returns void or wd::result<void>. The program sums the quantities of items as they stream, and keeps meta:

/** A callback that prints what it receives and where. */
constexpr auto print = [](const wd::const_value& v, wd::path_view where) {
    std::cout << "  " << where.to_string() << ": " << v.stringify() << '\n';
};
constexpr std::string_view text =
    R"({"meta":{"page":1},"items":[{"id":"a","qty":2},{"id":"b","qty":3}],"done":true})";
wd::parser p;
std::int64_t total = 0;
const wd::result<void> taken =
    p.on("$.items[*]", [&total](const wd::const_value& item, wd::path_view where) {
        print(item, where);
        total += item["qty"].value_or(std::int64_t{0});
    });
const wd::result<void> kept = p.observe("$.meta", print);
if (taken.has_error() || kept.has_error() || p.write(text).has_error()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "total " << total << '\n';
finished(p);
  $['meta']: {"page":1}
  $['items'][0]: {"id":"a","qty":2}
  $['items'][1]: {"id":"b","qty":3}
total 5
finish: {"meta":{"page":1},"items":[],"done":true}

A scalar is delivered when its token ends, and an array or an object when it closes. A value inside another that also matches is delivered first, since it completes first; if on took it, the outer value no longer holds it. A path’s indices are those of the text, which on does not renumber:

wd::parser rows;
if (rows.on("$.rows[*][1]", print).has_error() ||
    rows.observe("$.rows[*]", print).has_error() ||
    rows.write(R"({"rows":[[1,2,3],[4,5,6]]})").has_error()) {
    return 1;
}
finished(rows);
  $['rows'][0][1]: 2
  $['rows'][0]: [1,3]
  $['rows'][1][1]: 5
  $['rows'][1]: [4,6]
finish: {"rows":[[1,3],[4,6]]}

on("$") takes the root, and finish then returns a document that holds undefined. A number at the top of the text completes only when the text ends, since another digit could follow, so it is delivered by finish:

wd::parser whole;
if (whole.on("$", print).has_error() || whole.write("[1,2]").has_error()) {
    return 1;
}
finished(whole);  // the root was taken
whole.reset();    // the selectors stay
if (whole.write("12").has_error()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "12 written\n";  // a number at the top ends only with the text
finished(whole);
  $: [1,2]
finish: undefined
12 written
  $: 12
finish: undefined

A failing callback

A failure a callback returns fails the parser: write returns it, and so does every later call, until reset. In a build with exceptions, an exception a callback throws fails the parser the same way: write or finish rethrows it, and every later call throws it again, until reset.

wd::parser strict;
const wd::result<void> subscribed =
    strict.on("$[*]", [](const wd::const_value& v, wd::path_view) -> wd::result<void> {
        if (!v.is_number()) {
            return wd::errc::type;
        }
        return {};
    });
if (subscribed.has_error()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << "write: " << strict.write(R"([1,"two",3])").error().message() << '\n';
finished(strict);  // a failed parser stays failed until reset
write: a value of another kind
finish: a value of another kind

In bounded memory

A value on takes is erased from the document once delivered, its blocks zeroed and freed, so the next one takes the same room: a stream of any length needs the memory of one element at a time. A callback that must keep a value copies it, into a document of its own, with set or clone.

wd::parser stream;
std::uint64_t count = 0;
if (stream.on("$[*]", [&count](const wd::const_value&, wd::path_view) { ++count; })
        .has_error() ||
    stream.write("[").has_error()) {
    return 1;
}
for (std::uint64_t i = 0; i < 100'000; ++i) {
    const std::string element =
        std::string(i == 0 ? "" : ",") + R"({"id":)" + std::to_string(i) + "}";
    if (stream.write(element).has_error()) {
        return 1;
    }
}
if (stream.write("]").has_error()) {
    return 1;
}
const wd::result<wd::document> streamed = stream.finish();
if (streamed.has_error()) {
    return 1;
}
std::cout << count << " delivered, " << streamed->stringify()
          << " left, image under 64 KiB: " << std::boolalpha
          << (streamed->image().size() < 65'536) << '\n';
100000 delivered, [] left, image under 64 KiB: true

Traits

A document’s traits choose what it stores and how: the C++ types of its scalars, the encoding of its strings, how it writes bytes, and the order of an object’s keys. wd::basic_document<Traits, Storage> takes them first; wd::document is wd::basic_document<wd::default_traits, wd::owned>, and its handles wd::value and wd::const_value are those of the default traits too.

Member wd::default_traits wd::js_traits

boolean

bool

bool

integer

std::int64_t

std::int64_t

number

boost::decimal::decimal128_t: exact, 34 significant digits

double: JavaScript’s own numbers

string

wd::utf8

wd::utf16, as JavaScript holds strings

date

wd::date_ms

wd::date_ms

bytes

wd::base64

wd::javascript_bytes, as JSON.stringify writes a Uint8Array

object

wd::javascript_order

wd::javascript_order

array

wd::dense

wd::dense

js_traits derive from the default traits, and a program’s traits do the same, changing what they need:

/** The default traits, but every key in the order it was created, whatever it is. */
struct insertion_traits : wd::default_traits {
    using object = wd::insertion_order;
};

/** The default traits, but keys sorted by their code units, and bytes written as base64url. */
struct canonical_traits : wd::default_traits {
    using object = wd::sorted;
    using bytes = wd::base64url;
};

Key order parses a text with both, and Bytes writes bytes with the second. The concept wd::document_traits says what traits must give, and a document of traits that do not satisfy it does not compile. This version fixes boolean, integer and date to bool, std::int64_t and wd::date_ms; number is the traits’ choice, a type that satisfies wd::stored_scalar, trivially copyable, of 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 bytes, with a wd::scalar_codec that stores it the same way on every target and a wd::number_codec that reads it from JSON text and writes it as JavaScript writes numbers. string, bytes and object are one of the encodings and policies Strings, dates and bytes and Key order list, and array is wd::dense, the one array policy.

Traits are part of the image

A document’s image records its traits: its header holds a tag that hashes the size and the codec of each scalar, the encoding, the bytes policy and the object policy, with the sizes of the tree’s nodes. An image written with other traits is refused with errc::incompatible_document, never read wrongly (What is refused). Copies between documents need the same traits, and a document’s handles carry them in their type, so a handle of one traits cannot be given to a document of another.

Images

A document lives in one block of memory, its image: a header of 64 bytes, then a heap that holds the tree, its nodes, its indices and its strings. Every pointer inside is an offset from where it is stored, and every size a 64-bit integer, so the image works at any 16-aligned address and has the same bytes on a 64-bit native target and on wasm32. A document can therefore live in memory it does not own, such as a browser’s, be copied as bytes, be written to a file and read back, and travel as binary between a program’s processes. This section teaches the image itself: its bytes, its header, what opening refuses, where it lives and how its size is managed. Images on the wire sends images over streams and Sharing shares them between threads and processes.

The bytes

doc.image() is the image, a std::span<const std::byte> valid until the document’s next change. wd::from_image(bytes) copies an image into a new owned document, from any address; doc.clone() does the same with a document’s own:

wd::result<wd::document> made = wd::parse(R"({"user":"Ada","langs":["Analytical","Note G"]})");
if (made.has_error()) {
    return false;
}
const std::span<const std::byte> image = made->image();
std::cout << image.size() << " bytes, sha-256 " << digest_of(image) << "...\n";

// An owned copy, at another address, which grows as any owned document does.
wd::result<wd::document> copy = wd::from_image(image);
if (copy.has_error() || !(*copy)["user"].set("Lovelace")) {
    return false;
}
std::cout << copy->stringify() << '\n' << made->stringify() << '\n';
4096 bytes, sha-256 ed85084394e7bf7f...
{"user":"Lovelace","langs":["Analytical","Note G"]}
{"user":"Ada","langs":["Analytical","Note G"]}

The same operations give the same image, byte for byte, at any address and on every target: the digest above is the one every target of webcpp’s continuous integration prints, natively with Clang and GCC, on emscripten, and on wasm32-wasip2 and wasm32-wasip3. Free memory is zero: a buffer is zeroed when it is made or grown, a block is zeroed before it is freed, and nodes are built in place. So an erased value, a secret among them, leaves none of its bytes in the image, and the image is a function of the operations alone.

After an operation that failed for want of room, the document’s content is as it was, but bytes of the heap’s free space may differ, where the heap keeps its own bookkeeping: compare documents with ==, not their raw images, after a failure.

The header

The header says what the bytes after it are, in the byte order of the machine that wrote it:

Offset Size Field

0

8

the magic, WCPPDOC and a zero byte

8

4

the format version, 1

12

4

the byte-order mark, 0x01020304 as the writer’s machine writes it

16

4

reserved, zero; an image whose reserved bytes are not zero is refused

20

4

the layout tag: a hash of the sizes and alignments of the tree’s node, its container and the heap, and of the traits (Traits are part of the image)

24

8

the size of the image

32

8

the offset of the tree’s container, the heap’s first block, the same in every image

40

8

the id the next node takes; ids are never reused

48

8

the seal: zero for an image that is not sealed, else the high bit and the CRC-32C of the image, with these eight bytes taken as zero (Sealed images)

56

8

zero

The format version is the library’s: webcpp::document::format_version, which the library raises when the layout of an image changes, and then provides a migration from the previous version. The Boost release an image was written with is not in the header, and a Boost upgrade does not change the version, since the structures the image holds, Boost.Interprocess’s rbtree_best_fit blocks and Boost.MultiIndex’s ordered index nodes, rarely change. The library watches them: its format test compares the compact image of a fixed document, under each traits, with golden images committed with the tests, and fails when a Boost release changes one byte of them. The bytes at offset 16 are kept for a future version.

What is refused

wd::open and wd::from_image refuse bytes shorter than the header or than the size it states, and another magic, with errc::not_a_document; and an image of another format version, byte order, layout tag or nonzero reserved bytes, with errc::incompatible_document. A mismatch is refused, never read or converted. Then the heap’s own check of its structure runs, and a container offset other than the heap’s first block, or a pointer to the root that leaves the image, is errc::not_a_document too, refused before anything is read through it. A sealed image whose bytes do not match its seal is errc::damaged_document, and is checked first of all (Sealed images).

std::cout << "16 zero bytes: " << wd::from_image(std::array<std::byte, 16>{}).error().message()
          << '\n';
std::cout << "other traits: " << wd::from_image<wd::js_traits>(image).error().message() << '\n';
16 zero bytes: not a document's image
other traits: an image of another format, layout, byte order or traits

Each refusal has its own cause, and a program tells them apart by the errc of the error. This program makes one of each and prints the code and the message: an image of other traits, an image of another format version, text that is longer than a header and has no magic, zeroed memory, a buffer that is not 16-aligned (since open reads in place), an image cut short, a header that states a size larger than the bytes it is given, and a header that names a container outside the heap. The last line is the same image cut short after it was sealed (Sealed images):

// An image written with default_traits is no image of js_traits: the layout tag differs.
if (!refused("js_traits", wd::from_image<wd::js_traits>(image))) {
    return false;
}
// The format version is the header's field at offset 8; another version is not read.
std::span<std::byte> bytes = copy_into(storage, image);
set_field(bytes, offsetof(wd::image_header, version), std::uint32_t{2});
if (!refused("format version 2", wd::open(bytes))) {
    return false;
}
// Bytes that are not an image, and are longer than a header, have no magic.
constexpr std::string_view text =
    "this text is not an image, and it is longer than the 64 bytes of a header";
if (!refused("garbage", wd::from_image(std::as_bytes(std::span(text))))) {
    return false;
}
// Memory that was never written reads as zeros, which are no magic either.
alignas(16) std::array<std::byte, 256> zeros{};
if (!refused("zeroed memory", wd::open(zeros))) {
    return false;
}
// open reads the image in place, so its buffer must be 16-aligned: this one starts 8 bytes in.
bytes = copy_into(std::span<std::byte>(storage).subspan(8), image);
if (!refused("misaligned buffer", wd::open(bytes))) {
    return false;
}
// Cut short, an image that is not sealed is no image at all.
bytes = copy_into(storage, image);
if (!refused("truncated, unsealed", wd::open(bytes.first(bytes.size() - 16)))) {
    return false;
}
// A header that states a size larger than the bytes it is given is refused before it is read.
bytes = copy_into(storage, image);
set_field(bytes, offsetof(wd::image_header, size), std::uint64_t{image.size() + 4096});
if (!refused("size", wd::open(bytes.first(image.size())))) {
    return false;
}
// A header that names a container outside the heap is refused before anything is read there.
bytes = copy_into(storage, image);
set_field(bytes, offsetof(wd::image_header, container), std::uint64_t{image.size()});
return refused("container offset", wd::open(bytes));
// Cut short, a sealed image is a torn write: damaged, not merely no image.
std::span<std::byte> bytes = copy_into(storage, made->image());
if (!refused("truncated, sealed", wd::open(bytes.first(bytes.size() - 16)))) {
    return false;
}
js_traits: incompatible_document, an image of another format, layout, byte order or traits
format version 2: incompatible_document, an image of another format, layout, byte order or traits
garbage: not_a_document, not a document's image
zeroed memory: not_a_document, not a document's image
misaligned buffer: not_a_document, not a document's image
truncated, unsealed: not_a_document, not a document's image
size: not_a_document, not a document's image
container offset: not_a_document, not a document's image
truncated, sealed: damaged_document, a sealed image whose bytes do not match its seal

An image is trusted input. Those checks cannot prove sound every offset inside the tree, so an image travels only between a program’s own processes and peers it trusts; untrusted data enters as JSON text, which the parser checks entirely. A seal (Sealed images) catches bytes that changed by accident and is not authentication: never open an image from a source you do not trust.

Owned and external storage

A document’s second template parameter is its storage:

Storage The buffer When it is full

wd::owned, the default

the document’s own, 16-aligned

it grows: a buffer twice the size, or what the operation needs if more, the image copied and the heap grown, up to the max_bytes of create or from_image, 1 GiB unless told otherwise; past it, errc::capacity

wd::external

a std::span<std::byte> its user owns and keeps alive, such as a browser’s memory, 16-aligned

the operation returns errc::capacity and changes nothing

wd::format(buffer) makes a new, empty document in a buffer, holding null; wd::open(buffer) opens the image a buffer holds, in place; wd::parse_into(buffer, text) parses into one. Every operation finds its room before it allocates, so a full buffer is an error value, never a half-made change. A buffer that is not 16-aligned is errc::capacity to format, which finds no room for an image there, and errc::not_a_document to open.

// A buffer the program owns, such as a browser's memory, 16-aligned.
alignas(16) std::array<std::byte, 8192> buffer{};
using external_document = wd::basic_document<wd::default_traits, wd::external>;
wd::result<external_document> formatted = wd::format(buffer);
if (formatted.has_error() || !formatted->root().set(wd::array{})) {
    return false;
}
wd::basic_value<wd::default_traits, wd::external> list = formatted->root();
std::uint64_t pushed = 0;
wd::result<std::uint64_t> length = list.push("an element of the list");
for (; length.has_value(); length = list.push("an element of the list")) {
    ++pushed;
}
const std::string before = formatted->stringify();
std::cout << pushed << " pushed, then: " << length.error().message() << '\n';
// A failed operation changes nothing of the content.
std::cout << "unchanged: " << std::boolalpha
          << (list.splice(0, 1, wd::array{1, 2, 3}).error() == wd::errc::capacity) << ' '
          << (formatted->stringify() == before) << '\n';

// The buffer holds the image, which another document opens in place.
wd::result<external_document> opened = wd::open(buffer);
if (opened.has_error()) {
    return false;
}
std::cout << "opened in place: " << opened->root().size() << " elements\n";
31 pushed, then: no room left
unchanged: true true
opened in place: 31 elements

Reserving

A document that is to be built large grows by doubling: each time the image is full, a buffer twice the size is made, the image is copied into it and the old one is freed. reserve(bytes) is std::vector::reserve for an image: it makes the image hold at least bytes in one step, so that a batch of insertions of a known size moves nothing, and capacity() says how large the image is. A reservation moves the image once, which invalidates every std::string_view read from a value but no handle or iterator, and clears a seal; a reservation within the capacity changes nothing. A request past the document’s max_bytes, or past an external image’s size, is errc::capacity and changes nothing.

This program inserts ten thousand members into two objects, one without a reservation and one with a reservation of 256 bytes a member, and asks whether the image grew:

// The batch's size is known, so the image is reserved once, before the insertions: they then
// move nothing. Without the reservation, the same insertions grow the image.
