constexpr std::int64_t batch = 10'000;
constexpr std::uint64_t bytes_per_member = 256;

wd::result<wd::document> plain_made = wd::parse("{}");
if (plain_made.has_error()) {
    return fail(plain_made);
}
wd::document& plain = *plain_made;
wd::result<wd::object_ref> as_plain = plain.root().as_object();
if (as_plain.has_error()) {
    return fail(as_plain);
}
const std::uint64_t plain_before = plain.capacity();
for (std::int64_t i = 0; i < batch; ++i) {
    const auto added = as_plain->insert("k" + std::to_string(i), i);
    if (added.has_error()) {
        return fail(added);
    }
}
std::cout << "without reserve, " << batch
          << " insertions grew the image: " << (plain.capacity() != plain_before) << '\n';

wd::result<wd::document> reserved_made = wd::parse("{}");
if (reserved_made.has_error()) {
    return fail(reserved_made);
}
wd::document& reserved = *reserved_made;
wd::result<wd::object_ref> as_reserved = reserved.root().as_object();
if (as_reserved.has_error()) {
    return fail(as_reserved);
}
const std::uint64_t reserved_before = reserved.capacity();
const auto reservation = reserved.reserve(static_cast<std::uint64_t>(batch) * bytes_per_member);
if (reservation.has_error()) {
    return fail(reservation);
}
const std::uint64_t reserved_capacity = reserved.capacity();
std::cout << "reserve grew the image: " << (reserved_capacity != reserved_before) << '\n';
for (std::int64_t i = 0; i < batch; ++i) {
    const auto added = as_reserved->insert("k" + std::to_string(i), i);
    if (added.has_error()) {
        return fail(added);
    }
}
std::cout << "after the reserve, " << batch
          << " insertions grew it: " << (reserved.capacity() != reserved_capacity) << '\n';
without reserve, 10000 insertions grew the image: true
reserve grew the image: true
after the reserve, 10000 insertions grew it: false

Shrinking

A document that is parsed starts at 4096 bytes, and a document that is built grows from there as it needs. doc.shrink_to_fit() gives back the free space at the end of an owned image, and only that: blocks are never moved, so a value that sits at the end of the heap keeps the image as large as its end. For a small document it is the whole story, a few values shrinking to little more than a kilobyte. For a document that grew and then let its values go, it may leave an image nearly as large as it was, and a deep copy into a new document packs the content, as compact does in place (Compacting):

wd::result<wd::document> made = wd::parse("{}");
if (made.has_error()) {
    return false;
}
for (std::uint64_t i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) {
    if (!(*made)[std::to_string(i)].set(std::string(100, 'x'))) {
        return false;
    }
}
const std::uint64_t grown = made->image().size();
if (!made->root().set(wd::object{{"kept", true}}) || !made->shrink_to_fit()) {
    return false;
}
std::cout << "grown to " << grown << " bytes, shrunk to " << made->image().size() << ": "
          << made->stringify() << '\n';

// Blocks never move: a deep copy into a new document packs the content.
wd::result<wd::document> packed = wd::document::create();
if (packed.has_error() || !packed->root().set(*made)) {
    return false;
}
std::cout << "packed: " << packed->image().size() << " bytes\n";
grown to 524288 bytes, shrunk to 352864: {"kept":true}
packed: 4096 bytes

Compacting

doc.compact() rebuilds an owned image as the compact image of its content: the nodes in document order, their ids numbered from the first, each block right after the last with no hole between, and the image exactly as large as they are. Where shrink_to_fit can only trim the free tail, compact takes out every hole, so a document that lost most of its values is smaller compacted than shrunk. Measured, the same on a 64-bit target and on wasm32: a small document of 60 members after 54 of them were erased is 15,312 bytes after shrink_to_fit and 2,352 after compact; a large one, with 90% of its members erased, is 2,080,304 bytes and 209,424.

Compacting also makes the image a function of the content alone. Two documents of equal content have byte-identical images after it, whatever edits made them, whether they were parsed, or built by set, erase and splice, or had values replaced; and a compact image compacts to itself. Equal documents can then be compared, hashed or stored by their bytes, and a seal over a compact image is the same everywhere.

compact_size() is the exact size of the compact image, which it reads from the nodes without allocating anything, so a program sizes a block with it before it builds the image. compact_into(buffer) writes the compact image into a 16-aligned buffer of the program’s own and opens it there, as an external document, zeroing the rest of the buffer and leaving the document as it was: it is the way to compact a document that cannot reallocate, such as one leased from a pool or held in a shared block, or to send an image without waste. It is errc::capacity for a buffer that is smaller than compact_size() or not aligned, and writes nothing then.

Compacting removes holes, not the 192 bytes of each node (Memory per value), so it does not change how an image compares in size with the JSON text of the same document (The sizes on the wire).

compact() builds the new image before it replaces the old one, so a failure changes nothing. As a vector’s reallocation does, it invalidates every handle, every std::string_view read from a value and every iterator, and, the bytes having changed, it clears a seal: sealing again is the caller’s. The image’s size afterwards is compact_size(), which is also its capacity(), so the next change that needs room grows it.

A moved document takes the image of the one it is moved from, which then holds nothing: its handles, and those of the document moved into, are invalid.

Images on the wire

A document is its image, and its image can be sent as it is: the sender writes the bytes, and the receiver reads them into a block of memory and opens the document there. Nothing is parsed, no tree is built, and nothing is allocated for the values or for the message; the receiver’s work is the copy of the bytes off the stream and, for a sealed image, one pass to check the seal. JSON text needs a parse on arrival and allocates for each value it holds.

That is the use document’s image is built for, between programs that trust each other: a page and its Worker, the threads of a process, the processes of a machine, two machines on a fast local link whose receiver’s CPU is the bottleneck (Binary transmission). It is not the use for a narrow network: an image is many times the size of its JSON text, and larger than the compressed text (The sizes on the wire), so there the text is the smaller payload. The benchmarks measure what the receiver saves on each side of the trade (Reading the results).

This section sends images over a stream with Boost.Asio and receives them into a pool of blocks; sealing them, what a reader refuses and how big a block must be follow. Sharing shares images between threads and processes without any stream.

An image frames itself

An image states its size in its header (The header), so a stream of images needs no separator and no length prefix: the images follow one another, and a reader that has the first 64 bytes of one knows where it ends. wd::async_write_image(stream, doc, token) seals the document and writes its image as one buffer. wd::async_read_image(stream, pool, token) reads the header of the next image into a block of a pool, checks it before it reads another byte, reads the rest of the image into the same block and opens the document there. It reads exactly the bytes the image needs, so the stream is left at the end of the image it completed.

Both are composed operations of Boost.Asio, in <webcpp/document/asio.hpp>, which take any completion token, and are built natively only, as the rest of that header is (With Boost.Asio). async_write_image completes with an error_code; async_read_image completes with an error_code and a wd::leased_document<>, which holds the document and the block it lives in.

Pools of blocks

wd::image_pool::create(block_bytes, blocks) allocates a pool once: blocks blocks of block_bytes bytes each, 16-aligned and zeroed, in one allocation. A block is leased to each image a reader receives, and goes back when the leased_document that holds it goes, its bytes zeroed. The pool therefore allocates nothing per message; a receiver that can hold two images at once makes a pool of two blocks:

/** A pool of two blocks: the most the client leases at once. */
wd::image_pool pool_of_two() {
    return wd::image_pool::create(block_bytes, 2).value();
}

When every block is leased, async_read_image completes with errc::capacity and reads nothing: this is the backpressure of a stream of images, and the stream is read again when a block is given back. A pool outlives its leases and its readers, and is not thread-safe: a block is leased and given back, a lease destroyed included, on one thread at a time. For blocks that threads and processes share, see Shared documents.

A leased_document is moved, never copied, and reads and writes as any document does within its image; a change that needs more room than its block has returns errc::capacity. The sans-IO wd::image_reader under async_read_image is the same reader without Asio: write(bytes) takes the bytes of a stream and opens each image they complete, and prepare() and commit() let a socket read straight into the block, with no copy at all.

Sizing a block

A block holds the largest image the pool will receive, a multiple of 16 and at least 64: an image larger than a block is refused with errc::capacity. What a document costs on the wire is its image, whatever it holds.

A document that is parsed starts at 4096 bytes, as the parser gives it room, so a document of a few values sent as it is travels as 4096 bytes. shrink_to_fit() gives back the free space at the end of the image, and only that: for a small document it brings the image down to little more than a kilobyte (Shrinking). compact() rebuilds the image with no hole in it, and compact_size() says how large that image is before it is built (Compacting), so a program sizes its blocks, and what it sends, to what a document holds. This function makes the documents of the next example, parsing each and shrinking it before it is sent:

/**
 A document parsed from JSON text and shrunk to its size, so that its image holds what the document
 needs and no more.
*/
wd::document document_of(std::string_view text) {
    wd::document made = wd::parse_or_throw(text);
    // A shrink that fails leaves the document as valid as it was, only larger.
    static_cast<void>(made.shrink_to_fit());
    return made;
}

/** The documents the server sends, in order. */
std::vector<wd::document> documents() {
    std::vector<wd::document> sent;
    sent.push_back(document_of(ada));
    sent.push_back(document_of(grace));
    sent.push_back(document_of(alan));
    return sent;
}

Sending and receiving

The example sends three documents over a connection on the loopback address, in one program, and receives them twice, once in a coroutine and once with a callback. The receiver prints each document with stringify while its image is held in its block, whether the image is sealed, and the blocks the pool has free then:

/**
 Prints a document as the client holds it: its text, whether its image is sealed, and the blocks the
 pool has free while the image's block is leased.
*/
void print_held(const wd::leased_document<>& image, const wd::image_pool& pool) {
    std::cout << image.get().stringify() << ": " << (image.sealed() ? "sealed" : "not sealed")
              << ", blocks available: " << pool.available() << '\n';
}

The coroutine sends each image, awaiting each write, and shuts the write side down at the end, which the reader sees as eof. The receiver awaits async_read_image in a loop. Each image is printed while its block is leased, and the block goes back when the iteration ends:

/** Sends each document's image, awaiting each write, then shuts the write side down. */
asio::awaitable<void> send_in_coroutine(tcp::socket& server, std::vector<wd::document>& sent) {
    for (wd::document& document : sent) {
        auto [ec] =
            co_await wd::async_write_image(server, document, asio::as_tuple(asio::use_awaitable));
        if (ec) {
            std::cout << "error: " << ec.message() << '\n';
            co_return;
        }
    }
    server.shutdown(tcp::socket::shutdown_send);
}

/**
 Receives images until eof, awaiting each read in turn. Each image is printed while its block is
 leased, and the block goes back when the loop's iteration ends.
*/
asio::awaitable<void> receive_in_coroutine(tcp::socket& client, wd::image_pool& pool, bool& done) {
    for (;;) {
        auto [ec, image] =
            co_await wd::async_read_image(client, pool, asio::as_tuple(asio::use_awaitable));
        if (ec == asio::error::eof) {
            std::cout << "eof, blocks available: " << pool.available() << '\n';
            done = true;
            co_return;
        }
        if (ec) {
            std::cout << "error: " << ec.message() << '\n';
            done = true;
            co_return;
        }
        print_held(image, pool);
    }
}

/** Sends the documents over a link and receives them in a coroutine. */
bool images_in_coroutine(asio::io_context& io, tcp::acceptor& acceptor,
                         std::vector<wd::document>& sent) {
    std::cout << "images, received in a coroutine:\n";
    link c(io, acceptor);
    wd::image_pool pool = pool_of_two();
    bool done = false;
    asio::co_spawn(io, send_in_coroutine(c.server, sent), asio::detached);
    asio::co_spawn(io, receive_in_coroutine(c.client, pool, done), asio::detached);
    return drain_until(io, [&done] { return done; });
}
images, received in a coroutine:
{"name":"Ada","born":1815,"langs":["Analytical"]}: sealed, blocks available: 1
{"name":"Grace","langs":["COBOL"]}: sealed, blocks available: 1
{"name":"Alan","n":1500}: sealed, blocks available: 1
eof, blocks available: 2

With a pool of two blocks and one document held, one block is free, and at eof both are. With callbacks, the next write and the next read are posted rather than called, so that none starts inside the callback of the one before it:

/**
 Sends each document's image with async_write_image, the next one started after the last one
 completed, then shuts the write side down. The next write is posted, not called, so that no write
 starts inside the callback of the one before it.
*/
class callback_sender {
public:
    callback_sender(tcp::socket& server, std::vector<wd::document>& sent)
        : server_(server), sent_(sent) {}

    /** Starts the first write. */
    void start() { send_next(); }

private:
    void send_next() {
        if (next_ == sent_.size()) {
            server_.shutdown(tcp::socket::shutdown_send);
            return;
        }
        wd::async_write_image(server_, sent_[next_], [this](boost::system::error_code ec) {
            if (ec) {
                std::cout << "error: " << ec.message() << '\n';
                return;
            }
            ++next_;
            asio::post(server_.get_executor(), [this] { send_next(); });
        });
    }

    tcp::socket& server_;
    std::vector<wd::document>& sent_;
    std::size_t next_ = 0;
};

/**
 Receives images with async_read_image, the next read started after the last one completed, until
 eof. The image is printed inside its callback, where its block is leased; the block goes back when
 the callback returns.
*/
class callback_receiver {
public:
    callback_receiver(tcp::socket& client, wd::image_pool& pool, bool& done)
        : client_(client), pool_(pool), done_(done) {}

    /** Starts the first read. */
    void start() { read_next(); }

private:
    void read_next() {
        wd::async_read_image(
            client_, pool_, [this](boost::system::error_code ec, wd::leased_document<> image) {
                if (ec == asio::error::eof) {
                    std::cout << "eof, blocks available: " << pool_.available() << '\n';
                    done_ = true;
                    return;
                }
                if (ec) {
                    std::cout << "error: " << ec.message() << '\n';
                    done_ = true;
                    return;
                }
                print_held(image, pool_);
                asio::post(client_.get_executor(), [this] { read_next(); });
            });
    }

    tcp::socket& client_;
    wd::image_pool& pool_;
    bool& done_;
};

/** Sends the documents over a link and receives them with a callback. */
bool images_with_callback(asio::io_context& io, tcp::acceptor& acceptor,
                          std::vector<wd::document>& sent) {
    std::cout << "images, received with a callback:\n";
    link c(io, acceptor);
    wd::image_pool pool = pool_of_two();
    bool done = false;
    callback_sender sender(c.server, sent);
    callback_receiver receiver(c.client, pool, done);
    sender.start();
    receiver.start();
    return drain_until(io, [&done] { return done; });
}
images, received with a callback:
{"name":"Ada","born":1815,"langs":["Analytical"]}: sealed, blocks available: 1
{"name":"Grace","langs":["COBOL"]}: sealed, blocks available: 1
{"name":"Alan","n":1500}: sealed, blocks available: 1
eof, blocks available: 2

Several images in one write

wd::async_write_images(stream, documents, token) writes the images of a range of documents in one gather write. Every document is sealed first, and when one fails to seal the operation completes with its error and writes nothing. The images are not copied: Boost.Asio sends them with writev and carries on over partial writes. The operation completes with the bytes written, which are the sum of the images’ sizes; on an error, they are the bytes that reached the stream, and the whole documents among them are the leading ones whose images fit in that count. The range is taken by lvalue reference, and its documents stay unchanged until the write completes. The example sends its three documents this way:

/**
 Sends the three images in one gather write with async_write_images, then receives them in a
 coroutine, as the first exchange does.

 Tip: the write reads the images in place and completes with the bytes it wrote, so the documents
 stay unchanged until it completes.
*/
bool images_in_one_write(asio::io_context& io, tcp::acceptor& acceptor,
                         std::vector<wd::document>& sent) {
    std::cout << "images, sent in one write:\n";
    link c(io, acceptor);
    wd::image_pool pool = pool_of_two();
    bool done = false;
    wd::async_write_images(c.server, sent, [&c](boost::system::error_code ec, std::size_t bytes) {
        if (ec) {
            std::cout << "error: " << ec.message() << '\n';
        } else {
            std::cout << "written: " << bytes << " bytes\n";
        }
        c.server.shutdown(tcp::socket::shutdown_send);
    });
    asio::co_spawn(io, receive_in_coroutine(c.client, pool, done), asio::detached);
    return drain_until(io, [&done] { return done; });
}
images, sent in one write:
written: 4176 bytes
{"name":"Ada","born":1815,"langs":["Analytical"]}: sealed, blocks available: 1
{"name":"Grace","langs":["COBOL"]}: sealed, blocks available: 1
{"name":"Alan","n":1500}: sealed, blocks available: 1
eof, blocks available: 2

Sealed images

doc.seal() writes a seal into the image’s header: the CRC-32C (Castagnoli) of the image’s bytes, with the seal’s own eight bytes taken as zero, and a marker in the high bit. async_write_image seals the document it sends. Opening a sealed image, with wd::open, wd::from_image or the image reader, checks the seal first of all, before anything else its header states is trusted, and refuses an image whose bytes do not match with errc::damaged_document. A flipped bit on a disk or a wire, a torn write, a stray write over a buffer and an image cut short are all damage, and none of the image is read:

// A sealed image with one byte changed is refused as damaged, by open and by from_image.
const auto found =
    std::ranges::search(bytes, std::as_bytes(std::span(std::string_view("Ada"))));
if (found.empty()) {
    return false;
}
found.front() = std::byte{'a'};
if (!refused("one byte changed", wd::open(bytes))) {
    return false;
}
one byte changed: damaged_document, a sealed image whose bytes do not match its seal

The seal holds until the document’s next change, which clears it: an image is then simply not sealed, never wrongly sealed, and sealed() says which. It costs a pass over the image, about 600 MB/s, and checking it when the image is opened costs the same. A program that trusts its memory, such as one that opens an image it has just written, skips the check with wd::verify::none. The changed byte of the example then reads as it is:

// verify::none skips the seal: the caller trusts the source, and the changed byte reads as is.
wd::result<wd::document> trusted =
    wd::from_image(bytes, wd::default_max_bytes, wd::verify::none);
if (trusted.has_error()) {
    return false;
}
std::cout << "verify::none, accepted: " << trusted->stringify() << '\n';
verify::none, accepted: {"user":"ada","langs":["Analytical","Note G"]}

A sealed image left in reused memory, which a later use wrote over in part, is refused too, since the seal shows that the bytes changed since the image was written. An image that is not damaged opens in place, and is still sealed:

// An old sealed image left in memory, which a later use wrote over in part, is refused as
// damaged: the seal shows that the bytes changed since the image was written.
bytes = copy_into(storage, made->image());
std::ranges::fill(bytes.subspan(2048, 64), std::byte{0xAA});
if (!refused("reused memory", wd::open(bytes))) {
    return false;
}
// An intact sealed image opens in place, and is still sealed.
bytes = copy_into(storage, made->image());
wd::result<wd::basic_document<wd::default_traits, wd::external>> opened = wd::open(bytes);
if (opened.has_error()) {
    return false;
}
std::cout << "opened, sealed " << std::boolalpha << opened->sealed() << ": "
          << opened->stringify() << '\n';
reused memory: damaged_document, a sealed image whose bytes do not match its seal
opened, sealed true: {"user":"Ada","langs":["Analytical","Note G"]}

A seal is a checksum against accidental damage, and is not authentication. Anyone can compute a valid seal for any bytes, so a sealed image from a source that is not trusted is no safer than an unsealed one. Never open an image from an untrusted source: the checks of What is refused cannot prove sound every offset inside a tree, and an image travels only between programs that trust each other. Untrusted data enters as JSON text, which the parser checks entirely.

What a reader refuses

The completion of async_read_image says what happened, and on every error the lease it carries is empty:

Error When

none

An image was read and opened; the lease holds it.

asio::error::eof

The stream ended between two images.

errc::capacity

Every block of the pool is leased, and the stream is not read; or an image is larger than a block. The end of the stream is reported this way too while the pool is full, since the reader needs a block to learn that the stream ended.

errc::not_a_document

Bytes that are not an image, or an image whose heap is not sound.

errc::incompatible_document

An image of another format version, byte order, reserved bytes or traits.

errc::damaged_document

A sealed image whose bytes do not match its seal.

another

The error of a read.

The refusal of an image ends the reader, as an error ends a stream of documents (Errors), because a stream of images that has lost its place cannot find the next header. The refusals are the ones of What is refused, which that section shows one by one.

Sharing

JavaScript shares an object by sharing a reference to it, and its collector decides when the object goes. A C++ program that shares a document between threads or processes needs the same two things, a reference that several holders have and a moment when the last one lets go, and document gives them without a collector and without copying the document. Its image is relocatable and holds offsets, not addresses, so it is the same bytes in every thread and in every process that maps it, at whatever address.

Threads

A document that moves from one thread to another moves its handle and never the bytes of its image. A producer parses documents and pushes each into a queue; the consumer receives them and keeps them. The queue is the program’s, of any kind; this one wakes the consumer on a push and tells it when nothing more comes:

// A queue for one producer and one consumer: a push wakes the consumer, and close tells it that
// nothing more comes.
template <class T>
class queue {
public:
    void push(T value) {
        {
            const std::scoped_lock lock(mutex_);
            items_.push_back(std::move(value));
        }
        ready_.notify_one();
    }

    void close() {
        {
            const std::scoped_lock lock(mutex_);
            closed_ = true;
        }
        ready_.notify_all();
    }

    // The oldest value, waiting while the queue is open; nothing once it is closed and empty.
    std::optional<T> pop() {
        std::unique_lock lock(mutex_);
        ready_.wait(lock, [this] { return closed_ || !items_.empty(); });
        if (items_.empty()) {
            return std::nullopt;
        }
        T value = std::move(items_.front());
        items_.pop_front();
        return value;
    }

private:
    std::mutex mutex_;
    std::condition_variable ready_;
    std::deque<T> items_;
    bool closed_ = false;
};

What the producer sends is the document and the address of its image before the push, so that the consumer can show the image did not move:

// What the producer sends: a document, and the address of its image before the push. Moving a
// document moves its handle and never the bytes of its image, so the consumer finds them there.
struct parcel {
    wd::document doc;
    const std::byte* image = nullptr;
};

// What the consumer keeps: the documents in arrival order, how many of them still have their image
// where the producer left it, and how many texts failed to parse.
struct exchanged {
    std::vector<wd::document> documents;
    std::size_t same_image = 0;
    std::size_t failed = 0;
};

// The producer parses each text and pushes the document; the consumer keeps each one it receives.
// The two threads write different members of the result, and main reads it after both are joined.
exchanged through_a_queue(std::array<std::string_view, 3> texts) {
    queue<parcel> arrivals;
    exchanged result;
    std::thread consumer([&arrivals, &result] {
        while (std::optional<parcel> next = arrivals.pop()) {
            if (next->doc.image().data() == next->image) {
                ++result.same_image;
            }
            result.documents.push_back(std::move(next->doc));
        }
    });
    std::thread producer([&arrivals, &result, texts] {
        for (const std::string_view text : texts) {
            wd::result<wd::document> parsed = wd::parse(text);
            if (parsed.has_error()) {
                ++result.failed;
                continue;
            }
            const std::byte* image = parsed->image().data();
            arrivals.push(parcel{.doc = std::move(*parsed), .image = image});
        }
        arrivals.close();
    });
    producer.join();
    consumer.join();
    return result;
}
queue: 3 received, 3 with the image the producer sent, 0 failed to parse
{"id":1,"name":"Ada"}
[1,2,3]
{"id":3,"tags":["queue","thread"]}

Every document arrived with the image the producer sent: no byte was copied and nothing was parsed on the consumer’s side.

Shared documents

Several threads that read one document share it with wd::shared_document<>, which is std::shared_ptr for a document: copies share one image, a count says how many hold it, and the last holder to let go gives the image back. The images live in the blocks of a wd::shared_pool, over a region of memory the program gives, the process heap or a segment of shared memory. A pool is formatted once, wd::shared_pool::format(region, block_bytes), with a 16-aligned region; its region_bytes(block_bytes, blocks) sizes the region for a number of blocks, blocks(), block_bytes() and available() describe it, and wd::shared_pool::attach(region) is how another view of the same region, in this thread or another process, joins it.

A block is a header of 64 bytes, which holds the count of references to its image, and the room of one image. The pool works through offsets from the region’s start and never addresses, its counts are lock-free atomics and its free blocks a lock-free stack: no lock is held at any moment, so no thread or process waits on another, and one that dies leaves no lock behind. A block that is free is all zero, and a block given back is zeroed.

shared_document<>::from_image(pool, bytes) copies an image into a free block, create(pool) makes a new empty document in one, and use_count() says how many hold the document, in every process. Copying a shared_document adds a reference, destroying one drops it, and a reader takes a const reference and never writes. A reader holds its copy until it returns:

// The name and birth year of a shared document, read through a const reference: a reader never
// writes.
std::string describe(const wd::shared_document<>& doc) {
    return std::string(doc["name"].value_or(std::string_view("nobody"))) + " was born in " +
           std::to_string(doc["born"].value_or(std::int64_t{0}));
}

// A reader holds its copy until it returns, then drops it in its own thread.
void reader_task(const wd::shared_document<>& holder, std::string& out) {
    out = describe(holder);
}

The image of a parsed document keeps the room the parser gave it, 4096 bytes at first, and a block of 2048 would refuse it, so the example shrinks the image to its content before it copies it into the pool (Shrinking). Four readers then share the document, and the count is the number of holders:

// The image is copied into a block of the pool; the document it makes holds the one reference.
wd::result<wd::shared_document<>> stored =
    wd::shared_document<>::from_image(pool, parsed->image());
if (stored.has_error()) {
    std::cout << "error: " << stored.error().message() << '\n';
    return 1;
}
wd::shared_document<> shared = std::move(*stored);
std::cout << "stored: use_count " << shared.use_count() << ", " << pool.available() << " of "
          << pool.blocks() << " blocks free\n";

// Each reader gets its copy here, before any thread starts, so the count printed is exact.
constexpr std::size_t reader_count = 4;
std::vector<wd::shared_document<>> copies(reader_count, shared);
std::cout << "with " << reader_count << " readers: use_count " << shared.use_count() << '\n';

std::array<std::string, reader_count> read{};
std::vector<std::thread> readers;
readers.reserve(reader_count);
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < reader_count; ++i) {
    readers.emplace_back(reader_task, std::move(copies[i]), std::ref(read[i]));
}
for (std::thread& reader : readers) {
    reader.join();
}
std::cout << "after the readers: use_count " << shared.use_count() << ", " << pool.available()
          << " of " << pool.blocks() << " blocks free\n";
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < reader_count; ++i) {
    std::cout << "reader " << i << ": " << read[i] << '\n';
}
pool: 7 blocks of 2048 bytes
stored: use_count 1, 6 of 7 blocks free
with 4 readers: use_count 5
after the readers: use_count 1, 6 of 7 blocks free
reader 0: Ada was born in 1815
reader 1: Ada was born in 1815
reader 2: Ada was born in 1815
reader 3: Ada was born in 1815

Copy on write

A holder that wants to write calls make_mutable(). When it is the only holder, the document is its own and nothing happens. When others hold the image, make_mutable copies it into a free block of its own, the copy including the seal, and the holder changes the copy while the others keep the document as it was. It is errc::capacity when every block is leased.

The library does not synchronise writers. A block that has several writers, or a writer and readers of that same block, must wait for each other by the program’s own means, such as a mutex; the writer below changes only the copy that make_mutable made, which no other holder reads:

// make_mutable copies the image into a block of the writer's own when other holders exist, so the
// writer changes its copy and the others keep the document as it was. The library does not
// synchronise writers: a block with several writers, or a writer and readers of that same block,
// must wait for each other by the program's own means, such as a mutex. This writer changes only
// its copy, which no other holder reads.
void writer_task(wd::shared_document<> holder, std::string& out) {
    if (holder.make_mutable().has_error() || holder["name"].set("Lovelace").has_error()) {
        out = "error";
        return;
    }
    out = describe(holder);
}
// The writer takes its reference before its thread starts; its change leaves the shared
// document, which main still reads, as it was.
wd::shared_document<> writer_copy = shared;
std::string written;
std::thread writer(writer_task, std::move(writer_copy), std::ref(written));
writer.join();
std::cout << "writer: " << written << '\n';
std::cout << "after the writer: " << describe(shared) << ", use_count " << shared.use_count()
          << ", " << pool.available() << " of " << pool.blocks() << " blocks free\n";

// The last copy gives its block back to the pool, zeroed.
shared = wd::shared_document<>();
std::cout << "last copy dropped: " << pool.available() << " of " << pool.blocks()
          << " blocks free\n";
writer: Lovelace was born in 1815
after the writer: Ada was born in 1815, use_count 1, 6 of 7 blocks free
last copy dropped: 7 of 7 blocks free

The change was made to the writer’s copy, so the document that main holds still reads Ada, and the last holder to let go returned its block to the pool.

Processes

A pool in a segment of shared memory is shared by processes, each of which maps the segment at an address of its own, and a document is passed between them by the offset of its image. The program below is its own consumer: the producer formats a pool of eight blocks of 4096 bytes in Boost.Interprocess’s shared memory, parses or builds four documents in blocks of it, seals each, and sends the offsets through a message queue, and then runs itself again as the consumer, which attaches to the same segment. The constants say how many blocks and how large, and the end of the stream is an offset no image has:

// The room of each block's image, and the blocks of the pool: 8 blocks of 4096 bytes, the size of
// a parsed document's image.
constexpr std::size_t block_bytes = 4096;
constexpr std::size_t blocks = 8;

// The queue holds every offset at once, the end of the stream included.
constexpr std::size_t queue_messages = 8;

// The end of the stream: no document's image is at offset 0.
constexpr std::uint64_t end_of_stream = 0;

The producer makes each document in a block of the pool. release() gives up the producer’s reference without dropping it, and returns the offset of the image, which is the document now as far as the consumer is concerned:

// The document a JSON text makes: parsed, its image copied into a block of the pool, then sealed.
wd::result<wd::shared_document<>> sealed_from_text(wd::shared_pool pool, std::string_view text) {
    wd::result<wd::document> parsed = wd::parse(text);
    if (parsed.has_error()) {
        return parsed.error();
    }
    wd::result<wd::shared_document<>> made =
        wd::shared_document<>::from_image(pool, parsed->image());
    if (made.has_error()) {
        return made.error();
    }
    if (made->seal().has_error()) {
        return wd::errc::type;
    }
    return made;
}

// Releases a document's reference and sends its offset, the document now the consumer's.
void hand_over(bip::message_queue& queue, wd::shared_document<>& doc) {
    const std::uint64_t offset = doc.release();
    queue.send(&offset, sizeof offset, 0);
}

// The producer: it makes the documents, hands each over and runs the consumer, which prints them.
int produce(const char* program) {
    const names run = names_for(std::to_string(bip::ipcdetail::get_current_process_id()));
    remove_names(run);
    const remover cleanup(run);

    const wd::result<std::size_t> size = wd::shared_pool::region_bytes(block_bytes, blocks);
    if (size.has_error()) {
        std::cout << "error: " << size.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    bip::shared_memory_object memory(bip::create_only, run.segment.c_str(), bip::read_write);
    memory.truncate(static_cast<bip::offset_t>(*size));
    const bip::mapped_region mapped(memory, bip::read_write);
    const std::span<std::byte> bytes(static_cast<std::byte*>(mapped.get_address()),
                                     mapped.get_size());
    const wd::result<wd::shared_pool> formatted = wd::shared_pool::format(bytes, block_bytes);
    if (formatted.has_error()) {
        std::cout << "error: " << formatted.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    const wd::shared_pool pool = *formatted;
    bip::message_queue queue(bip::create_only, run.queue.c_str(), queue_messages,
                             sizeof(std::uint64_t));

    // Three documents parsed or built in place, and a fourth whose sealed image is then damaged.
    wd::result<wd::shared_document<>> ada =
        sealed_from_text(pool, R"({"name":"Ada","born":1815,"langs":["Analytical"]})");
    wd::result<wd::shared_document<>> grace =
        sealed_from_text(pool, R"({"name":"Grace","langs":["COBOL"]})");
    wd::result<wd::shared_document<>> alan = wd::shared_document<>::create(pool);
    wd::result<wd::shared_document<>> edsger = sealed_from_text(pool, R"({"name":"Edsger"})");
    if (ada.has_error() || grace.has_error() || alan.has_error() || edsger.has_error()) {
        std::cout << "error: a document could not be made\n";
        return 1;
    }
    if (alan->root().set(wd::object{{"name", "Alan"}, {"n", 1500}}).has_error() ||
        alan->seal().has_error()) {
        std::cout << "error: a document could not be made\n";
        return 1;
    }

    // One byte of the sealed image changes after the seal; any change breaks a seal.
    constexpr std::size_t damaged_byte = 100;
    pool.region()[edsger->offset() + damaged_byte] ^= std::byte{0xff};

    hand_over(queue, *ada);
    hand_over(queue, *grace);
    hand_over(queue, *alan);
    hand_over(queue, *edsger);
    queue.send(&end_of_stream, sizeof end_of_stream, 0);

    std::cout << "available before the consumer: " << pool.available() << '\n' << std::flush;

    // The consumer is this program run again, as Boost.Interprocess's own tests run theirs; the
    // parent waits for it, so its output comes before the parent's last line.
    const std::string command =
        "\"" + std::string(program) + "\" consumer " + run.segment + " " + run.queue;
    // NOLINTNEXTLINE(bugprone-command-processor,cert-env33-c)
    if (std::system(command.c_str()) != 0) {
        std::cout << "error: the consumer failed\n";
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "available after the consumer: " << pool.available() << '\n';
    return 0;
}

The consumer attaches to the segment, and for each offset it receives, adopt takes over the reference release gave up, opens the image in place, and checks its seal. The document is read where it is and dropped, which returns its block to the pool. One image of the example was damaged after it was sealed: adopt refuses it with errc::damaged_document, and the reference it was handed is still counted, so the consumer gives it back by offset with pool.drop(offset), which reads nothing of the image and returns the block:

// The consumer: it adopts each offset the producer sends, prints the document and drops it, so
// that its block returns to the pool; an offset the seal refuses is dropped by the pool, unread.
int consume(const char* segment, const char* queue_name) {
    const bip::shared_memory_object memory(bip::open_only, segment, bip::read_write);
    const bip::mapped_region mapped(memory, bip::read_write);
    const std::span<std::byte> bytes(static_cast<std::byte*>(mapped.get_address()),
                                     mapped.get_size());
    const wd::result<wd::shared_pool> attached = wd::shared_pool::attach(bytes);
    if (attached.has_error()) {
        std::cout << "error: " << attached.error().message() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    const wd::shared_pool pool = *attached;
    bip::message_queue queue(bip::open_only, queue_name);

    for (;;) {
        std::uint64_t offset = 0;
        std::size_t received = 0;
        unsigned int priority = 0;
        queue.receive(&offset, sizeof offset, received, priority);
        if (offset == end_of_stream) {
            return 0;
        }

        wd::result<wd::shared_document<>> adopted = wd::shared_document<>::adopt(pool, offset);
        if (adopted.has_value()) {
            std::cout << adopted->get().stringify() << ": use count " << adopted->use_count()
                      << '\n';
        } else {
            std::cout << "refused: " << adopted.error().message() << '\n';
            // A refused reference stays counted until it is given back: the pool drops it by its
            // offset, without reading the image, and the block returns to the pool.
            if (const wd::result<void> dropped = pool.drop(offset); dropped.has_error()) {
                std::cout << "error: " << dropped.error().message() << '\n';
                return 1;
            }
        }
    }
}
available before the consumer: 4
{"name":"Ada","born":1815,"langs":["Analytical"]}: use count 1
{"name":"Grace","langs":["COBOL"]}: use count 1
{"name":"Alan","n":1500}: use count 1
refused: a sealed image whose bytes do not match its seal
available after the consumer: 8

Before the consumer ran, the pool had four free blocks of the eight, the four documents’ blocks being leased; after it, all eight are free. The reference count of each document read was one, the consumer’s.

A process that dies holding references leaves their blocks counted for good, as Boost.Interprocess’s own shared_ptr does; recovering them is the program’s. Images in shared memory are trusted input, as every image is (Sealed images): the processes that map a pool trust one another.

Compared with Boost.JSON

Boost.JSON is the JSON library of Boost, and document reads JSON with its parser. Its document, boost::json::value, is built for speed, and document is built to behave as JavaScript does and to move as bytes: the two make different choices, and this section puts them side by side. Each part of the program below runs the same JSON through both libraries and prints both outputs. The line of document is what JavaScript gives where the part says nothing else, and the line of Boost.JSON is what that library gives. It uses Boost.JSON by <boost/json.hpp>, beside document’s header:

#include <webcpp/document.hpp>

#include <boost/json.hpp>

#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <span>
#include <string>
#include <string_view>

namespace wd = webcpp::document;
namespace json = boost::json;
/** Prints the document's line of a section, under the label that names it. */
void print_document(std::string_view text) {
    std::cout << "  document:   " << text << '\n';
}

/** Prints the Boost.JSON line of a section, under the label that names it. */
void print_boost(std::string_view text) {
    std::cout << "  Boost.JSON: " << text << '\n';
}

/** The text Boost.JSON writes for `text` once parsed, or the error it reports without throwing. */
std::string boost_text(std::string_view text) {
    boost::system::error_code ec;
    const json::value v = json::parse(text, ec);
    return ec ? ec.message() : json::serialize(v);
}

Key order

boost::json::object keeps the keys in the order they came. JavaScript puts the keys that are array indices first, ascending, then the others in the order they were created, and document does the same (Key order):

constexpr std::string_view text = R"({"b":1,"2":2,"a":3,"1":4})";
wd::result<wd::document> made = wd::parse(text);
if (made.has_error()) {
    return false;
}
std::cout << "1. Key order\n";
print_document(made->stringify());
print_boost(boost_text(text));
1. Key order
  document:   {"1":4,"2":2,"b":1,"a":3}
  Boost.JSON: {"b":1,"2":2,"a":3,"1":4}

A key that is repeated keeps the last value, in the place of the first, as JavaScript does:

constexpr std::string_view text = R"({"b":1,"2":2,"b":3,"1":4})";
wd::result<wd::document> made = wd::parse(text);
if (made.has_error()) {
    return false;
}
std::cout << "6. Repeated keys\n";
print_document(made->stringify());
print_boost(boost_text(text));
6. Repeated keys
  document:   {"1":4,"2":2,"b":3}
  Boost.JSON: {"b":3,"2":2,"1":4}

Erasing keeps the order

boost::json::object::erase copies the last member into the gap, so d comes before b and c. JavaScript’s delete keeps the order of the others, and so does document’s erase:

constexpr std::string_view text = R"({"a":1,"b":2,"c":3,"d":4})";
wd::result<wd::document> made = wd::parse(text);
if (made.has_error() || !made->root().erase("a")) {
    return false;
}
std::cout << "2. Erase keeps the order of the other members\n";
print_document(made->stringify());

// Boost.JSON's erase copies the last member into the gap, so d comes before b and c.
boost::system::error_code ec;
json::value v = json::parse(text, ec);
json::object* object = v.if_object();
if (ec || object == nullptr) {
    return false;
}
object->erase("a");
print_boost(json::serialize(v));
2. Erase keeps the order of the other members
  document:   {"b":2,"c":3,"d":4}
  Boost.JSON: {"d":4,"b":2,"c":3}

Exact numbers

Boost.JSON stores a number as a double when it is not an integer, and writes it back as 1E-1. document keeps the digits that were sent, and writes them as JavaScript writes a number (Numbers):

constexpr std::string_view text =
    R"([0.1000000000000000000000000000000001,12345678901234567890123])";
wd::result<wd::document> made = wd::parse(text);
if (made.has_error()) {
    return false;
}
// The digits are the ones read; 23 of them are written in JavaScript's exponent form.
std::cout << "3. Exact numbers\n";
print_document(made->stringify());
print_boost(boost_text(text));
3. Exact numbers
  document:   [0.1000000000000000000000000000000001,1.2345678901234567890123e+22]
  Boost.JSON: [1E-1,1.2345678901234568E22]

Array methods

boost::json::array has insert and erase, which make the same edit as splice and unshift but return no removed values. document has the array methods of JavaScript (Arrays):

wd::result<wd::document> made = wd::parse("[1,2,3,4]");
if (made.has_error()) {
    return false;
}
wd::value a = made->root();
const wd::result<std::uint64_t> length = a.unshift(0);
// splice removes two elements from index 1, returns them, and inserts "x" in their place.
const wd::result<wd::document> removed = a.splice(1, 2, "x");
if (length.has_error() || removed.has_error()) {
    return false;
}
std::cout << "4. Array methods\n";
print_document("unshift(0) -> " + std::to_string(*length) + "; splice(1, 2, \"x\") removes " +
               removed->stringify() + "; a = " + a.stringify());

// Boost.JSON's array has insert and erase, which make the same edit but return no removed
// values.
json::array arr{1, 2, 3, 4};
arr.insert(arr.begin(), 0);
arr.erase(arr.begin() + 1, arr.begin() + 3);
arr.insert(arr.begin() + 1, json::value("x"));
print_boost(
    "no splice or unshift; insert and erase make the edit, without the removed "
    "values: a = " +
    json::serialize(arr));
4. Array methods
  document:   unshift(0) -> 5; splice(1, 2, "x") removes [1,2]; a = [0,"x",3,4]
  Boost.JSON: no splice or unshift; insert and erase make the edit, without the removed values: a = [0,"x",3,4]

An image copied and opened in place

A boost::json::value points into its memory resource, so its bytes cannot be copied to another buffer: the only way to move it is to serialize it and parse it again. document’s image is the document, and a copy of its bytes in a buffer of the program’s own, opened there, is the same document with no parse (Images):

constexpr std::string_view text = R"({"user":"Ada","langs":["Analytical","Note G"]})";
wd::result<wd::document> made = wd::parse(text);
if (made.has_error()) {
    return false;
}
const std::span<const std::byte> image = made->image();
// A buffer of the program's, 16-aligned, large enough for the image.
alignas(16) std::array<std::byte, 8192> buffer{};
if (image.size() > buffer.size()) {
    return false;
}
std::ranges::copy(image, buffer.begin());
// Opened in place: the buffer becomes the document, with no parse.
wd::result<wd::basic_document<wd::default_traits, wd::external>> opened =
    wd::open(std::span<std::byte>(buffer.data(), image.size()));
if (opened.has_error()) {
    return false;
}
std::cout << "5. An image copied to another buffer and opened in place\n";
print_document(opened->stringify());
// A Boost.JSON value points into its memory resource, so its bytes cannot be copied: the
// only way to move it is to serialize it and parse it again.
print_boost(boost_text(made->stringify()));
5. An image copied to another buffer and opened in place
  document:   {"user":"Ada","langs":["Analytical","Note G"]}
  Boost.JSON: {"user":"Ada","langs":["Analytical","Note G"]}

Errors are values

document’s operations return a result, neither a bad parse nor a bad write throws, and the core never throws at all. Boost.JSON’s parse reports through an error_code when it is given one, but its accessors, at and as_string among them, throw (Errors):

// The document's operations return result; neither a bad parse nor a bad write throws.
const wd::result<wd::document> broken = wd::parse("[1,");
wd::result<wd::document> number = wd::parse("5");
if (broken.has_value() || number.has_error()) {
    return false;
}
const wd::result<std::uint64_t> pushed = number->root().push(1);
std::cout << "7. Errors are values\n";
print_document("parse(\"[1,\") -> " + broken.error().message() + "; push on a number -> " +
               pushed.error().message());

// Boost.JSON's parse reports through error_code, but its value accessors (at, as_string)
// throw, so this section stays with the error_code overload.
boost::system::error_code ec;
static_cast<void>(json::parse("[1,", ec));
print_boost("parse(\"[1,\", ec) -> " + ec.message());
7. Errors are values
  document:   parse("[1,") -> malformed JSON text; push on a number -> a value of another kind
  Boost.JSON: parse("[1,", ec) -> incomplete JSON

What Boost.JSON does better

document is not a fast JSON tree. Boost.JSON parses faster, stringifies faster, finds a key faster (it hashes, where document walks an ordered tree) and splices an array faster, and its values are smaller than document’s images: a node of an image takes 192 bytes whatever it holds (Memory per value). The benchmarks measure each of these against Boost.JSON and against JavaScript (Benchmarks, and Reading the results for where document is slower and why). The reasons to choose document are the ones above, and the ones that no parser has: an image that is sent as it is, opened in place and shared between threads and processes, which Images on the wire and Sharing teach.

The sugar that throws

document has two layers. The core, every function this page has shown so far, never throws and exists in every build: each operation that can fail returns a result. The sugar reads as JavaScript reads, and throws as JavaScript throws, so it exists only in a build with exceptions:

Sugar Its core function

h = x

h.set(x)

h = other, doc["a"] = doc["b"]

h.set(other): a deep copy of the other handle’s value

h.as<T>()

h.get<T>()

h.as_string()

h.get<std::string_view>()

h.as_bool()

Each member is its core function, then, on failure, the exception of the core’s error: errc::syntax throws wd::syntax_error, which also holds the byte offset; errc::type throws wd::type_error, errc::range wd::range_error, errc::capacity wd::capacity_error, and errc::not_a_document and errc::incompatible_document wd::image_error. Each derives from wd::error, which derives from std::runtime_error and holds the code (Errors). A member that throws has changed nothing, since its core function completes or changes nothing.

wd::document doc = wd::parse_or_throw(R"({"n":1,"user":{"name":"Ada"}})");
doc["n"] = 2;                      // doc.n = 2
doc["user"]["nick"] = "Countess";  // creates the member
const auto n = doc["n"].as<std::int64_t>();
const std::string_view name = doc["user"]["name"].as_string();
std::cout << n << ' ' << name << '\n';

// Assignment writes at the handle's place, a deep copy, and never rebinds the handle.
wd::value place = doc["n"];
place = doc["user"]["name"];
show("doc.n", doc["n"]);
doc["user"]["nick"] = wd::undefined;  // erases the member
show("doc.user", doc["user"]);

try {
    doc["n"]["x"]["y"] = 1;  // a write through nothing
} catch (const wd::type_error& e) {
    std::cout << "TypeError: " << e.what() << '\n';
}
try {
    static_cast<void>(doc["user"].as<bool>());
} catch (const wd::type_error& e) {
    std::cout << "TypeError: " << e.what() << '\n';
}
try {
    static_cast<void>(wd::parse_or_throw("[1,]"));
} catch (const wd::syntax_error& e) {
    std::cout << "SyntaxError: " << e.what() << " at " << e.offset() << '\n';
}

const wd::document empty;  // holds null
wd::document twin = doc;   // an equal and independent copy
twin["n"] = 3;
std::cout << empty.stringify() << ' ' << doc.stringify() << ' ' << twin.stringify() << '\n';
2 Ada
doc.n -> "Ada"
doc.user -> {"name":"Ada"}
TypeError: a value of another kind
TypeError: a value of another kind
SyntaxError: malformed JSON text at 3
null {"n":"Ada","user":{"name":"Ada"}} {"n":3,"user":{"name":"Ada"}}

Its rules

  • Assignment writes; it never rebinds. h = x stores x at the place h names, and h still names that place afterward. h = other, with other a handle, stores a deep copy of the value other names, as doc["a"] = doc["b"] does: never an alias (Copies, never aliases).

  • = wd::undefined erases a member, as set(wd::undefined) does.

  • as_string() reads UTF-8 strings only: it returns a std::string_view, which a UTF-16 string cannot give. Under js_traits, a program uses as<std::u16string_view>() or as<std::string>().

  • wd::document d; holds null, and the copy constructor gives an equal and independent copy. Both are for owned documents only: an external document has no buffer to be made or copied into.

  • An external document throws wd::capacity_error when it is full, where set would return errc::capacity.

Without exceptions

In a build without exceptions, the sugar is not there: each member carries the constraint detail::exceptions_enabled, which no such build satisfies, so a call does not compile, and the compiler’s note names the constraint. For as<std::int32_t>(), Clang writes "no matching member function for call to 'as'", with the note "because 'int' does not satisfy 'exceptions_enabled'", and the test no_exceptions holds what it writes for each member (Testing). A generic program can ask whether the sugar is there:

/** Whether a handle of type `H` has the sugar `as<T>()`, which throws. */
template <class H>
concept has_as = requires(const H& h) { h.template as<std::int64_t>(); };

/** Whether a handle of type `H` can be assigned a value, `h = 1`, which throws on failure. */
template <class H>
concept assignable = requires(H h) { h = 1; };

static_assert(!has_as<wd::const_value>, "as<T>() needs exceptions");
static_assert(!assignable<wd::value>, "h = x needs exceptions");
static_assert(!std::is_default_constructible_v<wd::document>, "wd::document d; needs exceptions");
static_assert(!std::is_copy_constructible_v<wd::document>, "copying a document needs exceptions");

The core is the same in both builds, and an example of it is in Errors. A build has no exceptions when webcpp has none, or when the program defines WEBCPP_DOCUMENT_NO_EXCEPTIONS for document alone (Without exceptions).

Errors

Every operation of the core that can fail returns a wd::result<T>, Boost.System’s result: the value, or a boost::system::error_code. document’s own codes are the enumerators of wd::errc, of the category webcpp.document, whose values are fixed and never reused, so that a stored code keeps its meaning across versions. The error a sink or a selector’s callback returns is passed on unchanged, in its own category.

errc When JavaScript Exception, with exceptions only

syntax, 1

malformed JSON text, with Boost.JSON’s code as the parser’s cause() and the byte offset as its offset(); text after a finished parse

SyntaxError

wd::syntax_error, with offset()

type, 2

a value of another kind; a write through nothing; text invalid in the encoding; a malformed selector; a method of arrays on anything but an array

TypeError

wd::type_error

range, 3

a number that does not fit or is not exact; a date out of JavaScript’s range

RangeError

wd::range_error

capacity, 4

no room: a full external buffer, an owned document at its max_bytes, a parser’s limit

none; RangeError from the module

wd::capacity_error

not_a_document, 5

bytes that are not an image

none; TypeError from the module

wd::image_error

incompatible_document, 6

an image of another format version, reserved bytes, layout, byte order or traits

none; TypeError from the module

wd::image_error

damaged_document, 7

a sealed image whose bytes do not match its seal: changed, torn or cut short (Sealed images)

none; TypeError from the module

wd::image_error

The JavaScript column is the error JavaScript itself throws for the same fault; the module of Errors throws a SyntaxError, a RangeError or a TypeError for every code.

An errc converts to an error_code and compares with one, r.error() == wd::errc::type, and wd::error_category() is the category. The program below is built without exceptions, which example/Jamfile asks for it whatever the build asks, and makes each error once:

/** Prints what failed, its code's value and category, and its message. */
void print(std::string_view what, boost::system::error_code e) {
    std::cout << what << ": " << e.category().name() << ':' << e.value() << ", " << e.message()
              << '\n';
}
// errc::syntax: malformed text, and the parser's offset where it was found.
wd::parser p;
const wd::result<void> written = p.write("[1,]");
print("[1,]", written.error());
std::cout << "  at byte " << p.offset() << ", Boost.JSON's cause: " << p.cause().message()
          << '\n';

wd::result<wd::document> made = wd::parse(R"({"n":300})");
if (made.has_error()) {
    return 1;
}
wd::document& doc = *made;
// errc::type: a write through nothing, or a read of another kind.
print("doc.n.x.y = 1", doc["n"]["x"]["y"].set(1).error());
print("doc.n as a string", doc["n"].get<std::string>().error());
// errc::range: a number that does not fit, or a date out of JavaScript's range.
print("doc.n as int8_t", doc["n"].get<std::int8_t>().error());
// errc::capacity: a limit, here of depth.
wd::parse_options shallow;
shallow.max_depth = 1;
print("[[1]], max_depth 1", wd::parse("[[1]]", shallow).error());
// errc::not_a_document and errc::incompatible_document: bytes that are no image of these
// traits.
print("64 zero bytes", wd::from_image(std::array<std::byte, 64>{}).error());
print("another traits' image", wd::from_image<wd::js_traits>(doc.image()).error());
[1,]: webcpp.document:1, malformed JSON text
  at byte 3, Boost.JSON's cause: syntax error
doc.n.x.y = 1: webcpp.document:2, a value of another kind
doc.n as a string: webcpp.document:2, a value of another kind
doc.n as int8_t: webcpp.document:3, a number or index out of range
[[1]], max_depth 1: webcpp.document:4, no room left
64 zero bytes: webcpp.document:5, not a document's image
another traits' image: webcpp.document:6, an image of another format, layout, byte order or traits

An operation that fails changes nothing, so the program goes on with the document as it was:

// An error compares with an errc, and the document is as it was before the call that failed.
if (const wd::result<void> set = doc["n"]["x"].set(1); set.error() == wd::errc::type) {
    std::cout << "still " << doc.stringify() << '\n';
}
still {"n":300}

A failure of the process heap is not an error value. The image’s heap is never exhausted by surprise, since every operation finds its room first, but a few things live on the process heap: the text stringify returns, the key a handle of a missing member holds, and the parser’s frames. The standard library’s std::bad_alloc there is thrown with exceptions and ends the program without them, as it does for any C++ container.

Testing

A test of a program that uses document compares values: a document with ==, which compares structurally, or the text stringify writes, which is what JSON.stringify writes, byte for byte, so that an expected text can be measured with Node. Every failure is a value, which a test compares with an errc; nothing depends on a clock, a thread or global state; and the same operations give the same image, so that two runs, or two targets, can be compared byte for byte.

How document is tested

document’s tests are lightweight_test programs, one per subject, under test/, each declared in test/Jamfile with webcpp’s webcpp.run. The JavaScript facts they hold are Node 26’s:

Test What it checks

errors

The values of errc and kind, which are fixed, the category’s name and messages, and the conversion and the comparison with an error_code; built again with exceptions as errors_raise, the exception each errc raises.

number

Numbers read from JSON text exactly, at the edges of their text and of decimal128_t; written as JavaScript’s Number::toString writes them, row by row of Numbers; converted to and from every integer width and decimal type.

traits

Array-index keys; dates as Date.prototype.toJSON writes them; base64 against RFC 4648’s vectors; UTF-8 and UTF-16 validation and transcoding; the scalar and number codecs; the concept traits satisfy, and the tags that tell traits apart.

heap

The image’s heap: strings of exact size zeroed when freed, an allocator that hands out and frees zeros, probes that leave the heap as it was, regions owned and external, grown, copied and shrunk, the same bytes at any address, and the header’s check.

selector_grammar

The selectors’ grammar and matcher, apart from any parser: which texts parse into which steps, which are refused, and which paths each selector matches.

tree

The tree under each object policy, keys that look like array indices, elements renumbered, deep copies and literals, the header it keeps, and every operation, which completes or changes nothing, in buffers of every size and in owned images that grow.

literal

wd::object and wd::array before a document stores them: each form a value takes, nesting, members in the order written, and what a literal refuses at compile time.

convert

Every settable type stored by value, and every node read back as every readable type, with their type and range failures; text validated and transcoded; dates, bytes, and structural equality.

value

The handles: navigation that never fails, set that creates and replaces, numbers, strings, dates and bytes, value_or, erase and assign_from, deep copies, a handle kept while the image grows and moves, equality, iteration, a deep copy into external buffers of every size, a moved-from document and one that holds undefined.

order

The key order through the handles, with keys that look like array indices and one that holds a zero byte, under each object policy and both encodings, sorted keys by UTF-16 code units with either: assignment keeps a key’s place, and a key erased and created again takes a new key’s.

image

Images copied to another address and opened there, formatted, refused, the same for the same operations, no byte left of an erased secret, shrunk, a full external buffer, a buffer that is not 16-aligned, and a header whose container offset lies.

stringify

stringify and stringify_to against Node’s text: indentation, empty containers, escapes, numbers, dates, bytes under each policy, a lone surrogate under js_traits, an undefined root, every piece size from 1 to 64, a sink that fails or throws, and a document nested 100,000 levels deep.

parse

What parse accepts, written back as Node writes it, and what it refuses, with the offset; the limits of depth, bytes and image, exact; an object of 100,000 keys and a 64 MB string; the revivers; a parse into external buffers of every size. Built again with exceptions as parse_sugar, it checks parse_or_throw.

streaming

Every text of the corpus split at every byte, and written one byte at a time, gives the document a whole parse gives; a syntax error’s offset is the same however the text is split; a failed parser stays failed and a finished one takes no more text, nor a second text after its first; max_bytes counts every chunk; an external parser.

selector

Deliveries by on and observe, nested values first, scalars when their token ends, the root, a callback that fails or throws, a function as a callback, a callback that cannot write, a million elements under on within 64 KB of image, the same deliveries however the text is split, and paths that parse back as selectors.

stream

Streams of documents: each framing on its own rows, NDJSON’s rules one by one, indented records and bad ones in JSON text sequences, errors skipped with their lines or stopping the stream until a reset, the limits held per document, and every stream split at every byte and written one byte at a time giving what one write gives, through next() and through the push form alike.

stream_asio

Natively only: async_read_document over a loopback TCP connection, the writer sending NDJSON and concatenated JSON in odd-sized pieces, read with a callback and, with exceptions, in a coroutine with asio::use_awaitable; a skipped line reported with its line, eof at the end, and a completion that needs no read made after the call returns.

array

Each array method against Node’s results, with JavaScript’s index rules, on empty arrays and on anything but an array; a handle kept while pushes grow the image; and a splice into external buffers of every size, which completes or changes nothing.

sugar

Built with exceptions: assignment stores as set does and never rebinds, so std::swap of two handles writes through them, as, as_string and as_bool read as get does, a default-constructed document holds null, a copy is equal and independent, and each failure throws the exception of the core’s code and changes nothing.

no_exceptions

Built without exceptions, a test of the compiler’s diagnostics: each member of the sugar called once does not compile, and the note names exceptions_enabled (The sugar that throws).

oracle_cases

Node as the oracle, from C++: every case of the corpus parsed, changed by its operations through the core and written, under default_traits and js_traits, must give Node’s text and Node’s return values, byte for byte (Node as the oracle).

Each case is a function named after the rule it checks, such as handle_survives_growth, and main calls them all and returns boost::report_errors(). Every test is built and passes without exceptions too, but those that declare <exception-handling>on. Beside them, test/Jamfile compiles each public header alone, as the only include of its translation unit, so that a header that leans on an include it does not make fails, naming it. And example/Jamfile builds every program this page shows, runs it, and compares what it printed with the .expected beside it; a program that returns anything but 0 fails too.

Node as the oracle

test/oracle/ runs the same cases in Node and in C++. A case, test/fixtures/cases/<name>.json, is a JSON text, an indent, and a list of operations: set, erase, push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, reverse, the length set and Object.assign, each value written as JSON text, so that neither side reads a number through a double. oracle.mjs runs each case with JSON.parse, the operations in JavaScript and JSON.stringify, and writes what it gets to test/fixtures/expected/<name>.json, which is committed; the test oracle_cases runs each case through the document and must give those bytes. The cases written by hand follow the rules of this page, key order, numbers, arrays, strings, dates, bytes and indentation; the others are random documents and operations, which generate.mjs writes from a fixed seed. A case of numbers a double does not keep runs with js_traits alone; every other runs with both traits.

No case holds what the two sides do differently by design (Where document differs, on purpose): a lone surrogate, a number past a double’s range or past 34 digits, an operation JavaScript would throw on, or the key __proto__, which sets a prototype in JavaScript.

Without exceptions

That document works without exceptions is checked by the lint, which compiles every public header, and every test and example, which instantiate its templates, with exception-handling=off. <webcpp/document/config.hpp>, which every public header of document includes first, defines WEBCPP_DOCUMENT_NO_EXCEPTIONS when webcpp has no exceptions (WEBCPP_HAS_EXCEPTIONS is not defined: the compiler has none, or the program defined WEBCPP_NO_EXCEPTIONS), and a program may define it for document alone, as Boost.Asio’s BOOST_ASIO_NO_EXCEPTIONS does. The core never throws, so the macro removes only the sugar that throws and the exception types (The sugar that throws). The tests config, config_developer_defined and config_all_off check the three ways it is defined, and the lint refuses a throw in a public header: an exception goes through boost::throw_exception.

Targets

test/Jamfile and example/Jamfile declare the targets they are built for, webcpp.targets native emscripten wasip2 wasip3, and b2 builds each program for those alone. From the root of a webcpp checkout, each of these builds and runs:

b2 libs/document/test

The 63 tests natively: the lightweight_test programs, and each of the 28 public headers compiled alone. stream_asio, and asio.hpp compiled alone, are built natively only, as Boost.Asio is (With Boost.Asio).

b2 libs/document/example

The 20 examples, each built, run, and its output compared with the one beside it.

b2 libs/document/test libs/document/example toolset=emscripten

The same on emscripten: 65 tests and 13 examples, each run by node, b2’s toolset itself, except the 6 driven programs, the tests of the JavaScript API and the example of Fed from JavaScript, which the own lane js runs.

b2 libs/document/test/js//js toolset=emscripten

The own lane js (Using it from JavaScript): Node’s test runner on the module and on the module of shared documents, the npm package as a user receives it, and the two examples in headless Chromium, and Node over the example that binds a stream parser (example/document_stream_js.cpp). Each test builds the module it checks, so the lint and the CI compile it.

b2 libs/document/test libs/document/example toolset=clang-wasip2 testing.launcher=wasmtime

The same for wasm32-wasip2: 59 tests and 14 examples, each run by wasmtime. toolset=clang-wasip3 does the same for wasm32-wasip3: 59 tests and 14 examples.

b2 libs/document/test/oracle//oracle

The oracle lane: Node runs every case, and what it writes must be what test/fixtures/expected holds. It needs Node, and no package.

b2 libs/document/test/oracle//update-expected

Not a check: it writes Node’s results again, over the committed ones, after a case is added or changed.

b2 compares timestamps, so a result that counts is built from scratch, with b2 -a. b2 libs/document/test//value builds and runs one test alone, while working on it.

The test matrix

The continuous integration runs document’s tests and examples in lanes, one toolset each: the native compilers, emscripten, wasip2 and wasip3. Each lane builds from scratch and records what b2 built and ran:

b2 -a --dump-tests --out-xml=<lane>.xml toolset=<toolset> libs/document/test libs/document/example

webcpp’s tools/report/report.py merges the files of every lane into a matrix, published with the documentation at https://webcpporg.github.io/report/.

Benchmarks

document does what JavaScript does, and does it in C++: this section measures what that costs. Each operation is timed three ways: with Boost.JSON, the C++ library whose parser document uses, with document itself, and with JavaScript’s own objects in V8, the engine whose behaviour document reproduces. The C++ runs natively, and compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten in the same Node.js and the same headless Chrome as the JavaScript, so that each row compares the three where a web application would run them.

The operations of the survey and the data come from recognised benchmarks, never from document’s own tests; the operations of binary transmission, which no suite times, come from the case document is built for, and are the first results below. Every implementation must give the same answer to each before it is timed. One C++ program, bench/bench.cpp, holds the Boost.JSON and document sides; one JavaScript module, bench/bench.mjs, holds JavaScript’s and the same harness, which Node runs and Chrome runs in a page; and bench/run.mjs runs them all, checks their answers and writes the results below.

The operations

The fourteen operations of the survey of JSON and dictionary benchmarks that this section follows, each with the suites it is taken from. No recognised JSON suite times changes to a document (insert, update, delete, splice) or deep copies: those come from the hash-map suites, V8’s own js-perf-test and Dromaeo’s DOM tests. Equality, the survey’s fifteenth, is left out, since no suite times it. Three more, 15 to 17, are binary transmission: a document sent to another place and opened there. No suite times them, so the page takes them from the case the image is built for.

A * marks the closest form of an operation an implementation has no direct form of, as the survey names it; the results’ tables carry the same mark. Rows 15 to 17 have no *: each implementation has its own form of sending a document, and a - marks one that has none. Every array method of document but slice is a loop by hand: document has the methods that change an array (push, pop, splice and the others) and slice and concat, not the callbacks of map or filter. A loop that builds an array copies each element it keeps into a new document, where JavaScript’s map, filter and slice share the elements they keep with the array they read.

The data

  • nativejson-benchmark’s three files (Milo Yip’s, MIT): canada.json, 2.2 MB of GeoJSON, mostly numbers; citm_catalog.json, 1.7 MB of wide objects; twitter.json, 0.6 MB of strings, many of them Japanese, and escapes. The repository is a submodule pinned at 478d572, third_party/libs/nativejson-benchmark, which /webcpp/third_party//nativejson-benchmark gives a program: the files are read where the checkout holds them, never copied.

  • For the arrays, the largest ring of the polygon of canada.json, an array of 14,310 points, each an array of two numbers, and the 100 statuses of twitter.json.

  • For the dictionaries, Tessil’s synthetic objects: 10, 1,000 and 100,000 members whose keys are 15 or 50 characters long, a letter then letters and digits, so that none is an array index, each member’s value its index. The keys come from Mulberry32 with a fixed seed per object, in C++ and in JavaScript alike, bit for bit; the lookups take them in a shuffled order, from a seed of their own; the misses are as many keys of the same length from another seed. Beside them, the widest object of citm_catalog.json, events, of 184 members, whose keys are nine-digit integers: array indices to JavaScript, which keeps such keys in ascending order, as document does and as the file lists them.

  • A pass of operation 9 deletes every other key of the lookups’ order, at most 1,000 of them, then looks every key up: Boost.JSON’s stable_erase moves every member after the one it erases, and deleting half of 100,000 members takes it 25 s a pass.

The image is the larger on the wire in every row. It holds a node of a tree for each value, with its ids and offsets, where the text holds the value’s characters alone, so it is 8 to 17 times the text’s size uncompressed; compressed it is still 3 to 9 times larger for canada.json and twitter.json, and for citm_catalog.json the gzip and brotli of the image are 36 and 24 times the text’s. The sizes come from bench/wire.mjs, which reads the files that bench-native --wire <dir> writes; the results target does not write them.

A seal is a CRC-32C of the image’s bytes, which catches accidental damage (a flipped bit, a torn write). It is not authentication: anyone can compute a valid seal for any bytes, so an image from an untrusted source must not be opened, sealed or not.

Methodology

The survey’s section 4, which gathers the practice of the suites above:

  • Loading is never timed: the files are read, and the documents an operation reads are parsed and built, before its first pass. An operation that changes its input, such as delete, gets fresh copies, made before a sample and outside its time.

  • The first pass of each operation is timed alone, before any warm-up: the first-iteration time, as JetStream reports it, which tells how the code runs before the JIT or the caches have seen it. Its answer is then checked against every other implementation’s: the Stat counts of nativejson-benchmark for a parse, a stringify read back, a traversal, a copy or a document sent and received (sealed or not, and in a Worker, the Worker’s statistics of what it received); the queries’ answers; the members found and the sums of their values; lengths and checksums for the arrays. A run whose implementations disagree writes no results.

  • The warm-up doubles the passes of a sample until it lasts at least 10 ms, then runs one more sample, which is discarded. The result is the median of 10 samples of at least 10 ms, divided by the passes and by the operations of a pass.

  • JavaScript runs with --expose-gc (in Chrome, --js-flags=--expose-gc), and gc() runs before each sample; its passes add their results to a checksum, which the run prints, and the C++ passes write theirs to a volatile object, so that no compiler drops the work.

  • Chrome loads its page from a server of the run, on 127.0.0.1, which makes it cross-origin isolated (COOP and COEP headers): its performance.now then reads 5 us rather than 100 us. Node and Chrome share V8’s major version, 14: Node 26 and the Chrome for Testing 147 headless shell that Playwright 1.59 installs, which bench/package-lock.json pins.

  • Each implementation runs in a process of its own, or in a page of its own. The C++ is b2’s release variant: -O3 natively, and -O3 for Emscripten too, at compilation and at link.

  • document runs under default_traits: exact decimal numbers and UTF-8 text. Parse and stringify also run under js_traits, binary doubles and UTF-16, which JavaScript’s own representation is, in rows of their own.

  • A C++ pass frees the result of the pass before it, so its time includes freeing it, as Boost.JSON’s own benchmark does; JavaScript’s garbage is collected when V8 chooses, and gc() runs between samples.
