Reading the results

The figures below are this machine’s medians natively unless a place is named; the tables hold the rest. document is not a fast JSON tree, and this first version does not try to be one: it pays, on every operation, for what it guarantees, JavaScript’s behaviour, exact numbers and one relocatable image. Where it is slower, and why:

  • Binary transmission, which the image is built for. A document sent as its image is copied and opened in place: the receiver parses no text, builds no tree and allocates nothing per value, so its CPU cost is the copy and, for a sealed image, one CRC pass over the bytes (about 600 MB/s). Boost.JSON and JavaScript pay the parse on the receiving side, which the image does not. That is where the image wins: on the receiver’s CPU, in a Worker, where the image crosses as a transferred ArrayBuffer (row 17) and not as a structured clone of every node, and in shared memory, which is not measured here. The rows’ timings are in the tables above. Over a constrained network the text wins: the image is 8 to 17 times larger, and still larger compressed, so on a link that carries the bytes the text is faster unless the receiver’s parse costs more than the extra bytes take to cross. On a LAN it depends on the rate. For canada.json the image is 30 MB more than the text, which the link saves only when it carries more than about 143 MB/s (1.1 Gbit/s) against document’s own parse of canada, 209 ms; Boost.JSON’s 2.19 ms parse is never worth it. The seal is a CRC against accidental damage, not authentication: anyone can compute a valid seal, so an image from an untrusted source must not be opened.

  • Building and walking the tree. document parses canada.json in 209 ms, where Boost.JSON takes 2.19 ms and Node’s JSON.parse 3.58 ms: 95 times Boost.JSON’s time, 22 times on citm_catalog.json and 15 times on twitter.json. A full traversal is slower still, 37.0 ms against 186 us on canada.json. Every value is a node of a Boost.MultiIndex container inside the image, linked into three red-black trees by offset pointers: by its id, by its parent and position, and by its parent and key. Appending a value finds its parent by id and links the node into each tree, and a handle names a node by its id, so that every access looks it up again. A profile of the native parse of canada.json (macOS’s sample) spends most of its time looking nodes up by id, inserting into and rebalancing the trees, and converting numbers to exact decimals; under js_traits, whose numbers are doubles, the same parse takes 175 ms, so the tree, not the decimals, is the larger cost. Boost.JSON appends to contiguous arrays and keeps doubles.

  • Stringify is 20 times Boost.JSON’s time on canada.json (33.9 ms against 1.70 ms) and 5 times on twitter.json: it walks the same trees, and writes each exact decimal as JavaScript would write the number; js_traits brings canada.json down to 20.5 ms.

  • Dictionaries. A lookup finds its key in an ordered tree, by comparisons, where Boost.JSON and V8 hash it: 42 ns at 10 members, 576 ns at 100,000, against 10 to 28 ns for Boost.JSON and 5 to 24 ns for JavaScript. Insertion (0.4 to 1.4 us), assignment and iteration (17 to 258 ns a member, against under 1 ns for Boost.JSON’s contiguous members) pay the same trees and the same lookups by id. JavaScript is slower than Boost.JSON on the events of citm_catalog.json (41 ns a lookup): its keys are array indices, which V8 keeps apart from named properties.

  • Arrays. A splice in the middle of 14,310 points takes 666 us, against 2 or 3 us for Boost.JSON and JavaScript: every element after the splice is renumbered in the position tree. A push and a pop take 789 ns each, because pop returns the removed value as a document of its own, whose image it allocates; set_length would drop it without one. map and filter copy each element they keep into a new document, about 1 us an element, where JavaScript’s share them, as its slice does.

  • Where document is faster: a deep copy is one copy of the image, 441 us for canada.json, against 1.12 ms for Boost.JSON’s copy constructor and 5.43 ms for structuredClone in Node. And deleting from a large object keeps the order without moving the members: 709 ns a deletion from 100,000 members, where Boost.JSON’s stable_erase takes 644 us.

Across places: the C++ compiled to WebAssembly takes a median 1.26 times its native time, for Boost.JSON and for document alike, at most 2.7 times (Boost.JSON’s stringify of canada.json, whose doubles it formats more slowly in wasm32), and Node and Chrome run the same module within a quarter of each other, their V8 sharing a major version. Boost.JSON’s splice is even faster in WebAssembly (855 ns) than natively (1.82 us): its values are 16 bytes in wasm32, 24 natively, and a splice moves them. JavaScript’s first iteration is often several times its median, the time V8 takes to compile it, where the C++'s first pass runs close to its median. Chrome’s clock reads 5 us, so the first iteration of a pass shorter than that, such as ten lookups, reads in Chrome as 0 or 5 us divided by its operations.

These costs are the design’s, measured before any tuning, and the profile names where to begin: the lookup of a node by id behind every handle, the renumbering of positions on a splice, and the image that pop allocates.

Running them

b2 libs/document/bench//results
b2 libs/document/bench//smoke toolset=clang-wasip2 testing.launcher=wasmtime

The first measures on the machine it runs on, which took 9 minutes here, and writes doc/benchmark-results.adoc; it is explicit, so that neither a default build nor the continuous integration runs it. Node, npm and Emscripten’s toolset are needed beside the native one: npm installs Playwright, and Playwright its headless shell, once. The second is one verifying pass of every operation, on any target, which fails when Boost.JSON and document answer differently; the library’s tests run it on every target as bench, without the objects of 100,000 members, which run the same code as those of 1,000 and would take most of its time in a debug build.

Reference

Every name document declares, in the namespace webcpp::document, from the Doc Comments of its headers: each class, function, type and enumerator with its declaration, what it does, what it asks of its caller and how it fails. The other sections teach the library; this one is where a name is looked up.

Macros

Name Description

WEBCPP_DOCUMENT_NO_DANGLING

Marks a class that names a place in a document and owns what it needs to find it again, a handle or a range of a container’s children; empty outside GCC 14 and later, whose -Wdangling-reference it quiets.

WEBCPP_DOCUMENT_NO_EXCEPTIONS

Defined when document is built without exceptions: when webcpp has none (the compiler has none, or the developer defined WEBCPP_NO_EXCEPTIONS for every webcpp library), or when the developer defines it alone.

webcpp::document

Types

Name Description

array

An array, as JavaScript writes [...]: wd::array{1, "x", nullptr}.

base64

The bytes policy that writes bytes as base64, RFC 4648 with padding, the default.

base64url

The bytes policy that writes bytes as base64url, RFC 4648 section 5, without padding.

basic_array_ref

An array as a vector-like container: front, back, operator[], at, push_back, emplace_back, pop_back, insert, erase, resize, clear and iteration both ways.

basic_const_value

A read-only handle: one place in one document, cheap to copy, which reads what is there now.

basic_document

A JSON document: one value, in one relocatable image.

basic_image_reader

Reads a stream of images, one after another with nothing between them, into the blocks of an image_pool, and opens each in place as a leased_document.

basic_object_by_key

The members of an object in lexicographic key order, by UTF-16 code units whatever the encoding, with find, lower_bound, upper_bound and equal_range: prefix and range queries over keys.

basic_object_ref

An object as a sorted-map-like container, in the traits’ key order (JavaScript’s by default): find, insert, insert_or_assign, try_emplace, erase, iteration both ways, and by_key() for prefix and range queries in lexicographic key order.

basic_parser

The streaming parser: write takes the text in chunks, finish returns the document.

basic_stream_parser

The parser of a stream of documents: write takes the bytes in chunks of any size, down to one byte, and each document is delivered as soon as the bytes that end it are consumed.

basic_value

A handle that reads and writes: one place in one document, as basic_const_value, with JavaScript’s assignment, delete, Object.assign and the array methods.

capacity_error

No room left: a full external buffer, a document at its limit, a parser’s limit.

decimal_digits

A finite decimal number as JavaScript’s Number::toString sees it: its value is 0.d1 d2 ... dk times ten to the power point, with k the count of its significant digits.

default_traits

The default traits: exact numbers, UTF-8 strings, base64 bytes and JavaScript’s key order.

dense

The array policy: no holes, and writing past the end fills with null.

error

What every exception of document derives from: a std::runtime_error holding its code.

external

The storage of a document whose image is a buffer its user owns, such as a browser’s memory: when it is full, an operation returns errc::capacity and changes nothing.

image_error

Bytes that are not a document’s image, an image of another format, or a damaged one.

image_header

The 64 bytes at the start of every image, in the byte order of the machine that wrote it.

image_pool

Fixed blocks for images, 16-aligned and zeroed, allocated once: block_bytes times blocks.

insertion_order

The object policy that keeps every key in the order it was created, whatever the key.

javascript_bytes

The bytes policy that writes bytes as JSON.stringify writes a Uint8Array: {"0":1,"1":2}.

javascript_order

The object policy of JavaScript: array-index keys ascending, then the others as created.

js_traits

The traits of JavaScript itself: doubles, UTF-16 strings, and bytes written as a Uint8Array.

leased_document

A document opened in place in a block of an image_pool, holding the block’s lease: when the document goes, the block goes back to the pool, its bytes zeroed.

literal

One value of a literal, converted implicitly from the C++ value it is written as.

null_t

The type of null, JavaScript’s null.

number_codec

How the traits’ number type is read from JSON text, written as JavaScript writes it, and converted; the primary template has none.

number_text

Text of at most 64 characters, held by value, so that writing a number or a date allocates nothing.

object

An object, as JavaScript writes {...}: wd::object{{"city", "Recife"}, {"zip", "50000"}}.

object_member

One member of an object literal: its key, in UTF-8, and its value.

owned

The storage of a document that owns its image: a buffer of its own, 16-aligned, which grows, twice the size each time, up to its max_bytes.

parse_options

The limits and the revivers of a parse.

path_view

The path in the text of a value a selector delivers: each step a member’s key or an element’s index in the text, which on does not renumber.

pool_block

A lease of one block of an image_pool; the block is its holder’s until the lease is destroyed or assigned, and then goes back to the pool, its bytes zeroed.

range_error

JavaScript’s RangeError: a number that does not fit, or an index out of range.

scalar_codec

How a scalar type is stored in a node: its name in the image’s layout tag, its size, and its bytes, written the same on every target.

shared_document

A document in a block of a shared_pool, holding one reference to it, as std::shared_ptr holds its object: copying adds a reference, destroying drops one, and the last reference zeroes the block and gives it back to the pool.

shared_pool

A pool of blocks for shared documents, over a region of memory the program gives: the process heap, or a region of shared memory that several processes map, each at an address of its own.

sorted

The object policy that orders keys by their UTF-16 code units, with either encoding, as JavaScript’s sort() and RFC 8785 do, for canonical JSON.

stream_options

The options of a stream: the limits and the revivers of each of its documents, its framing and its policy on errors.

syntax_error

JavaScript’s SyntaxError: malformed JSON text, at a byte offset.

type_error

JavaScript’s TypeError: a value of another kind, or a write through nothing.

undefined_t

The type of undefined, JavaScript’s undefined, which set takes to erase a member.

utf16

The encoding of strings and keys that stores UTF-16 code units, as JavaScript holds strings.

utf8

The encoding of strings and keys that stores UTF-8, the default.

webcpp::document::basic_array_ref

An array as a vector-like container: front, back, operator[], at, push_back, emplace_back, pop_back, insert, erase, resize, clear and iteration both ways.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/containers.hpp>

template<class Handle>
class basic_array_ref;

Description

Made by as_array() on a handle, it holds the document’s address and the array’s id, and is cheap to copy: a reference, like std::span, whose constness is its own, so a const view still writes; const_array_ref is the view that only reads. It is a std::ranges::bidirectional_range, a view and a borrowed range. The tree finds an element by its index in O(log n), so operator[] costs O(log n), not O(1), and the iterators are bidirectional, not random access, whose O(1) jumps they could not keep.

Iterators and handles hold ids, which no change reuses:

| Change | Iterators and handles | A std::string_view read from a value | | --- | --- | --- | | An element inserted, and any growth of the image | all follow their elements | invalid | | An element erased | those to it and its subtree; the others follow their elements | invalid | | An element’s value replaced | those to its old subtree | invalid | | The document moved from or destroyed | all | invalid |

What can fail returns result: an insertion, which needs room in the image, and at. An erasure needs no room and cannot fail. There are no throwing forms: they would differ from these only in their return type, which C++ does not overload on.

webcpp::document::basic_const_value

A read-only handle: one place in one document, cheap to copy, which reads what is there now.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/value.hpp>

template<
    class Traits = default_traits,
    class Storage = owned>
class basic_const_value;

Description

A handle names a node, a missing member or element of a container that exists (it reads undefined, and basic_value::set creates it), or nothing (it reads undefined, and set fails with errc::type). It holds the document’s address and node ids, so it stays valid when the document grows and its image moves; it reads undefined once its node is erased, and is invalid once its document is moved from or destroyed.

webcpp::document::basic_document

A JSON document: one value, in one relocatable image.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/document.hpp>

template<
    class Traits = default_traits,
    class Storage = owned>
class basic_document;

Description

The image is a 64-byte header and a heap that holds the tree, every pointer in it an offset, so that it works at any 16-aligned address and has the same bytes on 64-bit native and wasm32. A document is moved cheaply; moving it, or destroying it, invalidates its handles, as a container’s iterators would be. It is copied only with exceptions, or by clone.

webcpp::document::basic_document::compact

Rebuilds an owned image as the compact image of its content: the nodes in document order, ids numbered from the first, each block right after the last with no hole between, the image exactly as large as they are.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/document.hpp>

result<void>
compact() noexcept
requires std::same_as<Storage, owned>;

Description

Two documents of equal content, whatever edits made them, have byte-identical images after it, and a compact image compacts to itself. The copy is built before it replaces the image, so a failure changes nothing. As a vector’s reallocation does, it invalidates every handle, every std::string_view read from a value and every iterator, and, the bytes having changed, it clears a seal: sealing after it is the caller’s. The image’s size is compact_size afterwards, which is also its capacity, so the next change that needs room grows it.

Return Value

Success; errc::capacity when the new buffer cannot be allocated, and errc::type for a moved-from document.

See Also

"Images", in the guide.

webcpp::document::basic_document::seal

Seals the image: writes into its header the CRC-32C of its bytes, which open, from_image and the image reader then check, refusing an image whose bytes changed.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/document.hpp>

result<void>
seal() noexcept;

Description

The seal holds until the document’s next change, which clears it: the image is then simply not sealed, never wrongly sealed. It catches bytes changed inside an image (a flipped bit on a disk or a wire, a torn write, a stray write), not an old but valid image in reused memory, which carries a valid seal of its own. It costs a pass over the image, Boost.CRC’s table a byte at a time: measured natively at -O2 on one core of an Apple M5 Max, 1.7 ms per MiB (about 600 MB/s), and the check when an image is opened costs the same.

Return Value

Success; errc::type for a moved-from document, which has no image.

See Also

"Images", in the guide.

Declared in <webcpp/document/document.hpp>

shrink_to_fit() noexcept
requires std::same_as<Storage, owned>;

Description

Blocks never move, so the free blocks before the last one in use stay in the image: a document that grew and then let most of its values go may stay nearly as large. A deep copy into a new document, packed.root().set(doc), packs the content, and compact packs it in one order whatever the document’s history.

webcpp::document::basic_image_reader

Reads a stream of images, one after another with nothing between them, into the blocks of an image_pool, and opens each in place as a leased_document.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/image_stream.hpp>

template<class Traits = default_traits>
class basic_image_reader;

Description

Sans-IO: the bytes come from any source, copied by write, or read straight into the block by the source itself, through prepare and commit. The first 64 bytes of each image are checked as its header before a byte more is taken: its magic, format version, byte order, reserved bytes, the layout tag of Traits, and a size within a block. The rest of the image follows into the same block, and the image is opened there, a sealed one checked against its seal, and its heap checked. A refusal stops the reader with its error until reset, since the stream has lost its framing; the documents completed before it are still delivered.

The documents completed and not yet taken are queued in their own blocks, so the reader allocates nothing. When every block of the pool is leased, the reader takes no more bytes: that is the stream’s backpressure.

Note

Images are trusted input: this path is for peers the program trusts, and untrusted data enters as JSON text.

webcpp::document::basic_object_by_key

The members of an object in lexicographic key order, by UTF-16 code units whatever the encoding, with find, lower_bound, upper_bound and equal_range: prefix and range queries over keys.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/containers.hpp>

template<class Handle>
class basic_object_by_key;

Description

It reads the tree’s index by key, so each step and each bound costs O(log n). Under the sorted policy it is also the object’s own order. It is a std::ranges::bidirectional_range and a borrowed one, made by basic_object_ref::by_key; its iterators are invalidated as basic_object_ref’s are.

webcpp::document::basic_object_ref

An object as a sorted-map-like container, in the traits’ key order (JavaScript’s by default): find, insert, insert_or_assign, try_emplace, erase, iteration both ways, and by_key() for prefix and range queries in lexicographic key order.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/containers.hpp>

template<class Handle>
class basic_object_ref;

Description

Made by as_object() on a handle, it holds the document’s address and the object’s id, and is cheap to copy: a reference, like std::span, whose constness is its own, so a const view still writes; const_object_ref is the view that only reads. It is a std::ranges::bidirectional_range, a view and a borrowed range, so <algorithm> and <ranges> work on it, and an iterator outlives the view that made it. Its iterators are bidirectional, not random access: each step finds the next member in O(log n), so a jump of n costs n steps.

Iterators and handles hold ids, which no change reuses:

| Change | Iterators and handles | A std::string_view read from a value | | --- | --- | --- | | A member inserted, and any growth of the image | all stay valid | invalid | | A member erased | those to it and its subtree, which read undefined | invalid | | A member’s value replaced | those to its old subtree | invalid | | The document moved from or destroyed | all | invalid |

What can fail returns result: an insertion, which needs room in the image. A lookup returns an iterator, the end when nothing is found. There are no throwing forms: they would differ from these only in their return type, which C++ does not overload on.

webcpp::document::basic_parser

The streaming parser: write takes the text in chunks, finish returns the document.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/parser.hpp>

template<
    class Traits = default_traits,
    class Storage = owned>
class basic_parser;

Description

Boost.JSON’s basic_parser is fed each chunk, and its handler builds the document node by node, by ids, so that the document may grow and move between chunks. A failed write leaves the parser failed: every later call returns the same error, until reset. The parser raises nothing of its own, since its input is the network’s; an exception a callback throws propagates from write or finish, and leaves the parser failed: every later call throws it again, until reset.

webcpp::document::basic_stream_parser

The parser of a stream of documents: write takes the bytes in chunks of any size, down to one byte, and each document is delivered as soon as the bytes that end it are consumed.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/stream.hpp>

template<class Traits = default_traits>
class basic_stream_parser;

Description

It is sans-IO: it reads no socket or file, so it serves any source, a socket read by hand, an actor’s messages, or JavaScript through Emscripten; <webcpp/document/asio.hpp> reads it from Boost.Asio’s streams. Each document is parsed as parse parses one text, with the same key order, numbers and limits, into a new owned document. The parser reads one document at a time: at a document’s end it moves it to a queue that next takes from, or hands it to the callback of the push form, and begins the next on the bytes that follow, in the same chunk.

It raises nothing of its own, since its input is the network’s: every failure is returned. An exception the callback of the push form throws propagates; the bytes up to the document it was given are consumed, which offset counts, and the parser takes the rest by another write.

webcpp::document::basic_value

A handle that reads and writes: one place in one document, as basic_const_value, with JavaScript’s assignment, delete, Object.assign and the array methods.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/value.hpp>

template<
    class Traits = default_traits,
    class Storage = owned>
class basic_value
    : public basic_const_value<Traits, Storage>

Description

Every writing function returns result and either completes or changes nothing, a full heap included. Assignment to a handle writes to its place, with exceptions only: it never rebinds the handle.

So a handle is not a regular value, and must not be swapped or sorted: std::swap(x, y) assigns through both, leaving both places holding y’s value, and std::sort over handles writes the document’s values the same way.

Base Classes

Name Description

basic_const_value<Traits, Storage>

A read-only handle: one place in one document, cheap to copy, which reads what is there now.

The array as a vector-like container that reads and writes: push_back, insert, erase, resize, and iterators that <algorithm> and <ranges> take.

as_object

The object as a sorted-map-like container that reads and writes: find, insert, erase, bounds by key, and iterators that <algorithm> and <ranges> take.

Object.assign(v, source): sets each member of source here, in its order, as one operation.

at

Array.prototype.at: the element index, a negative index counting from the end.

Array.prototype.pop: removes the last element.

Array.prototype.push: appends each value.

reverse

Array.prototype.reverse: reverses the elements in place.

set

Stores a value at this place, v = x: a missing member is created, an element past the end fills the elements between with null, and an existing value is replaced.

a.length = n: truncates the array, or appends null up to n.

shift

Array.prototype.shift: removes the first element.

splice overloads

webcpp::document::basic_value::set

Stores a value at this place, v = x: a missing member is created, an element past the end fills the elements between with null, and an existing value is replaced.

requires detail::settable<Traits, T> || std::same_as<T, undefined_t>;

Description

Settable: bool; any integer type; the decimal types (finite, else errc::range); the traits’ number; std::string_view, const char*, std::string (valid UTF-8, else errc::type), std::u16string_view; std::span<const std::byte> (bytes); a date_ms (within JavaScript’s range, else errc::range); nullptr or null; the literals object and array; a handle or a document of the same traits, copied deeply; and undefined, which erases a member, stores null in an element and makes a root hold undefined. Numbers are stored by value.

webcpp::document::decimal_digits

A finite decimal number as JavaScript’s Number::toString sees it: its value is 0.d1 d2 ... dk times ten to the power point, with k the count of its significant digits.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/number.hpp>

struct decimal_digits;

Description

Zero has no digits: count is 0, point 0 and negative false. Any other value has between 1 and 34 digits, the first and the last of them not '0', so that every number has exactly one decimal_digits: 1.5, 1.50 and 15e-1 are all {false, "15", 2, 1}.

webcpp::document::image_pool

Fixed blocks for images, 16-aligned and zeroed, allocated once: block_bytes times blocks.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/image_stream.hpp>

class image_pool;

Description

A block is leased by acquire, or by a basic_image_reader for each image it reads, and goes back when its lease does. When every block is leased, the pool says errc::capacity, the backpressure of a stream of images, whose reader takes no more bytes until a block is given back. The pool must outlive its leases and its readers; moving it moves neither its blocks nor its leases.

Note

A pool is not thread-safe: a block is leased and given back, a lease destroyed included, on one thread at a time.

webcpp::document::leased_document

A document opened in place in a block of an image_pool, holding the block’s lease: when the document goes, the block goes back to the pool, its bytes zeroed.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/image_stream.hpp>

template<class Traits = default_traits>
class leased_document;

Description

The document is external: it reads and writes as any document does, within its image, and a change that needs more room than the image has returns errc::capacity. A leased document is moved, never copied; moving it invalidates its handles, and a moved-from one holds no document.

webcpp::document::literal

One value of a literal, converted implicitly from the C++ value it is written as.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/literal.hpp>

class literal;

Description

It holds bool, any integer (character types aside), the decimal types, a binary64 floating-point value (stored only by traits whose number is binary, such as js_traits), text in UTF-8 or UTF-16, a date_ms, bytes, nullptr or null, and an object or an array. Text and bytes are copied, so a literal owns what it holds.

Member Functions

Name Description

literal [constructor]

Constructors

visit

Calls f with the value this literal holds, as one of: null_t, bool, std::int64_t, std::uint64_t, const decimal_digits& (a finite decimal), detail::non_finite_decimal, detail::binary64, std::string_view, std::u16string_view, date_ms, std::span<const std::byte>, const object& or const array&.

webcpp::document::parse_options::max_depth

The deepest nesting of arrays and objects; one deeper is errc::capacity.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/parse.hpp>

uint64_t max_depth = 256;

webcpp::document::parse_options::max_document_bytes

The largest image an owned document grows to, 64 MiB; past it is errc::capacity.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/parse.hpp>

uint64_t max_document_bytes = std::uint64_t{64} << 20U;

Description

Each value takes at least 192 bytes of image, so a short value’s image is a hundred times its text or more: 2 MB of [0,0,...] makes an image of 268 MB. The default is low so that text from the network is refused early: under 1 GiB, 11 MB of such text cost 9 seconds and 2.2 GB of memory before it failed; under 64 MiB, 700 KB fails in 0.4 seconds with 137 MB. A program that parses larger documents raises it.

webcpp::document::shared_document

A document in a block of a shared_pool, holding one reference to it, as std::shared_ptr holds its object: copying adds a reference, destroying drops one, and the last reference zeroes the block and gives it back to the pool.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/shared.hpp>

template<class Traits = default_traits>
class shared_document;

Description

Every holder reads and writes the same image, in place: a write through one is every holder’s. Whether several holders may write at once is the program’s decision, and so is the synchronisation of writers, with each other and with readers, which the library does not do. A holder that wants a document of its own to change calls make_mutable, which copies the image into a new block when others hold it (copy on write). The references themselves are thread-safe: copies made and dropped on any number of threads and processes at once, as std::shared_ptr’s are. A reference passes to another process as its image’s offset in the region: release gives it up without dropping it, and adopt takes it over.

The document is external: a change that needs more room than its block has returns errc::capacity. A shared document allocates nothing; moving it invalidates its handles.

webcpp::document::shared_pool

A pool of blocks for shared documents, over a region of memory the program gives: the process heap, or a region of shared memory that several processes map, each at an address of its own.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/shared.hpp>

class shared_pool;

Description

The region holds a 64-byte header, then the blocks, each a 64-byte header, which counts the references to its document, and the room of one image. A shared_pool is a view of the region, copied freely: the pool is the region’s, and every view of it, in any process, is the same pool. Leasing a block and giving one back are lock-free and safe from any number of threads and processes at once; nothing is allocated, and a free block is all zero.

Note

A process that dies holding references leaves their blocks counted for good, as Boost.Interprocess’s shared_ptr does; recovering them is the program’s.

Synopsis

Description

The values start at 1, so an error_code of value 0 is no error. An errc converts to an error_code and compares with one: made.error() == wd::errc::syntax.

The values are fixed: they are never reused for a different meaning, so a stored value keeps its meaning across versions.

webcpp::document::async_read_document

Reads the next document of a stream: from the parser when it holds one, else from the stream, reading only while the parser has none ready.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/asio.hpp>

template<
    class AsyncReadStream,
    class DynamicBuffer,
    class Traits,
    boost::asio::completion_token_for<void(boost::system::error_code, basic_document<Traits>)> CompletionToken = boost::asio::default_completion_token_t<AsyncReadStream::executor_type>>
requires (boost::asio::is_dynamic_buffer_v1<DynamicBuffer>::value &&
             !boost::asio::is_dynamic_buffer_v2<DynamicBuffer>::value)
auto
async_read_document(
    AsyncReadStream& stream,
    DynamicBuffer& buffer,
    basic_stream_parser<Traits>& parser,
    CompletionToken&& token = boost::asio::default_completion_token_t<typename AsyncReadStream::executor_type>());

Description

It is a composed operation of Boost.Asio, which takes any completion token: a callback, asio::use_awaitable, asio::deferred, boost::cobalt::use_op. Its signature is void(boost::system::error_code, basic_document<Traits>), and it completes with the next document; with the error of a document dropped, under on_error::skip, after which the next call goes on with the stream; with the error that stopped the stream, under on_error::stop, every time; with asio::error::eof once the stream ended and the parser’s finish delivered what it held; or with the error of a read. On an error the document is empty. A completion is never called inside this function: one that needs no read is dispatched to the handler’s immediate executor, else posted to the stream’s.

The buffer is a dynamic buffer of either of Boost.Asio’s models, and the bytes it already holds, left by an earlier read of the same stream, are the parser’s before any read. A buffer of the first model, DynamicBuffer_v1 (asio::streambuf, Beast’s multi_buffer, whatever the pieces of its data), is taken by reference and used through it: the caller keeps it alive until the operation completes. A buffer of the second model, DynamicBuffer_v2 (grow, shrink, data(pos, n): what asio::dynamic_buffer makes of a string, or a vector, also when BOOST_ASIO_NO_DYNAMIC_BUFFER_V1 leaves out the first model) is taken by value, as Boost.Asio’s own reads take it, and the operation keeps its copy: the caller keeps alive the storage it names, the string, and the function never needs the original. A buffer of both models is a buffer of the second, as in Boost.Asio. One operation at a time reads a stream, its buffer and its parser, which outlive it.

Return Value

What the token makes of the operation.

Template Parameters

Name Description

AsyncReadStream

A stream of Boost.Asio’s AsyncReadStream: a socket, a pipe.

DynamicBuffer

A dynamic buffer of Boost.Asio’s first model, DynamicBuffer_v1, and not of the second.

Traits

The traits of the documents.

CompletionToken

The completion token.

Parameters

Name Description

The stream.

buffer

The buffer each read fills; the parser consumes what it holds before each read.

webcpp::document::async_read_image

Reads the next image of a stream into a block of a pool and opens it there, with no copy and no allocation.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/asio.hpp>

template<
    class AsyncReadStream,
    class Traits = default_traits,
    boost::asio::completion_token_for<void(boost::system::error_code, leased_document<Traits>)> CompletionToken = boost::asio::default_completion_token_t<AsyncReadStream::executor_type>>
auto
async_read_image(
    AsyncReadStream& stream,
    image_pool& pool,
    CompletionToken&& token = boost::asio::default_completion_token_t<typename AsyncReadStream::executor_type>());

Description

The image’s header is read into the block and checked before the rest of the image follows into the same block, which then holds the document. It reads exactly the bytes the reader asks for, so the stream is left at the end of the image it completed.

It is a composed operation of Boost.Asio, which takes any completion token. Its signature is void(boost::system::error_code, leased_document<Traits>): on success the document, which gives its block back when it goes; on error the empty lease (leased_document::empty), with the error: errc::capacity when every block of the pool is leased, in which case the stream is not read, errc::not_a_document or errc::damaged_document for an image the reader refuses, or the error of a read. The end of the stream is asio::error::eof, and it too is reported as errc::capacity when every block is leased: the reader needs a block to learn that the stream ended, so a pool that is full hides the end until a block is given back.

Images are trusted input: this path is for peers the program trusts.

Return Value

What the token makes of the operation.

Template Parameters

Name Description

AsyncReadStream

A stream of Boost.Asio’s AsyncReadStream: a socket, a pipe.

Traits

The traits of the images.

CompletionToken

The completion token.

Parameters

Name Description

stream

The stream.

pool

The pool whose blocks the image is read into; it outlives the operation and the document.

token

The completion token.

Writes a document’s image to a stream as one buffer, after sealing the document.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/asio.hpp>

template<
    class AsyncWriteStream,
    class Traits,

    AsyncWriteStream& stream,
    basic_document<Traits, Storage>& document,
    CompletionToken&& token = boost::asio::default_completion_token_t<typename AsyncWriteStream::executor_type>());

Description

The image carries a checksum of its bytes, which the reader checks, so a byte changed on the way is refused with errc::damaged_document. The document is changed by the seal, which is why it is taken by non-const reference.

It is a composed operation of Boost.Asio, which takes any completion token. Its signature is void(boost::system::error_code): the error of the seal, which writes nothing, or of the write. The caller keeps the document alive until the operation completes: the write reads its image.

webcpp::document::async_write_images

Writes the images of a range of documents to a stream in one gather write, after sealing every document of the range.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/asio.hpp>

template<
    class AsyncWriteStream,
    /* implementation-defined */ Range,
    boost::asio::completion_token_for<void(boost::system::error_code, std::size_t)> CompletionToken = boost::asio::default_completion_token_t<AsyncWriteStream::executor_type>>
auto
async_write_images(
    AsyncWriteStream& stream,
    Range& documents,
    CompletionToken&& token = boost::asio::default_completion_token_t<typename AsyncWriteStream::executor_type>());

Description

The seals come first: the first document that fails to seal completes the operation with its error, having written nothing. Otherwise the images are written as one gather write, which Boost.Asio sends with writev and continues over partial writes, with no copy of their bytes. The bytes are read in place, so the documents must not change until the operation completes.

It is a composed operation of Boost.Asio, which takes any completion token. Its signature is void(boost::system::error_code, std::size_t): the bytes written, the sum of the images’ sizes on success. On an error it is the bytes that reached the stream, which may end inside an image: the whole documents sent are the leading ones whose image sizes, added in order, do not exceed it. An empty range completes with 0 and writes nothing.

Return Value

What the token makes of the operation.

CompletionToken

The completion token.

Parameters

The range, read by this call only: the operation seals its documents, and the caller keeps them alive until it completes. A temporary range is refused.

webcpp::document::check_image

Checks that bytes are an image this build reads, reading nothing past the header before its size is known, and that a sealed image’s bytes match its seal.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/image.hpp>

result<void>
check_image(
    std::span<std::byte const> bytes,
    uint32_t layout,
    verify check = verify::seal) noexcept;

Description

A seal is checked first, before anything else its header states is trusted, so that a change anywhere in a sealed image, its magic and its size included, is reported as damage. Then the magic, the format version and the byte order, before the size, which an image of another version or byte order states in another way; then the reserved bytes and the layout.

Return Value

Success; errc::not_a_document for bytes shorter than the header or than the size it states, a size below 64, or another magic; errc::incompatible_document for another format version, byte order, nonzero reserved bytes or layout; errc::damaged_document for a sealed image whose bytes do not match its seal, or are fewer than its size, and for a seal that is neither zero nor marked.

Parameters

Name Description

bytes

The bytes, at any address.

layout

The layout tag this build expects.

check

Whether a sealed image’s bytes are checked against its seal.

webcpp::document::parse

JSON.parse(text): reads JSON text into a new owned document.

Declared in <webcpp/document/parse.hpp>

template<class Traits = default_traits>
result<basic_document<Traits, owned>>
parse(
    std::string_view text,
    parse_options const& o = {}) noexcept;

Description

It accepts what RFC 8259 and JSON.parse accept: no comments, no trailing commas, whitespace of space, tab, line feed and carriage return only. A key written twice keeps the last value in the first one’s place, as JavaScript does. A lone surrogate, "\ud800", is refused with either encoding, since Boost.JSON’s parser, which document uses, cannot deliver one.

The document; errc::syntax for malformed text, errc::range for a number the traits’ number refuses, errc::capacity past a limit.

webcpp::document::scan_number

Reads a JSON number’s text exactly, never through a double.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/number.hpp>

result<decimal_digits>
scan_number(std::string_view json_number) noexcept;

Description

The text follows JSON’s grammar, -? (0 | [1-9][0-9]*) (. [0-9]+)? ([eE][+-]? [0-9]+)?. Leading zeros and trailing zeros are dropped, so that 1.50, 1.5 and 15e-1 read the same.

Return Value

Its digits; errc::syntax for text outside the grammar, errc::range for a 35th significant digit, or for a number other than zero whose exponent or point leaves std::int32_t. Zero is zero whatever its exponent: 0e2147483648 reads as 0.

Parameters

Name Description

json_number

The number’s text, as a JSON parser delivers it.

webcpp::document::document_traits

What a document’s traits must give: the scalar types, each a stored_scalar, a number_codec for number, and one of the encodings and policies.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/traits.hpp>

template<class T>
concept document_traits = std::same_as<typename T::boolean, bool> && std::same_as<typename T::integer, std::int64_t> &&
    std::same_as<typename T::date, date_ms> && stored_scalar<typename T::number> &&
    requires { number_codec<typename T::number>::stores_non_finite; } &&
    (std::same_as<typename T::string, utf8> || std::same_as<typename T::string, utf16>) &&
    (std::same_as<typename T::bytes, base64> || std::same_as<typename T::bytes, base64url> ||
     std::same_as<typename T::bytes, javascript_bytes>) &&
    (std::same_as<typename T::object, javascript_order> ||
     std::same_as<typename T::object, insertion_order> ||
     std::same_as<typename T::object, sorted>) &&
    std::same_as<typename T::array, dense>;

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/config.hpp>

#define WEBCPP_DOCUMENT_NO_DANGLING

WEBCPP_DOCUMENT_NO_EXCEPTIONS

Defined when document is built without exceptions: when webcpp has none (the compiler has none, or the developer defined WEBCPP_NO_EXCEPTIONS for every webcpp library), or when the developer defines it alone.

Synopsis

Declared in <webcpp/document/config.hpp>

#define WEBCPP_DOCUMENT_NO_EXCEPTIONS

Description

document’s core never throws, so the macro changes none of it. It removes the members that throw (value::operator=, as, as_string, as_bool, parse_or_throw) and the exception types: a call to one of those members does not compile, and the compiler names detail::exceptions_enabled.

See Also

"Testing", in the guide.

Appendix A: Changelog

What changed in document in each version of webcpp, newest first, one line per change. "Unreleased" is what the next version brings. The release notes of every version are on webcpp’s index page.

Unreleased

webcpp 0.1.0

  • Added the library: a JSON document that behaves as JavaScript does.

  • Added traits that choose the stored types, and JavaScript’s key order.

  • Added handles, array methods and JavaScript-style sugar that throws, compiled only with exceptions.

  • Added object and array views that the standard algorithms read, with key-ordered queries.

  • Added stringify, parse, and selectors that stream in bounded memory.

  • Added streams of documents: NDJSON, JSON text sequences, concatenated JSON, Asio, Cobalt and xactor.

  • Added one relocatable binary image per document, with reserve, shrink_to_fit and compact.

  • Added sealed images, and Asio readers and writers that open them in place in pools of blocks.

  • Added shared documents, reference counted over shared memory, with copy on write.

  • Added a JavaScript module: exact decimals, key ranges, images, streams and Workers.
